en: Preface to the Sixteenth Assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Section on the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery.

Now, when we examine how diverse principles converge to govern their respective directions, yet all find a level path in returning to the One to measure our affairs, how could it ever be otherwise than to melt one's thoughts within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and stifle attachment to the dust of illusions?

Although the precepts of giving (*dāna*) and morality (*śīla*) are most solemn, and the practices of patience (*kṣānti*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are most refined, they ultimately rely upon real wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) for support and take the true exposition (*tattvavyākhyāna*) as their provisional path.

About to dispel the delusions of the "elephant's touch," there was again the assembly at Lake Rājagṛha; thus he illuminated the traces of the five [Hīnayāna] paths and caused beings to ascend the vehicle of the First [Dhyāna], molding and refining them from both extremes.
He gazed deeply into the subtle and profound, while his silence was as vast as the ocean, concealing all sound beyond the four propositions.
When the sprouts of various views are pruned, the obscuring petals fall like stars;
when the net of accumulated doubts is drawn aside, the veiling silk clouds part.

By realizing the emptiness of nature one practices constantly, and by awakening to the falsity of birth one benefits others perpetually; thus the four māras lose their way, and the six pāramitās arrive in a unified procession.
Through giving, one does not waste; that which is difficult to relinquish, one is able to relinquish.
Through precepts, one does not fail to restrain; that which is difficult to protect, one is able to protect.
Through patience, one does not harbor resentment; that which is unbearable, one is able to endure.
Through progress, there is no movement, yet it issues forth from non-issuance;
through concentration, there is no stillness, yet the three marks do not interact;
through wisdom, there is no illumination, yet the three wheels do not revolve.
Therefore, to realize it is to find that movement becomes ever more still; to err regarding it is for stillness to become ever more movement.
The Dharma is neither identical to nor separate from non-Dharma; how could practice be either one with or different from non-practice?
In its realization, the true mind merges into a single vision;
in its manifestation, the Dharma-treasures proliferate into myriad realms.

Thus there arise the two wisdoms, the three bodies, the four analytical knowledges, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine meditative concentrations, and the ten powers; further added are the eighteen unique qualities, the eighty minor marks, the knowledge of the twelve links of dependent origination, and the twenty modes of emptiness—all fashioned from *hi* and completed by *ta*, gathered within the *roma* [tuft of hair], and flowing forth from the golden lips of his instruction.

These have been compiled into eight fascicles; they were not translated anew, but as one of dull wit who has mistakenly joined the ranks of translators, I look back upon the magnificent banquet of the assembly and lament that I could not attend it in person. Yet, mindful of Your Majesty’s extraordinary favor, I record these remaining words: originating from the compassionate breath [of the Buddha] which spreads far and wide, and receiving them with veneration during this auspicious era, I shall ensure that the wondrous treasure is passed down in every household and the numinous pearl is held by every person. May the dust of worldly affliction be washed away throughout the eight regions, and may the profound nourishment of the Dharma rain down upon ten thousand generations.
May blessings protect the imperial throne and grant long life to the Emperor and Empress; may joy pervade the common people, and may the teachings of the Dharma flourish and expand.
It is hoped that scholars of limited capacity may cast aside their doubts at this moment of awe and terror,
and that guests of overweening pride may cease their slander during this period of profound compression.

Were it not for those who have long served under countless Buddhas like the sands of the Ganges and heard the teachings through successive generations, how could they open these volumes to offer their devotion, transcend words to enter into appreciation?
How tragic!
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Part One of the Sixteenth Division of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the side of the Śīrṣavatī Pond, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth, had gathered together from various buddha-fields.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat surrounded by a respectful assembly of many hundreds of thousands, preaching the Dharma for them.

At that time, among the great assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Suvīra. He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding a small portion of profound meaning. I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will grant permission for the question and deign to provide an answer!”
Thereupon, the Buddha said to Suvīra:
“The Tathāgata now grants you leave to ask whatever you wish; I shall answer according to your questions so as to bring joy to your heart.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you have everywhere proclaimed the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; what is meant by ‘*prajñāpāramitā*’?”
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom so as to bring it swiftly to fulfillment?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom such that no evil māras can find an opportunity, and all demonic activities are fully recognized?
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, swiftly fulfill all the qualities of omniscience?
At that time, the Blessed One praised the bodhisattva mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin, saying:
“Excellent!”
Excellent, noble son!
It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

For the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas attaining their purpose and benefit, for the sake of causing sentient beings to obtain benefit, and also for the sake of sentient beings obtaining peace and happiness; out of compassion for the great multitude of beings in the world, and for the benefit, peace, and happiness of gods and humans; and desiring to act as a lamp of illumination for bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the present and future—you have questioned the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing [the answer] yet questioning further, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra, saying:
"Son of good family!
With what intention do you inquire of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra said:

"Out of compassion for all sentient beings, and for the sake of bringing them benefit and happiness, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* universally encompasses all dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and perfectly awakened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will fully proclaim and explain the realm and wisdom of the Tathāgata!
If there are sentient beings whose disposition is fixed in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly realize their own stage of outflowlessness;
if there are sentient beings whose disposition is fixed in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly attain liberation by relying on their own vehicle.

If there are classes of sentient beings who are certain regarding the nature of the Unsurpassed Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

if there are classes of sentient beings who, though not yet entered into the state of correct determination and departure from birth, are indefinite as to their lineage among the three vehicles, having heard this Dharma, they shall all give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
I only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will answer this inquiry concerning the profound Prajñāpāramitā, so that the roots of goodness of all sentient beings may grow!
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
I do not now inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha for the sake of those sentient beings who possess inferior inclinations and understandings;
nor do I inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha for the sake of those sentient beings whose minds cling to poverty."
Nor is it for the sake of establishing those sentient beings who ride upon the vehicle of poverty that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings who are indolent and lazy that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings who are obscured by slothfulness that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, it is not for the sake of sentient beings who have fallen into the mire of evil views that one inquires of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who are bound by the snares of Māra that one inquires of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who lack a sense of shame and dread of blame that one inquires of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of sentient beings who lack integrity and frugality that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who have lost right mindfulness that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings whose minds are constantly deluded and distracted that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Nor do they inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of those sentient beings who are submerged in the mire of desire;
nor do they inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of those sentient beings who frequently practice deceit and crookedness;
nor do they inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of those sentient beings who frequently practice deception and delusion.
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of those sentient beings who do not know how to repay kindness that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings who have accomplished evil desires that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings who delight in practicing evil deeds that one asks the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings who have violated their ethical discipline that one inquires about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings whose morality is impure that one inquires about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
nor is it for the sake of those sentient beings who have destroyed right view that one inquires about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Furthermore, it is not for the sake of sentient beings who delight in wandering through the realms of Māra that they inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who take pleasure in self-praise that they inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who take pleasure in reviling others that they inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of sentient beings who crave and value gain and offerings that one questions the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who are greedily attached to robes and alms bowls that one questions the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who practice deceit and hypocrisy in secret that one questions the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, it is not for the sake of sentient beings who delight in flowery and deceptive speech that one questions the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who falsely manifest strange signs that one questions the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;
nor is it for the sake of sentient beings who seek by means of provocation and pressure that one questions the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of seeking profit through profit that they inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"Blessed One!
It is not for the sake of these various defiled and evil sentient beings that I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings whose deep minds take great delight in the knowledge of all modes, unattached knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, unequaled knowledge, and unsurpassed knowledge, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, concerning this profound Prajñāpāramitā for their sake;
for if these sentient beings cannot find anything even within what they themselves possess, how much less would they praise themselves!"
I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā;
for if sentient beings cannot find anything at all belonging to others, how much less would they revile or disparage them!
I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those sentient beings who have subdued their pride like a hornless bull; I now inquire of the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those sentient beings who seek to extract the various poisonous arrows of the afflictions.

If there are sentient beings whose minds are humble like those of the sons of Caṇḍālas, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for their sake;

if there are sentient beings whose minds are impartial like the four great elements or space, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for their sake;
if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not even apprehend or cling to any phenomena, how much less so to what is not a phenomenon!
I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,

regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose intention is pure, who are without guile and without deceit, and whose nature is straightforward; I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose minds are impartial and who have compassion for, and seek the benefit and happiness of, all sentient beings.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly demonstrate, exhort, encourage, and gladden all sentient beings in wholesome dharmas, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for their sake;

if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to bear the great burden, are able to mount the Great Vehicle, and are able to accomplish the great task, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for their sake.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, bring forth the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound perfection of wisdom for their sake;

if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to act as guides, supreme guides, and universal guides for all sentient beings, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound perfection of wisdom for their sake;
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not dwell in dependence upon any phenomena, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound perfection of wisdom for their sake.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no longing for any place of rebirth, I now ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for his sake;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is liberated from the snares of all evil Māras, I now ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for his sake;

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses great aspiration, is endowed with great diligence, and is always free from negligence, I now ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā for his sake.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to reach the ultimate further shore of all phenomena, I now, for their sake, inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to thoroughly sever and extinguish the entire web of doubt, I now, for their sake, inquire about the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses no pride, no grasping, and no attachment even toward the realization of buddha-wisdom, how much less so toward other forms of wisdom!
I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,

concerning the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have transcended all pride and attachment, who are able to abide in the right path, who are able to practice the right path, and who are able to teach the right path; I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,

concerning the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who constantly act for the benefit of all sentient beings, who are able to provide them with profit, who are able to provide them with peace and happiness, and who are able to bring them security.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

For the sake of universally bestowing upon all sentient beings undefiled peace and happiness, unsurpassed peace and happiness, peerless peace and happiness, the peace and happiness of nirvāṇa, the peace and happiness of all Buddhas, and the peace and happiness of the unconditioned, I inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā;

for the sake of forever severing the various nets of doubt, afflictions, and fetters of all sentient beings, I inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
In order to sever for myself the various nets of doubt, afflictions, and fetters, I have questioned the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

If my own net of doubt, afflictions, and fetters were forever severed, I would then be able to teach sentient beings, in accordance with reality, the various essential dharmas for severing their nets of doubt, afflictions, and fetters.

Why is this? Because all sentient beings delight in peace and happiness and loathe danger and suffering; all sentient beings employ skillful means to pursue peace and happiness. I do not see even the slightest portion of peace and happiness to be sought, except for the *prajñāpāramitā*;
I do not see even the slightest portion of peace and happiness to be sought, except for the vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"I do not see even the slightest portion of any other happiness worth seeking, except for the Mahāyāna.

Having now perceived such benefits and wishing to bestow sublime peace and happiness upon sentient beings, I inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā."

I now perceive such benefits for the entire assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; therefore, I inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā. I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant me an answer!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Noble son!

Since you have compassionately taken pity on the great assembly led by Mahājāti and have questioned the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā, you shall, by virtue of this cause, possess immeasurable merit."
“You should listen attentively!
Reflect upon this very well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Sudāṇa (Excellent Valor) said:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain it for us!”
“We would delight to hear it.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra:
“Regarding what you previously asked: ‘World-Honored One, in various places you have proclaimed the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; what is this *prajñāpāramitā*?’”
"Thus it is, you should know!
In reality, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be named 'Prajñāpāramitā,' for the profound Prajñāpāramitā transcends all paths of names and expressions."
Why is this? O Suvīra!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* truly cannot be said to "be" the *prajñāpāramitā*; nor can it be said to "belong to" that *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can it be said to "arise from" that *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can it be said to "proceed from" that *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because wisdom can reach far into the true nature of all phenomena, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
Even the wisdom of the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, let alone the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)!
"O Well-Valiant One!
'Wisdom' refers to the understanding of all phenomena and the knowledge of all phenomena; therefore, it is called prajñā."
"Excellent Valiant One!
How does wisdom understand all phenomena?
It means that as phenomena differ, their names and expressions also differ."

However, all phenomena do not transcend names and expressions; whether one understands or knows these phenomena, they are both inexpressible. Nevertheless, because one speaks in accordance with what sentient beings can understand, it is called *prajñā*.
"O Suvīra! Prajñā is a provisional designation; it is by means of provisional designation that it is called 'prajñā.
However, all phenomena are beyond designation, immovable, inexpressible, and unmanifestable. To know them in this way is called knowing them as they truly are."
"O Suvīra! Prajñā is neither knowing nor not-knowing; it is neither this nor any other place;
therefore it is named prajñā. Furthermore, O Suvīra!"
Prajñā is said to be that which is the range of wisdom and yet not the range of wisdom; it is neither the object of non-wisdom nor the object of wisdom, because wisdom is detached from all objects.
If wisdom were the object, it would not be wisdom; wisdom does not arise from non-wisdom, nor does non-wisdom arise from wisdom.
Non-wisdom does not arise from non-wisdom, nor does wisdom arise from wisdom.
One does not designate something as wisdom by virtue of being non-wisdom, nor does one designate something as non-wisdom by virtue of being wisdom.
It is not by means of non-wisdom that it is called "non-wisdom," nor is it by means of wisdom that it is called "wisdom.
Rather, it is precisely non-wisdom that is called "wisdom," and by virtue of this, it is precisely wisdom that is called "non-wisdom."

In this regard, wisdom cannot be manifested as "this is called wisdom," nor can it be manifested as that to which wisdom belongs, nor can it be manifested as that from which wisdom arises, nor can it be manifested as that by which wisdom proceeds. Therefore, within wisdom there is no real nature of wisdom, nor does a real wisdom abide within the nature of wisdom; both wisdom and the nature of wisdom are unattainable.

It is the same with regard to non-wisdom and its nature: it is certain that one does not become wise by means of non-wisdom. If one were called wise by virtue of non-wisdom, then all foolish people would possess wisdom.
If one, in accordance with reality, finds nothing to be apprehended in either knowledge or non-knowledge, and thoroughly knows knowledge and non-knowledge as they truly are, this is called knowledge.
However, the true nature of knowledge is not as it has been described.
Why is this? Because the true nature of wisdom is free from names and expressions.

Wisdom is not the object of wisdom, nor is it not the object of wisdom; because wisdom transcends all objects, it cannot be said to be either the wisdom that is the object or the wisdom that is not the object.
"O Suvīra! This is called the teaching of the characteristics of wisdom as they truly are.
Such characteristics of wisdom are in reality ineffable and cannot be demonstrated; nevertheless, they are taught and shown in accordance with what sentient beings can know."
Even that which is able to know cannot be described; since the object of wisdom does not exist, how much less can there be a knower!
If one can thus understand things as they truly are and realize them according to reality, this is called *prajñā*.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
If one can thus realize and witness through direct insight, this is called supramundane prajñā; yet this supramundane prajñā that has been described is also inexpressible."
Why is this? Since even the mundane world does not exist, how much less could there be that which transcends it!
Since that which is transcended does not exist, how much less could there be that which is able to transcend it!
For this reason, even supramundane prajñā does not exist. Why is this?

Because one cannot apprehend either the mundane or the supramundane—the means by which one transcends or that which is transcended—one may speak of it as "supramundane prajñā. If there were anything to be apprehended, it would not be called supramundane prajñā.
This nature of prajñā is also unattainable, for it is free from any attainable nature such as existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, Subhavyūha! "World" is a conventional designation;

there is no real world established by convention from which one could emerge. Rather, because one emerges from all conventions, it is called "transcending the world. Moreover, transcending the world does not mean that there is actually an emerging or a non-emerging within the world.

Why is this so? Because herein there is absolutely nothing that emerges, nor can even the slightest phenomenon that could emerge be found; therefore, it is called "transcending the world" (*lokottara*).
Furthermore, as for "transcending the world," there is neither world nor transcending the world, neither emergence nor non-emergence; therefore, it is called "transcending the world."
If one can understand in this way according to reality, this is called supramundane prajñā.
Such prajñā is not as it has been described. Why is that?
Because supramundane *prajñā* transcends all paths of names and expressions, although it is called "supramundane," there is nothing from which it emerges;

although it is called "*prajñā*," there is nothing known. Since that which emerges and that which is known cannot be apprehended, the one who emerges and the one who knows likewise cannot be apprehended. To know it thus, in accordance with reality, is what is called supramundane *prajñā*.
Because there is nothing that this prajñā does not bring forth, it is therefore called supramundane prajñā.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! This is also called the prajñā of thorough penetration."
What does such prajñā realize? It is said that this prajñā realizes nothing.

If this prajñā were to realize something, it would be a mere conceptual designation; if it were a conceptual designation, it could not be called the realization of prajñā. This is because within this there is absolutely nothing: no "this," no "that," and no middle; no one who realizes, no object realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and no realizer. Therefore, it is called "realization."
Furthermore, within this there is nothing at all: no one who practices, no place where one practices, no "this," no "that," and no middle; therefore, it is called "thorough penetration."

Furthermore, that which is called "penetrating wisdom" (pratisaṃvid) is itself non-existent; this penetrating wisdom has neither above nor below, neither slowness nor speed, neither progress nor retreat, and neither going nor coming. Therefore, it is named "penetration."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
What does one who has attained mastery through wisdom master?
It means that whatever is seen, all of it is thoroughly mastered."
By what is it realized?
It is by means of prajñā.
How is such prajñā realized?

This means that while one attains penetration through the establishment of conventional signs, all such conventionally established signs are in fact non-signs; thus, these non-signs are called "conventionally established signs.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
All those who achieve such prajñā are able to penetrate the three realms as they truly are.
How does one penetrate the three realms as they truly are?
It means that what are called the "three realms" are not, in fact, the three realms.
Why is this so? Because herein there are no elements (*dhātu*) that can be penetrated; the penetration of the three realms is itself the non-element.
Since one is able to penetrate the three realms in this manner, it is called the accomplishment of the wisdom of penetration (*prajñā*).
What is the accomplishment of the penetrating prajñā?

It means that there is not the slightest matter that is not well-penetrated; one is thoroughly proficient in all matters. Therefore, it is called penetrating prajñā, and such prajñā completely transcends all matters.
If one accomplishes such *prajñā*, all that is seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and cognized is thoroughly penetrated.
How is it penetrated? That is to say:

because they are impermanent, suffering, an abscess, a disease, an arrow, empty, obstructive, harmful, alien, subject to disintegration, of a nature to disintegrate, unstable, quickly perishing, selfless, unarisen, unceasing, and signless; and so forth.
"O Suvīra! If one can thoroughly penetrate this, it is called 'the cool state free from arrows.

It is like an excellent medicine named 'Free from Arrows' (Viśalyā): wherever it is applied, all arrows are removed, and no poison can remain therein, for it is driven out by the power of this medicine."

In this way, if there are bhikṣus who accomplish this dharma of coolness and freedom from the arrow—namely, accomplishing the penetration of prajñā, possessing the six constant abodes and penetrating prajñā, remaining far removed from all defiled attachments of the three realms, and transcending the snare-net of all Māras.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as a diamond, for the purpose of boring through objects, penetrates everywhere it is applied without obstruction;

likewise, if there are bhikṣus who possess the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), which is embraced by penetrating wisdom, they will penetrate every dharma they examine without exception."
This penetrative wisdom is embraced by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), such that there is no phenomenon it does not penetrate upon observation.

If one achieves this penetrative wisdom, one can transcend the world and correctly exhaust all suffering, proceeding toward the exhaustion of all suffering without any defilement or attachment; this penetrative wisdom is also called the "three knowledges" (*trividyā*).

"O Suvīra! 'Illumination' (vidyā) is a metaphor for the eternal cessation of ignorance; it is also said to be the thorough knowledge of ignorance, and it is further named a metaphor for that which can extinguish the aggregate of suffering."

For example, it is like a skilled physician who is intelligent and profoundly learned; whatever he undertakes, he observes with excellence because he has perfected the subtle wisdom of observation. He is well-acquainted with all medicines, thoroughly understands the causes of diseases, and skillfully knows the symptoms of illness, thereby able to rescue beings from their manifold sufferings; whatever disease he treats, there is none that is not cured.
Why is this? Because he has thoroughly mastered the methods regarding medicine, disease, causes, symptoms, and their proper combination; therefore, he is able to eliminate all suffering from illness.

Thus, if one accomplishes the third clarity (*vidyā*), which can extinguish all ignorance, can still all suffering, and can eliminate all birth, old age, sickness, death, as well as the states of grief, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair—this is called supramundane penetrating *prajñā*.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! It is with reference to this meaning and with this underlying intention that I have said:

'Among all things in the world, wisdom is supreme,' meaning that it is able to penetrate the true nature of all phenomena, and through this correct knowledge, it brings about the exhaustion of birth."
What is the designation for "one whose births are exhausted"?
It is the designation for "thoroughly penetrating emergence and disappearance.
What is meant by "thoroughly penetrating emergence and disappearance"?
This means that one thoroughly penetrates the fact that all phenomena which arise have the nature of ceasing; this is called penetrating emergence and disappearance.
O Well-Valiant One!

"Emergence" is a metaphorical designation for birth, and "disappearance" is a metaphorical designation for cessation. Although these terms are used, there is no actual emergence or disappearance as the words suggest.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
All that is accumulated is not a phenomenon that truly emerges. Why is this?

"O Suvīra! 'Arising' (samudaya) means arising equally; it is not that there is an equal emergence, nor is there an equal disappearance. Because it arises in accordance with equality, it is called 'arising.
As for 'arising in accordance with equality,' within this there is neither emergence nor disappearance."

Thus, the spontaneous disintegration of its own nature is what is called "cessation. In this context, cessation refers to the absence of any entity; it is called cessation because there is immediate extinction.
It is not that something which arises in one moment ceases in that very same moment that is called cessation;
rather, it is called cessation precisely because there is no arising.
Thus, one who penetrates [the truth] that there is neither arising nor ceasing in either emergence or subsidence is said to "penetrate emergence and subsidence.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
Regarding the term "thoroughly penetrating" (prativedha): it refers to being able to fully know all dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Because various phenomena arise by means of various conditions, it is called "dependent origination.

Such dependent origination is entirely non-existent; this is what is meant by "thoroughly penetrating dependent origination," which is also called "fully knowing dependent origination," meaning one can demonstrate that, in accordance with reality, there is no arising.

Because it is without arising, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*); because it is equal and without arising, it is called "dependent origination. This means that in this state, even arising does not exist, let alone cessation!

Following the awakening to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), neither the favorable nor the adverse can be apprehended; because there is no origination, it is called "dependent origination. If there is no origination, then there is no birth.

If there is no birth, then there is no past and no that which has already arisen. If there is no past and no that which has already arisen, then there is no cessation. If there is no cessation, then there is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); by virtue of this knowledge of non-arising, one does not give rise again, nor does one realize cessation.

Because there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation; it is only because there is arising that cessation is conventionally established. Since there is no arising, there is therefore no cessation.
To thus know, see, penetrate, and realize all phenomena in this way is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
“Suvīra! ‘Knowledge of exhaustion’ means that because ignorance is exhausted, it is called knowledge of exhaustion.
By what is it called ‘exhaustion’?
It is because of its inexhaustibility that it is called "exhaustion," for one does not perceive any dharma that can be called exhausted.
Nevertheless, apart from the absence of ignorance, it is termed "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*); that is, the very exhaustion of ignorance is termed "knowledge of exhaustion."

Because one thoroughly knows all dharmas that are ignorance, it is called the "exhaustion of ignorance"; by virtue of this exhaustion of ignorance, it is termed "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
It is not that there is an exhaustion or non-exhaustion of the dharmas that are ignorance; rather, because one is free from ignorance, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion.

Because one knows this dharma of ignorance as it truly is—namely, that it is entirely non-existent—it is called "freedom"; by means of such knowledge, knowing that there is no distinct entity to be found within the dharma of ignorance, it is called "freedom from ignorance."
However, since the dharma of ignorance is ultimately unattainable, even wisdom does not exist; how much less could there be ignorance!
If one can attain liberation within this exhaustion, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

Although it is spoken thus, it is not as it is spoken; all knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is ultimately ineffable, yet it is conventionally designated by the name "knowledge of the exhaustion of ignorance," and is also called "knowledge of exhaustion."

If one observes all phenomena with such inexhaustible knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), even that knowledge of exhaustion is non-existent. If one knows in this way, one departs from the knowledge of exhaustion and reaches the limit of the inexhaustible; this limit of the inexhaustible is itself the limitless and the limit of nirvāṇa.

Although it is spoken of in this way, it is not as it is spoken, because all phenomena are themselves the limitless and the limit of nirvāṇa; the eternal severance of all limits is called the limit of nirvāṇa.
Although it is spoken of in this way, it is not as it is spoken, because the limit of nirvāṇa is eternally free from names and phrases, and all names and phrases are eternally extinguished therein.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

Although the Tathāgata speaks of the realm of nirvāṇa, it is not as it is spoken of; for the realm of nirvāṇa is utterly ineffable, transcending all speech, and within the realm of nirvāṇa, all speech is forever severed."
To speak of the characteristics of the realm of nirvāṇa in such a manner is precisely what is called speaking of the characteristics of supramundane penetrating prajñā.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
It cannot be said that the realm of nirvāṇa exists in this place or that place; therefore, nirvāṇa is truly ineffable.
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
In this context, what is meant by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"
This Prajñāpāramitā does not have even a slight portion of a distant "other shore" that can be apprehended. Suvīra!
If this Prajñāpāramitā had even a slight portion of a distant "other shore" that could be apprehended, the Tathāgata would have said that the profound Prajñāpāramitā has a distant "other shore."
“Suvīra! This prajñāpāramitā cannot be found at a distance; therefore, it is not said that it has a ‘far shore.
Furthermore, Suvīra!”

That which is called "Prajñāpāramitā" refers to the activity of sublime wisdom that reaches the ultimate further shore of all phenomena; therefore it is named Prajñāpāramitā. Although it is explained in this way, it is not as it is described.
Why is this? It is not through speech nor through action that one can reach the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?
"O Suvīra! Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is ineffable.
Furthermore, O Suvīra!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* conforms to the awakening to all phenomena; yet, if one can so conform, that itself contradicts awakening. Why is this?

Because herein there is no entity that can be called "conforming to awakening. Since conforming to awakening does not exist, awakening likewise does not exist; thus, regarding all phenomena, there is no sense of "thorough penetration" (*prativedha*).
Because awakening to and penetrating the equal nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is bodhi, it is called "bodhi" because of the awakening to all phenomena.
How does this [awakening] awaken to all phenomena?
In this, there is no entity that can be named "awakening," and therefore, within this, there is also no subsequent realization. Why is this?
O Well-Valiant One!
If even a fraction of bodhi were obtainable, then one would have to obtain bodhi within bodhi;
however, within bodhi, bodhi does not exist. One should realize bodhi in this manner: it is called awakening because it is not a matter of sequential cognition, nor is it a matter of penetration.

Although this is said, it is not as it is expressed, because all phenomena cannot be followed or awakened to, nor can they be fully realized; furthermore, both phenomena and non-phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Because one awakens to this principle, it is called bodhi.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is not that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas can attain bodhi; [rather, they realize it].
It is not that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas can realize bodhi, for bodhi as it truly is cannot be realized and cannot be expressed;
nor is it that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas give rise to bodhi, for bodhi has the nature of being neither born nor arisen.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is unattached; within awakening, there is not even the slightest sentient being, nor any designation of a sentient being."

Since within enlightenment there is neither a sentient being nor the designation of a "sentient being," how can it be said that "this is a sattva belonging to enlightenment" or "this is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva"?
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
Within awakening, no awakening can be apprehended; within awakening, no sentient being can be apprehended. Why is this?

“Suvīra! Awakening is transcendent, awakening is unborn, awakening is unarisen, and awakening is signless. Within awakening there is no nature of a sentient being (*sattva*); within awakening no sentient being can be apprehended. Awakening is not designated by means of a sentient being, nor is a sentient being designated by means of awakening. Because one awakens to the fact that a sentient being has no intrinsic nature, it is called ‘awakening.’”
Knowing that within awakening there is truly no sentient being (sattva), one is therefore called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? O Well-Valiant One!
A bodhisattva is not manifested by the notion of a "being"; it is because one has eliminated the notion of a "being" that one is called a "bodhisattva. Although this is said, it is not as it is said.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is free from names and expressions.

A bodhisattva is free from the nature of a "being" (sattva), and a bodhisattva is free from the conceptualization of a "being"; it is because they know awakening (bodhi) that they are called a "Bodhisattva."
"How does a bodhisattva know awakening? It means knowing that awakening transcends all things;

awakening is unconditioned, awakening is unborn, and awakening is unceasing. It is not that the nature of awakening can comprehend awakening, nor is awakening something that is manifested. Because it cannot be manifested, cannot be designated, and cannot be diverted, it is called 'awakening'."

If one can correctly awaken to and penetrate [reality] without inversion, such that there is no conceptualization and conceptualization is forever severed, for this reason one is called a bodhisattva; yet, although it is so described, it is not as the description suggests.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
If there were a bodhisattva to be apprehended, then one could likewise apprehend that "this is enlightenment," "this belongs to enlightenment," "this is a sattva," or "this belongs to a sattva.

However, it cannot be said that "this is enlightenment" or "this belongs to enlightenment," nor can it be said that "this is a sattva" or "this belongs to a sattva. Because one awakens to the fact that in reality there is no sattva—being without the nature of a sattva and detached from the nature of a sattva—one is called a "bodhisattva. Since there is no sattva and the notion of a sattva has been eliminated, one is called a "bodhisattva."
"Why is this? O Suvīra!

The realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) is a designation for the absence of real sentient beings; there is no nature of a sentient being within sentient beings. Because sentient beings do not exist, it is called the 'realm of sentient beings.'"
If sentient beings possessed the nature of being sentient beings, then one should not speak of a "realm of sentient beings" (*sattvadhātu*).
The "realm of sentient beings" reveals the absence of a realm, because the realm of sentient beings has the nature of being no-realm.
If the realm of sentient beings existed by way of its own elemental nature, then there would truly be a life-principle identical to the body;
if the realm of sentient beings existed apart from its elemental nature, then there would truly be a life-principle distinct from the body.
However, the realm of sentient beings has no real elemental nature; it is merely designated as a "realm" through conventional usage.
Within the non-sentient realm there can be no nature of a realm, nor does the nature of a realm contain the sentient realm;
the nature of a realm is not itself the sentient realm, nor is the sentient realm apart from the nature of a realm, because all phenomena lack the nature of a realm.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
Based on this meaning, I have spoken with intentional ambiguity:
'The realm of sentient beings cannot be established as either decreasing or increasing.'"
Why is this so? Because the realm of sentient beings is not of an existent nature, and because the realm of sentient beings is devoid of an existent nature.

Just as it is impossible to designate the realm of sentient beings as either diminishing or increasing, so too it is with all phenomena; it is impossible to designate them as either diminishing or increasing, because all phenomena lack any real intrinsic nature and thus cannot be said to diminish or increase.
If one can thus awaken to all phenomena accordingly, this is called awakening to the Buddha-dharma accordingly.
Based on this meaning and with this underlying intention, I have said:
"Just as it cannot be established that the realm of sentient beings diminishes or increases, so too it cannot be established that all phenomena diminish or increase."
If all phenomena are neither diminished nor fulfilled, and by means of their lack of reality, they are thus the Buddha-dharma which is neither diminished nor fulfilled.

Because one awakens to all phenomena in this way, it is called the Buddha-dharma that is neither diminished nor fulfilled; since all phenomena are without diminution or fulfillment, they are designated as the Buddha-dharma.
The "Buddha-dharma" is a mere designation for what is not Buddha-dharma; among all Buddha-dharmas, there is no entity that can cause them to either decrease or increase.

Why is this? Because it is precisely through the thorough awakening to all phenomena (*dharma*). If one can thoroughly awaken to the nature of all phenomena, therein no phenomenon can either decrease or increase.
One should know that "all phenomena" is a synonym for the dharma-realm; that dharma-realm neither decreases nor increases. Why is this?
Because that dharma-realm is without limit.

No distinction between the realm of sentient beings and that dharma-realm can be apprehended; nor can the realm of sentient beings and that dharma-realm be diminished, increased, attained, or found to exist. To awaken accordingly to this is called bodhi.
For this reason, it is said:
"The Buddha-dharmas cannot be conceived as having either decrease or increase.
Furthermore, Suvīra!

If one can, in accordance with reality, remain without conceptual discrimination regarding the nature of neither decrease nor increase, one should be known as a "seer of reality as it is. Within this state, there is no possibility of grasping or rejecting; such awakening to reality is called *bodhi*.
“Suvīra! Awakening is itself the mark of a Buddha. What is the mark of a Buddha?
It is that all marks are ultimately markless; this is the mark of a Buddha.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because ultimate signlessness and the characteristic of bodhi are by nature dissociated.
Thus, awakening in accordance with reality is called bodhi; yet, although it is described in this way, it is not as it is described.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because one is able to awaken to such dharmas accordingly, one is called a bodhisattva.
If there is a bodhisattva who does not truly understand such dharmatā, yet claims:
"I am able to awaken to them accordingly as they truly are," [he is not a true bodhisattva].

One who claims to be a bodhisattva should be known as one who is far from the stage of a bodhisattva and far from the qualities of a bodhisattva; by using the name "bodhisattva," they deceive and delude devas, humans, asuras, and others.
“Furthermore, Suvīra!
If one could become a bodhisattva merely by claiming to be a bodhisattva through empty words, then all sentient beings would necessarily be bodhisattvas.”
Furthermore, Suvīra!
It is not merely by empty words that one enters the bodhisattva stages and attains the bodhisattva dharmas; it is not through speech alone.

One can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet this is not attained through the verbal act of self-proclaiming one's name; nor is it through such verbal self-proclamation that one enters the bodhisattva stages or attains the bodhisattva dharmas.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
All sentient beings who practice the conduct of awakening, yet do not know and do not awaken to the true nature of all phenomena, are not called bodhisattvas."
Why is this? Because they do not know that sentient beings are non-sentient beings.
If they knew the nature of sentient beings as being non-sentient, they would become bodhisattvas by practicing the conduct of enlightenment.

However, because all sentient beings are subject to perversion, they are unable to realize their own conduct, their own objects, and their own spheres of activity. If one were to understand one’s own conduct as it truly is, one would no longer engage in conduct characterized by conceptual discrimination.
Due to such discriminative conduct, all foolish worldlings give rise to perverted actions by taking false objects as their conditions, and they also give rise to prideful attachment toward bodhi.
Because they give rise to perverse conceited conduct and discriminative conduct by taking false objects as conditions, they cannot even attain the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, much less attain bodhi!

If one can thoroughly understand such dharmas, then one will no longer give rise to conduct conditioned by the false, nor will one again give rise to conceit by taking various dharmas as conditions; this is called the bodhisattva practicing non-practice.
A bodhisattva should not give rise to conceptual activity through conceptualization; if there is no conceptualization regarding a certain object, there is no activity therein;
if one does not give rise to conceptualization regarding a certain object, there is likewise no activity therein.
Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practice all activities without making any conceptual distinctions, all forms of pride never arise.

When a Bodhisattva knows all phenomena in this way, they no longer grasp at them, no longer discriminate them, and neither wander through nor tread upon them; this is called the true practice of a Bodhisattva, for it takes non-action as its skillful means.
If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, this is called the true bodhisattva practice.
Why is that? O Well-Valiant One!
Because one who can thus awaken to all phenomena and penetrate all phenomena is called a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Suvīra!
You should know that "the absence of sentient beings" is a synonym for a bodhisattva, because they have been able to eliminate all conceptualizations.

Why is this so? Because one is able to thoroughly comprehend that all sentient beings are not truly sentient beings; that all sentient beings are in fact non-sentient beings; that all sentient beings are sentient beings through the attachment of inversion; that all sentient beings are sentient beings grasped by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); that all sentient beings are sentient beings whose objects of perception are false; that all sentient beings are sentient beings whose own conduct is ruined; and that all sentient beings are sentient beings for whom volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Why is this? O Well-Vigorous One!

If a phenomenon and all sentient beings do not exist such that various classes of sentient beings create that phenomenon, this is called "sentient beings for whom ignorance conditions volitional formations."
What phenomena do not exist?
They are the self as it is grasped, the "mine" as it is grasped, and that which is grasped and relied upon by the grasping at self and "mine"—those phenomena do not exist.

If those phenomena existed, all sentient beings would grasp at them as "I" and as "mine"; that which is grasped and relied upon by the grasping at "I" and "mine" would all be truly existent and could not be called false.

However, because those phenomena do not exist, yet sentient beings falsely grasp at them as "I" and as "mine," that which is grasped and relied upon by the grasping at "I" and "mine" is entirely non-existent and is purely false. Therefore, it is said:
"All sentient beings are not truly sentient beings; all sentient beings are sentient beings whose formations are conditioned by ignorance."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

There is no real dharma whatsoever that is designated as a 'sentient being' which could be grasped as a self, or as belonging to a self, or as that which is grasped or relied upon by those two types of grasping;
because there is no real dharma, it can be said that all sentient beings are not real sentient beings."
That which is "not a sentient being" should be understood as a metaphorical designation for "not real";
that which is "not real" should be understood as a metaphorical designation for "not a sentient being.
Furthermore, within the perception of unreal sentient beings, all sentient beings falsely cling to them as real; therefore, this statement is made:
All sentient beings are not truly sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhānavīrya!
To say they are "not real" means that within them there is no reality and no arising, because all phenomena are devoid of true reality and are without arising.
In this regard, sentient beings are bound by their own false attachments; therefore, it can be said that all sentient beings are sentient beings whose objects of perception are false.
Because they cannot comprehend their own conduct, it may be said that those who are not truly sentient beings lack the sense of universal awakening therein.
One should know that those who possess universal awakening regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) may be called Bodhisattvas.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 593. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two of the Sixteenth Division on Prajñāpāramitā: "Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can awaken to the Dharma in this way, they may be called a true bodhisattva.
To speak of a "bodhisattva" is a designation for one who is able to conformingly awaken to the fact that sentient beings are without reality and without arising.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva is also able to know all phenomena as they truly are, just as a Buddha does.
How does a bodhisattva know them as a Buddha does?
It means knowing, as it truly is, that the nature of all phenomena is without reality, without arising, and without falsehood.

Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas know the nature of all phenomena as it truly is—neither as it is grasped by foolish ordinary beings nor as it is attained by foolish ordinary beings—they are called Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
For awakening (bodhi) is without attachment, without conceptual differentiation, without accumulation, and without attainment.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

It is not that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained even the slightest thing regarding the nature of awakening; because all phenomena are unattainable, the non-attainment of phenomena is designated as 'awakening.'"
The enlightenment of all Buddhas should be described in this way, yet it is not described as such, because it is free from all signs.
Furthermore, Suvīra! If bodhisattvas resolve upon the mind of enlightenment, they should form this thought:
"I have now resolved to attain bodhicitta. This is bodhi;
for the sake of proceeding toward this bodhi, I now resolve to cultivate the mind of practice.
Because these bodhisattvas perceive things as having objective existence, they are not called "bodhisattvas," but may only be termed "mad beings" (khalita-sattva).
Why is this? O Suvīra!

It is because that bodhisattva resolutely clings to the existence of an initiator, resolutely clings to the existence of the mind generated, and resolutely clings to the existence of the nature of awakening.

If bodhisattvas, having generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), harbor any attachment, they may only be called *sattvas* who possess attachment to the mind of enlightenment; they are not called true bodhisattvas who have generated the pure mind of enlightenment.
Because he generates the mind of enlightenment through mere effort, he is therefore called an "effort-sattva" (kṛt-sattva) and not a bodhisattva;
because he generates the mind of enlightenment through application (prayoga), he is therefore called an "application-sattva" (prayoga-sattva) and not a bodhisattva.
Why is this? O Suvīra!

Because those bodhisattvas have given rise to the mind of awakening through grasping at something, they may only be called "beings who have resolved their minds" (cittotpādika-sattva), but they are not called "bodhisattvas."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
There is no one who can truly give rise to the bodhicitta, because the bodhicitta cannot be given rise to; for awakening is unarisen and devoid of mind."
Those bodhisattvas cling only to the arousal of the mind of awakening, yet they do not understand the meaning of the non-arising nature of the mind of awakening.
Furthermore, Subhānavīrya!
If the arising of equality is itself true equality, if true equality is itself the equality of the mind, and if the equality of the mind is itself awakening.
If there is suchness within this, then within this there is no conceptual differentiation;

if there is a conceptualizing mind and bodhicitta, one then becomes attached to that mind and bodhicitta. One who generates the resolve for enlightenment based on these two types should be known as not truly generating the resolve.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! Awakening and the mind are not distinct from one another;

there is no real awakening within the mind, nor is there a real mind to be found within awakening. Awakening and the mind, according to reality and in accordance with the principle, can both be described neither as 'awakening' nor as 'mind.'"

Because, through suchness-realization, both awakening and the mind are unapprehendable—neither arising nor non-arising—one is called a bodhisattva, a mahāsattva, and a sentient being according to reality.
Why is this? Because one knows, as it truly is, that they do not possess a real intrinsic nature.
Whom does one know, as it truly is, to lack a real intrinsic nature?
It means that all worlds are not substantially existent, are not comprised of substantiality, and do not arise from substantiality; they are merely conventionally established.
In what way do the worlds not arise from substantiality but are merely conventionally established?
That which is not truly existent has no real arising.
Because there is no real arising and because it is not truly existent, all phenomena are said to be without reality and without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Since one knows them as they truly are—namely, that they lack a truly existent nature—one may also be called a "sentient being who knows reality as it is" (*yathābhūtajña sattva*).
Because one does not cling even to that which exists as real, one may further be described as a sentient being who accords with reality as it is.
Yet, although this is said, it is not [exactly] as it is said. Why is this so?
In accordance with the reality of things, there is not even the slightest sentient being or mahāsattva.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because one who has realized and entered the Mahāyāna is called a mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! What is called the Great Vehicle?
It is omniscience that is designated as the Great Vehicle."
What is omniscience?

It refers to all forms of knowledge whatsoever—whether conditioned knowledge or unconditioned knowledge, worldly knowledge or supramundane knowledge; one who is able to realize and enter into such knowledge as these is called a Mahāsattva.

Why is this? Because one who is able to remain far removed from the great perception of a sentient being is called a mahāsattva; because one is able to remain far removed from the great aggregate of ignorance is called a mahāsattva; because one is able to remain far removed from the great aggregate of volitional formations is called a mahāsattva; because one is able to remain far removed from the great aggregate of unknowing is called a mahāsattva; and because one is able to remain far removed from the great aggregate of suffering is called a mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! One who can remain far removed from the notion of a 'great being' is called a Mahāsattva.
Although such a person finds nothing to be apprehended among any minds or mental factors, they are nonetheless able to realize the fundamental nature of the mind."
Although he has no attainment of either awakening or the factors conducive to awakening, he is nonetheless able to understand the intrinsic nature of awakening.

By means of this wisdom, he does not perceive awakening within the mind, nor does he perceive awakening apart from the mind; he does not perceive a real mind within awakening, nor does he perceive a real mind apart from awakening.

Thus, one dispels [all things] such that there is nothing to be cultivated and nothing to be dispelled; regarding both what is cultivated and what is dispelled, one finds nothing to be apprehended, nothing to rely upon, and nothing to cling to. Although one does not perceive a "bodhicitta-nature" as existing, one is nonetheless able to give rise to the great bodhicitta.
If one can thus give rise to the bodhicitta, one may then be called a true bodhisattva.
Although such a person gives rise to the bodhicitta in this way, they do not actually initiate anything with respect to bodhi.
Why is this? O Well-Vigorous One!
Because they have already become firmly established in great enlightenment.

If one can thus remain without attachment, perceiving no distinction whatsoever between the arising and ceasing of the mind and bodhi, and seeing no one who generates the resolve to advance toward great bodhi—being without views, without grasping, and without conceptual discrimination—one should know that such a person already dwells in unsurpassed bodhi.
If one can thus remain without attachment, giving rise to resolute conviction and a mind of liberation, one should be known as a true bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
If bodhisattvas give rise to the thought of enlightenment while not being free from the perception of mind and the perception of enlightenment, they are far from enlightenment and not near to it.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
If bodhisattvas do not perceive that awakening is either distant or near, it should be known that they are close to unsurpassed awakening and are truly those who have generated the bodhicitta.
Based on this meaning and with this underlying intention, I have said:
"If one can personally know the non-dual characteristic, they will know all Buddha-dharmas as they truly are. Why is this so?

When one is able to realize that both oneself and sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature, one is then able to fully know that all phenomena are non-dual. By virtue of this full knowledge of the non-duality of all phenomena, one will certainly comprehend that oneself, sentient beings, and all phenomena all take the absence of intrinsic nature as their very nature, such that there is no distinction in principle between them.
If one can realize that all phenomena are non-dual, one can realize all Buddha-dharmas;
if one can thoroughly know that all phenomena are non-dual, one can thoroughly know all Buddha-dharmas.
If one can fully know the self, one will fully know the triple world.
Furthermore, Suvīra! If one fully knows the self, one will be able to reach the further shore of all phenomena.
What is called "the other shore of all phenomena"?
It refers to the equal, true nature of all phenomena.

If one neither attains this nor clings to this, and neither attains the other shore nor clings to the other shore, that person is called one who has attained the other shore through universal knowledge. Although it is described in this way, it is not as the description suggests.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

Bodhisattvas should approach the bodhisattva stages in this way, and they should realize the bodhisattva stages in this way; you should know that this is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattvas. That is to say, within this there is not the slightest dharma that can be approached or realized, because within this it is impossible to designate any coming or going."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Those who possess signs of overweening pride should not harbor fear regarding what the Buddha has taught."
Then, Śāriputra said to Ānanda:
"This is not the domain of those who possess signs and are characterized by overweening pride; why would they be afraid?"

Why is this? Those who harbor fear are free from overweening pride, yet they are influenced by evil friends; unable to fathom the profound Dharma when they hear it, they fear losing what they seek and thus give rise to terror.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Those who practice correctly with the desire to sever overweening pride may experience fear; those who exert themselves with diligence with the desire to sever overweening pride likewise experience fear."

Why is this so? Because they are already aware of the fault of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), yet in their pursuit of non-arrogance and their quest to sever arrogance, they are unable to fathom the profound Dharma when they hear it; fearing that they might lose what they seek, they consequently give rise to fear.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If there is one who does not perceive conceit, who has no reliance and no grasping, that person will have neither fear nor dread regarding all phenomena."
Furthermore, Ānanda!
The Tathāgata does not teach such a Dharma for those possessed of overweening pride; therefore, they have no occasion for fear regarding this.
Those who, desiring to sever overweening pride, diligently practice the path, will, upon hearing such a Dharma, be able to understand it correctly and likewise remain without fear.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

You should know that the term 'conceited' (adhimāna) indicates the superimposition of superior qualities. If anyone manifests conceit, they necessarily manifest the superimposition of superior qualities, because their practice is one of superimposition rather than impartial practice."
Those who practice the conduct of establishing joy while practicing equanimity will harbor doubts regarding this profound Dharma; they will neither feel terror nor accept it with faith.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If one finds nothing to be apprehended within both the equal and the unequal, if one relies on nothing within both the equal and the unequal, and if one grasps at nothing within both the equal and the unequal, then one will not be startled, alarmed, terrified, or afraid regarding all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

This profound Dharma is not the sphere of activity for foolish worldlings; this profound Dharma is not the domain of foolish worldlings; this profound Dharma is not what foolish worldlings can comprehend, because it transcends all that is practiced, grasped, and perceived by foolish worldlings."
Those who are inclined toward the Śrāvaka vehicle, though they practice the profound Dharma, this profound Dharma is not what they practice.
Those who are inclined toward the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, though they practice the profound Dharma, this profound Dharma is not what they practice.

Those who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, if they practice with signs, remain far removed from virtuous friends, and are influenced by evil friends, will be unable to practice even such a dharma free from attachment, for it is not within their sphere.
Ānanda, you should know this:

with the sole exception of those śrāvakas who have seen the truths and seek great bodhi, as well as those who are embraced by spiritual friends of the bodhisattva vehicle and are able to give rise to faith and understanding toward this profound Dharma, to practice in accordance with this profound Dharma, and to deeply realize and penetrate this profound Dharma.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If bodhisattvas distance themselves from all signs and abide in signlessness, practicing without differentiation, they will ultimately emerge from the various nets of doubt, conceptualization, and attachment regarding the profound Dharma. They will be able to accomplish whatever they desire; they will find nothing to be apprehended in either the mind or awakening (bodhi); they will have no differentiated understanding of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), nor will they give rise to differentiated practices. Whatever direction they turn toward, they will be able to penetrate it."
Regarding such profound Dharma-gates, they are all able to receive and uphold them with minds free from doubt or confusion. Why is this?

Because they abide in accordance with all phenomena without any opposition; if anyone raises various questions concerning the Dharma, they are able to provide corresponding answers in each case, harmonizing this and that so that they do not contradict one another.
"It is for their sake that the Buddha has taught this profound Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"You should receive and uphold what Śāriputra has spoken; his teaching is no different from my own."
“Ānanda, you should know that those with overweening pride cannot enter into this Dharma teaching, because it is not their domain and not their sphere.
Ānanda, you should know this!”
Such a teaching accords with the nature of all phenomena and accords with the Bodhi of the Buddha; it serves as a supportive companion to the Buddha’s Bodhi.
However, sentient beings of inferior inclination and resolve do not mentally penetrate this profound and vast Buddha-Dharma, and are unable to receive or practice it.

Ānanda, you should know that those of inferior resolve and those possessed of overweening pride dwell in opposition to the Buddha’s enlightenment and the profound Dharma; whatever they do follows from their overweening pride, and thus they are unable to believe in or accept this profound Dharma.

“Ānanda, you should know that this present assembly is most excellent and pure, far removed from all defilements. They have, under many past Buddhas, made great vows and planted immeasurable, sublime roots of goodness; they have served boundless Buddhas of the past, long since developed faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, and have already matured their practice of the profound path.”

Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha now entrusts this assembly with full confidence and without suspicion; he clearly elucidates all the Dharma-gates he teaches, and without any sense of stinginess or concealment, he expounds the essential points of the Dharma.

Ānanda, you should know that this present assembly is firm and pure; it is devoid of anything like rubble or saline wasteland, for these beings have already made offerings to many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and are firmly established in the teachings of all Buddhas.
Ānanda, you should know that "tiles and rubble" is a metaphor for foolish worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), who lack the capacity to receive the profound Dharma.
"Salt-encrusted wasteland" and the like should be understood as a metaphor for sentient beings of overweening pride (*abhimānika*), because they are unable to cultivate the profound practice.
"Ānanda, you should know that this present assembly is free from overweening pride; it has arisen from the accumulation of vast roots of goodness and is a profound vessel for the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"

For example, when the Nāga King Anavatapta has a cause or condition for great joy, he experiences the pleasures of the five senses within his own palace; because of that joy, he causes a great rain endowed with the eight meritorious qualities to fall from his palace.

At that time, those sons each went to their own palaces and likewise enjoyed themselves, experiencing the pleasures of the five senses, sporting together and causing a great rain of sweet nectar to fall.
In this same way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, causes a great rain of Dharma to fall for the sake of the assembled multitudes.

At that time, having heard this and gathered together, the immeasurable assembly of elder sons, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, either remained within this Sahā world-system to rain down the great rain of Dharma before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha for the sake of the assembled multitudes, or they went to their respective Buddha-fields to rain down the great rain of Dharma before the various Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas for the sake of their own assemblies.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Just as when the Nāga King of the Ocean is filled with joy, he causes a great rain to fall within his own palace.
All the nāgas who have long resided within that palace receive this falling rain with joy, for they well understand its proper measure.
Those dragon princes were also each filled with joy, being capable of receiving the great rain sent down by their father-king. Why was this?
Because there were other dragons who did not know the limits of the falling rain, and were likewise unable to receive it with joy and endurance.
In this way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, dwells amidst the great assembly and rains down the profound treasure of the Dharma.

There is a host of great Bodhisattvas, the eldest sons of the Buddha, who have long planted immeasurable and most excellent roots of goodness, who have grown within the gateways of the exceedingly profound Dharma, and who have accomplished various kinds of vast aspirations. They are capable of receiving the rain of the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-gate; having heard it, they rejoice and well understand its proper measure.
For this purpose, the Tathāgata now lets out a great lion’s roar amidst this pure assembly, raining down the great rain of Dharma to bring about great benefit.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like a wheel-turning monarch who has many sons, whose maternal lineage is pure and whose physical appearance is dignified and handsome.
At times, when that king has accumulated vast treasuries of jewels, he summons all his sons and distributes them among them, his mind entirely free from deception, delusion, or partiality.
At that time, having obtained the various treasures, the princes felt a redoubled sense of deep respect and affection for their father, the king, and each thought to themselves:
"We now know for certain that our father, the king, shares our interests."

Thus, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is the Great Lord of Dharma and the Great King of Dharma, spontaneously summons the true sons of all Buddhas and distributes the great treasury of Dharma to them, his mind entirely free from deception, delusion, or partiality.
At that time, having obtained the sublime Dharma, the sons of the Buddha felt a redoubled sense of deep reverence and affection for the Tathāgata. Each of them thought:
