"We now know with certainty that the Tathāgata shares our welfare; we should now exert ourselves with fervent diligence to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas so that it shall never be severed."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
This Dharma-treasure is so subtle, wondrous, and profound that it cannot be believed or accepted by other sentient beings.

Those of inferior faith and resolve, those with overweening pride, those who practice evil views, those who practice with signs, those who practice with the notion of attainment, those ruined by the conceit of 'I,' those overcome by greed, hatred, and delusion, and those who have strayed from the path—all such as these are called 'other sentient beings,' and they are unable to believe and accept this Dharma-gate."
Ānanda, you should know this:

sentient beings of inferior inclination and resolve cannot feel reverence or affection for the wealth and treasures of a wheel-turning monarch; it is only toward the prince of the wheel-turning monarch that they give rise to such reverence and affection.
Ānanda, you should know this:

how could poor and lowly sentient beings ever covet the wheel-treasure, elephant-treasure, horse-treasure, jewel-treasure, woman-treasure, householder-treasure, and military-commander-treasure belonging to a universal monarch, as well as other various kinds of exquisite garments and precious riches such as mani-jewels, pearls, gold, silver, coral, and lapis lazuli?

If that poor person should happen to obtain it, he feels such shame that he cannot use it; even if he were to try to sell it, he does not know its value and accepts whatever meager price is offered. Alternatively, because he lacks the discernment to recognize the jewel, his mind becomes weary and contemptuous, and he casts it aside.
Ānanda, you should know that those impoverished people not only failed to understand the value of the jewel, but they were also ignorant of its name.
"In this same way, Ānanda!"

Only the sons of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who possess the Dharma-body; or those Śrāvakas who have already seen the truth and seek great Bodhi; or those Bodhisattvas who are sustained by true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends—only these are able to believe and accept this treasury of the Dharma Jewel.

They deeply revere and love the jewel of the Dharma that accords with the emptiness of the unattainable; they are also able to enjoy the principles and teachings of the truly pure Buddha-dharma, and they are able to practice all bodhisattva deeds characterized by non-attachment and non-clinging toward all phenomena.
Ānanda, you should know this!

How could those sentient beings who are poor and lowly—those who lack authentic hearing, those whose authentic hearing has been destroyed, and those who are deluded and sightless—possibly hope for the treasure-trove of the True Dharma?

Even if one should encounter it and obtain it, one does not know how to revere it; one treats other sentient beings with contempt and sells them, or, with a mind of aversion and disdain, abandons them.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!..."

Whether they be caṇḍālas, pukkāsas, various craftsmen, or others who live in poverty and engage in base livelihoods, they are ultimately unable to seek out precious jewels of high value; even if they should happen to obtain them, they do not use them for themselves, but instead sell them to others for a small price as soon as they acquire them, or else grow weary of them and simply cast them away.
Ānanda, you should know that the term "caṇḍālas" and so forth is a metaphor for all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as well as for their various disciples;

and those others who are poor, lowly, and live by ignoble means are metaphors for foolish worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). They are constantly submerged in the mire of evil views, always practicing with the notion of attainment, delighting in being bound by signs, and performing practices characterized by signs. Their every destination is a deviation from the path; they cannot joyfully seek the treasures of the noble Dharma. Even if they encounter them or obtain them, they are unable to utilize them—either deeply loathing and discarding them, or giving them away contemptuously to others.
Ānanda, you should know this!

If the sons of the Buddha practice the sphere of the Buddhas’ conduct, desiring to maintain the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and other boundless Buddha-dharmas so that they shall not be severed or exhausted, they seek to obtain such a profound treasury of the Dharma-jewels.

Regarding this profound treasury of the Dharma-jewels, they conceive of it as a true jewel; with deep-seated affection and respect, they are well able to utilize it, and they diligently guard it so that it shall not be destroyed or lost.
“Ānanda, you should know that a jackal cannot learn the lion’s roar; only a son born of the lion king can learn this roar.
Ānanda, you should know!”

The term "jackal" is a metaphor for those foolish ordinary beings with false views; they are certainly unable to diligently apply skillful means to learn the great lion’s roar of the Perfectly Enlightened One. Only the sons of the Buddha, born from the spontaneous wisdom of the Perfectly Enlightened One, are able to diligently learn the great lion’s roar of the Perfectly Enlightened One. In this way, such sons of the Buddha are well able to enjoy the unsurpassed Dharma-wealth of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to assemble such a pure assembly.
How marvelous!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to assemble such a most excellent assembly, a spontaneous assembly, an invincible assembly—an assembly that is immovable, unchanging, and undisturbed like a diamond—to teach the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"You have skillfully praised the merits of this assembly.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I cannot praise the merits of this assembly. Why is this?
This assembly has accomplished immeasurable and boundless merit; it is like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be fully described even by praise.”
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

This present assembly has accomplished boundless, pure, rare, and sublime virtues, such that even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, could not exhaustively praise them; how much less so other sentient beings!
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This present assembly was not gathered by the power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, nor did the Tathāgata desire to gather them for this assembly; rather, they have come to this gathering solely through the power of their own roots of goodness to hear my name.

Furthermore, this great assembly has not come for the sake of the Buddha, nor have they been summoned by the supernatural powers of the Tathāgata; rather, they have arrived here through the awakening power of their own roots of goodness.

Furthermore, it is the natural law that whenever the Buddha, the World-Honored One, intends to preach such profound and wondrous Dharma, there will certainly be these great Bodhisattvas who come from various Buddha-lands to assemble.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whether in the past, future, or present, or throughout the worlds of the ten directions, whenever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, intend to reveal the subtle, profound Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka that severs all doubts, there will invariably be such an assembly of immeasurable, boundless, and most supreme, pure merits.

If there is such an assembly of immeasurable, boundless, and most excellent pure merits, he will surely proclaim this subtle, profound, and wondrous Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, which severs all doubts.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra, saying:
“In various places, I have proclaimed the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, so that they may diligently practice and study it.”
What is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is the object of study for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
If one can reach far into the true nature of all phenomena, this is called the perfection of wisdom.
This Prajñāpāramitā is subtle, profound, and truly ineffable.

Now, in accordance with the sphere of your knowledge and through worldly words and phrases, I shall skillfully expound this profound Prajñāpāramitā, so that the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard it, may apply themselves with skillful diligence to its cultivation and study.
“Suvīra! The aggregate of form is not the perfection of wisdom; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also not the perfection of wisdom.
Apart from the aggregate of form there is no perfection of wisdom; apart from the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is also no perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!

The perfection of the aggregate of form is not identical to the aggregate of form; likewise, the perfection of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not identical to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
As it is with the further shore of the aggregate of form, so too is the aggregate of form;

as it is with the further shores of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, so too are the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"O Suvīra! In this context, that the *pāramitā* of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is not itself the aggregate of form is said to be the dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) from the aggregate of form;

likewise, that the *pāramitā* of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not itself the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is said to be the dissociation from the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

When it is said that "as the other shore of the aggregate of form is, so too is the aggregate of form," this explains that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregate of form is such, meaning that the aggregate of form’s *yathāvadbhāva* (the state as it is) and its fundamental nature are unapprehendable.

When it is said that "as the other shores of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are, so too are the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," this explains that the intrinsic natures of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are such, meaning that the *yathāvadbhāva* and fundamental natures of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable.
Just as the suchness and intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form cannot be apprehended, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise;

just as the suchness and intrinsic nature of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
“Suvīra! The eye-base itself is not the perfection of wisdom; likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are also not the perfection of wisdom.
Apart from the eye-base, there is no perfection of wisdom; apart from the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases, there is also no perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!

The perfection of the eye-base is not identical to the eye-base; likewise, the perfection of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases is also not identical to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.
As it is with the other shore of the eye-base, so too is the eye-base;
as it is with the other shore of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases, so too are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.
“Suvīra! In this context, that which is the ‘other shore’ of the eye-base is not the eye-base itself; this is said to be the dissociation from the eye-base.

That which is the ‘other shore’ of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases is likewise not the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases themselves; this is said to be the dissociation from the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.”

"Just as the other shore of the eye-base is so, the eye-base is likewise" means that the intrinsic nature of the eye-base is thus described; it means that the suchness and the fundamental nature of the eye-base are unapprehendable.

"Just as the other shore of the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base is so, the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base are likewise" means that the intrinsic nature of the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base is thus described; it means that the suchness and the fundamental nature of the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base are unapprehendable.
Just as the suchness and intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye are unapprehendable, so too should one know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise;
just as the suchness and intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unapprehendable, so too should one know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
“Suvīra! The sense-base of form is not the perfection of wisdom; likewise, the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are also not the perfection of wisdom.
Apart from the sense-base of form, there is no perfection of wisdom; apart from the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, there is also no perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!

The further shore of the sphere of form is not itself the sphere of form; likewise, the further shore of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is not itself the sphere of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
As it is with the other shore of the sense-base of form, so too is the sense-base of form;
as it is with the other shores of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, so too are the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
"O Suvīra! In this context, that which is the 'other shore' of the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not itself the sphere of form; this is said to be the dissociation from the sphere of form.

Likewise, that which is the 'other shore' of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is not itself the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects; this is said to be the dissociation from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects."

The sense base of the eye is neither a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay nor a phenomenon not subject to transformation and decay; the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay nor phenomena not subject to transformation and decay.
"In this way, the six internal sense bases are neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay, nor are they phenomena not subject to transformation and decay;
this is called the perfection of wisdom, O Well-Valiant One!"

The sphere of visible form is neither a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay nor a phenomenon not subject to transformation and decay; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay nor phenomena not subject to transformation and decay.
In this way, the six external sense bases are neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay nor phenomena not subject to transformation and decay; this is called the perfection of wisdom.

The eye-element is neither a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay, nor is it a phenomenon not subject to transformation and decay; the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are likewise neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay, nor phenomena not subject to transformation and decay.
"In this way, the six internal elements are neither subject to transformation nor not subject to transformation; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
O Well-Valiant One!"

The form realm is neither a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay nor a phenomenon not subject to transformation and decay; likewise, the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects are neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay nor phenomena not subject to transformation and decay.

In this way, the six external elements are neither phenomena subject to transformation and decay, nor are they phenomena not subject to transformation and decay; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!

The eye-consciousness element is neither a dharma subject to transformation and decay nor a dharma not subject to transformation and decay; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise neither dharmas subject to transformation and decay nor dharmas not subject to transformation and decay.
In this way, the six consciousness elements are neither subject to transformation and decay nor are they not subject to transformation and decay; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
All phenomena are neither subject to transformation and decay nor not subject to transformation and decay.
That all phenomena are neither subject to transformation and decay nor not subject to transformation and decay is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

The aggregate of form is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure."

Thus, these five aggregates are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The eye-base is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure.”

Thus, the six internal sense bases are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, and neither pure nor impure; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The sphere of form is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure. The spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure.”

“Suvīra! All phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure.”

In this way, all phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, and neither pure nor impure; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

The aggregate of form is neither a phenomenon characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion, nor is it a phenomenon free from lust, hatred, and delusion. The aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise neither phenomena characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion, nor are they phenomena free from lust, hatred, and delusion."

Thus, these five aggregates are neither dharmas characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they dharmas free from greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The sense-base of the eye is neither a phenomenon characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion, nor is it a phenomenon free from lust, hatred, and delusion. The sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise neither phenomena characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion, nor are they phenomena free from lust, hatred, and delusion.”

Thus, the six internal sense bases are neither phenomena characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they phenomena free from greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The eye-element is neither a dharma characterized by desire, hatred, and delusion, nor is it a dharma free from desire, hatred, and delusion. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are likewise neither dharmas characterized by desire, hatred, and delusion, nor are they dharmas free from desire, hatred, and delusion.”

Thus, the six internal elements are neither dharmas characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they dharmas free from greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

"Furthermore, Suvīra! The aggregate of form is not an agent, nor does it cause another to act; it is not an originator, nor does it cause another to originate; it is not a cognizer, nor does it cause another to cognize; it is not an experiencer, nor does it cause another to experience; it is neither a knower nor a seer.

The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not agents, nor do they cause others to act; they are not originators, nor do they cause others to originate; they are not cognizers, nor do they cause others to cognize; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause others to experience; they are neither knowers nor seers."

Thus, these five aggregates are not an agent nor one who causes another to act; they are not an originator nor one who causes origination; they are not a cognizer nor one who causes cognition; they are not an experiencer nor one who causes experience; they are neither knowers nor seers—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The sense base of the eye is not an agent, nor does it cause an agent; it is not an originator, nor does it cause origination; it is not a cognizer, nor does it cause cognition; it is not an experiencer, nor does it cause experience; it is neither a knower nor a seer.

The sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise not agents, nor do they cause agents; they are not originators, nor do they cause origination; they are not cognizers, nor do they cause cognition; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers.”

This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The sense-sphere of form is not an agent, nor does it cause an agent; it is not an originator, nor does it cause origination; it is not a cognizer, nor does it cause cognition; it is not an experiencer, nor does it cause experience; it is neither a knower nor a seer.

The sense-spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise not agents, nor do they cause agents; they are not originators, nor do they cause origination; they are not cognizers, nor do they cause cognition; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers.”

Thus, the six external sense bases are not an agent, nor do they cause an agent; they are not an originator, nor do they cause origination; they are not a perceiver, nor do they cause perception; they are not an experiencer, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The eye-element is not an agent, nor does it cause an agent; it is not an originator, nor does it equally originate; it is not a cognizer, nor does it cause cognition; it is not an experiencer, nor does it cause experience; it is neither a knower nor a seer.

The ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are likewise not agents, nor do they cause agents; they are not originators, nor do they equally originate; they are not cognizers, nor do they cause cognition; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers.”

Thus, these six internal elements are not an agent, nor do they cause an agent; they are not an originator, nor do they cause origination; they are not a cognizer, nor do they cause cognition; they are not an experiencer, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! The realm of form is not an agent, nor does it cause an agent; it is not an originator, nor does it cause origination; it is not a perceiver, nor does it cause perception; it is not an experiencer, nor does it cause experience; it is neither a knower nor a seer.

The realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise not agents, nor do they cause agents; they are not originators, nor do they cause origination; they are not perceivers, nor do they cause perception; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers.”

Thus, these six external elements are not an agent, nor do they cause an agent; they are not an originator, nor do they cause origination; they are not a perceiver, nor do they cause perception; they are not an experiencer, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! The eye-consciousness element is not an agent, nor does it cause an agent; it is not an originator, nor does it cause origination; it is not a perceiver, nor does it cause perception; it is not an experiencer, nor does it cause experience; it is neither a knower nor a seer.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise not agents, nor do they cause agents; they are not originators, nor do they cause origination; they are not perceivers, nor do they cause perception; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause experience; they are neither knowers nor seers.”

This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Suvīra! All phenomena are not agents, nor do they cause others to act; they are not originators, nor do they cause others to originate; they are not perceivers, nor do they cause others to perceive; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause others to experience; they are neither knowers nor seers.”

In this way, all phenomena are not agents, nor do they cause others to act; they are not originators, nor do they cause others to originate; they are not perceivers, nor do they cause others to perceive; they are not experiencers, nor do they cause others to experience; they are neither knowers nor seers—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

The aggregate of form is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite."
These five aggregates are neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"O Well-Valiant One!

The eye-base is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base are likewise neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite.
"In this way, the six internal sense bases are neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; this is called the perfection of wisdom, O Well-Valiant One!"

The sphere of form is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite.
In this way, the six external sense bases are neither annihilated nor permanent, neither finite nor infinite; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"O Well-Valiant One!

The eye-element is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; likewise, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are also neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite.
In this way, the six internal elements are neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"O Well-Valiant One!

The realm of form is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; likewise, the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite.
In this way, the six external elements are neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "O Suvīra!

The eye-consciousness element is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite; the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise neither annihilated nor eternal, neither finite nor infinite.

"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The aggregate of form is neither a pursuit of views nor the abandonment of views; it is neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases are likewise neither the pursuit of views nor the abandonment of the pursuit of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.

Thus, the six internal sense bases are neither the pursuit of views nor the abandonment of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

The sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither paths of views nor the abandonment of paths of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.”

Thus, the six external sense bases are neither the pursuit of views nor the abandonment of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Suvīra! The eye-element is neither a sphere of views nor the abandonment of a sphere of views; it is neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.
The ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements are likewise neither spheres of views nor the abandonment of a sphere of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.”

Thus, these six internal elements are neither the pursuit of views nor the abandonment of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Suvīra! The realm of form is neither a path of views nor severed by views; it is neither craving nor severed by craving.
The realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither paths of views nor severed by views; they are neither craving nor severed by craving.”

In this way, the six external elements are neither the pursuit of views nor the abandonment of views, neither craving nor the abandonment of craving; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Suvīra! The eye-consciousness element is neither a path of views nor the abandonment of a path of views; it is neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise neither paths of views nor the abandonment of paths of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.”

Thus, the six consciousness elements are neither the pursuit of views nor the abandonment of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Suvīra! All phenomena are neither views nor the abandonment of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.
In this way, all phenomena being neither views nor the abandonment of views, and neither craving nor the abandonment of craving—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The aggregate of form is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
Thus, these five aggregates are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"O Well-Valiant One!
The sense base of the eye is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
In this way, the six internal sense bases are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"O Well-Valiant One!
The sense base of form is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
In this way, the six external sense bases are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"O Well-Valiant One!
The eye-element is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are likewise neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
In this way, the six internal elements are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"O Well-Valiant One!
The element of form is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are likewise neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
Thus, the six external elements are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"O Well-Valiant One!
The eye-consciousness element is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
In this way, the six consciousness elements are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
All phenomena are neither wholesome nor unwholesome."
In this way, all phenomena are neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Great *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, Fascicle 595, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Four of the Sixteenth Division on the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "Furthermore, Su-vīra!..."

The five aggregates cannot be established as having going or coming, or staying or not staying; likewise, the twelve bases and eighteen elements, etc., also cannot be established as having going or coming, or staying or not staying.
Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are without going and without coming, without abiding and without non-abiding; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

It cannot be established that the five aggregates have a distance or a further shore; likewise, it cannot be established that the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth, have a distance or a further shore."
Thus, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements have neither a far shore nor a near shore; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!..."

One cannot designate that within the five aggregates there is craving, aversion, fear, or delusion; nor can one designate that within the twelve bases or the eighteen elements, etc., there is craving, aversion, fear, or delusion.
Thus, when the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are without craving, without anger, without fear, and without delusion, this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!..."

The five aggregates are without giving and without taking, without observing precepts and without violating precepts, without patience and without impatience, without diligence and without laziness, without meditative concentration and without mental distraction, and without sublime wisdom and without false wisdom. The twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise without giving and without taking, without observing precepts and without violating precepts, without patience and without impatience, without diligence and without laziness, without meditative concentration and without mental distraction, and without sublime wisdom and without false wisdom.

Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are without giving and without taking; there is no observance of precepts and no violation of precepts; no patience and no impatience; no diligence and no indolence; no meditative concentration and no mental distraction; no sublime wisdom and no false wisdom—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The five aggregates are neither inverted nor non-inverted; the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth are likewise neither inverted nor non-inverted."
Thus, that the aggregates, bases, and elements are neither inverted nor non-inverted is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!..."

The five aggregates lack the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and path factors; likewise, the twelve bases and eighteen elements also lack the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and path factors.

Thus, the absence of mental fixation regarding the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, as well as the applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and factors of the path—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The five aggregates are without ignorance and without liberation; the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth are likewise without ignorance and without liberation."
Thus, when the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are without ignorance and without liberation, this is called the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvīra!

The five aggregates have no meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, or attainments; the twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, likewise have no meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, or attainments.
Thus, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, being devoid of dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti, are called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra! The five aggregates are neither finite nor infinite;

they possess neither supernormal powers nor the absence of supernormal powers. The twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise neither finite nor infinite; they possess neither supernormal powers nor the absence of supernormal powers."

Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are neither finite nor infinite; they are neither supernatural powers nor the absence of supernatural powers—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

The five aggregates are neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized by marks nor markless, neither aspirational nor non-aspirational. The twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized by marks nor markless, neither aspirational nor non-aspirational."

Thus, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized by marks nor markless, and neither characterized by aspiration nor aspirationless; this is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! The five aggregates are neither conditioned nor unconditioned;

they are neither with outflows nor without outflows; they are neither mundane nor supramundane; they are neither bound nor liberated. Likewise, the twelve bases and the eighteen elements, etc., are neither conditioned nor unconditioned; they are neither with outflows nor without outflows; they are neither mundane nor supramundane; they are neither bound nor liberated."

Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither with outflows nor without outflows; neither mundane nor supramundane; neither bound nor liberated. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

The five aggregates are neither with attachment nor without attachment, neither with wisdom nor without wisdom; the twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise neither with attachment nor without attachment, neither with wisdom nor without wisdom."
Thus, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are neither with attachment nor without attachment, neither with wisdom nor without wisdom; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

The five aggregates are without grasping, without fluctuation, and without conceptual proliferation; likewise, the twelve bases and the eighteen elements are also without grasping, without fluctuation, and without conceptual proliferation."
Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements, being without grasping, without fluctuation, and without conceptual proliferation—this is called the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
The five aggregates are neither with perception nor without perception; the twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise neither with perception nor without perception.
That these aggregates, bases, and elements are neither with perception nor without perception is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The five aggregates are neither quiescent nor non-quiescent; the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise neither quiescent nor non-quiescent."
Thus, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are neither tranquil nor non-tranquil; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
The five aggregates are neither nirvāṇa nor non-nirvāṇa; the twelve bases and eighteen elements, and so forth, are likewise neither nirvāṇa nor non-nirvāṇa.
That these aggregates, bases, and elements are neither nirvāṇa nor non-nirvāṇa is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
That which is described as being comprised within the arising of the five aggregates is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Rather, the suchness (tathatā), non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is (yathāvadbhāvikatā) that is comprised within the arising of the five aggregates as they are described—that is called the perfection of wisdom."
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, as they are subsumed under origination, are not what is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Rather, the suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity, immutability, and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) that are subsumed within those twelve bases, eighteen elements, and so forth as they arise—this is what is called the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
That which is described as being comprised within the arising of dependent origination is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Rather, the suchness (tathatā), non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is (yathāvadbhāvikatā) that are comprised within the arising of dependent origination as it is described—this is called the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is described as being comprised of the arising of perversions is not called the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Rather, the suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity, immutability, and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) that are comprised within what is described as the arising of perversions—this is called the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is described as being comprised by the arising of the various hindrances is not called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Rather, the suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) that is comprised within the arising of the various hindrances—this is called the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
That which is described as being comprised of the arising of the thirty-six modes of craving is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Rather, the suchness (tathatā), non-falsity, immutability, and the nature of things as they are (yathāvadbhāvikatā) that are comprised within the arising of those thirty-six modes of craving—this is called the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
That which is comprised by the arising of the sixty-two views as they have been described is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Rather, the suchness (tathatā), the non-falsity, the immutability, and the suchness-as-it-is (yathāvadbhāva) of all that is comprised by the arising of the sixty-two views as they have been described—this is called the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
What has been described as dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

The suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is of all the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments that have been taught—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is called the four immeasurables and the five supernormal powers is not what is meant by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Rather, the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, and the suchness-as-it-is of those four immeasurables and five supernormal powers—this is what is called the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is spoken of as being comprised of all mundane roots of virtue and so forth, and as being comprised of their arising, is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

The suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is (yathāvadbhāvikatā) encompassed by all the roots of goodness and other phenomena of the conditioned world that arise as described—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

That which is spoken of as being comprised by the arising of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the branches of the path is not what is called the perfection of wisdom."

The suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is (yathāvad-bhāvikatā) comprised within the arising of the mindfulness establishments, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path that have been taught—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is spoken of as the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Rather, the suchness, the non-falsity, the unchanging nature, and the suchness-as-it-is of these noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—this is called the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

That which is described as the purity of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation is not what is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

The suchness, non-falsity, immutability, and suchness-as-it-is of the purity of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation that have been taught—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
Those supramundane, non-reliant, and untainted dharmas that are said to be subsumed within the unconditioned are not what is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

The suchness, non-falsity, non-alterability, and suchness-as-it-is of all supramundane, supportless, untainted dharmas subsumed within the unconditioned as described—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The teachings on emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and the unconditioned are not what is called the perfection of wisdom."

The suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, and suchness-as-it-is of all that is spoken of as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and the unconditioned—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
That which is explained as liberation, detachment, cessation, and nirvāṇa is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Rather, the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, and the suchness-as-it-is of that which is explained as liberation, detachment, cessation, and nirvāṇa—this is called the perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
This perfection of wisdom is not subsumed within the aggregate of form, nor is it subsumed within the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It is not subsumed under the sense-base of the eye, nor is it subsumed under the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
it is not subsumed under the sense-base of form, nor is it subsumed under the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena;
it is not subsumed under the element of the eye, nor is it subsumed under the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It is not subsumed under the realm of form, nor is it subsumed under the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects;
it is not subsumed under the realm of eye-consciousness, nor is it subsumed under the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness;
it is not subsumed under the earth element, nor is it subsumed under the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness.
It is not comprised within the desire realm, nor is it comprised within the form or formless realms;
it is not comprised within the conditioned, nor is it comprised within the unconditioned;
it is not comprised within the mundane, nor is it comprised within the supramundane.
It is not comprised within the outflows, nor is it comprised within that which is without outflows;
it is not comprised within wholesome dharmas, nor is it comprised within those that are not wholesome dharmas;
it is not comprised within the realm of sentient beings, nor is it comprised within that which is not the realm of sentient beings.
Nor is there a separate *prajñāpāramitā* that exists apart from or is distinct from such dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhavyūha,
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is neither subsumed by these various dharmas, nor is it not subsumed by them.
The suchness, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, and the suchness-as-it-is of all phenomena—both those so included and those not so included—is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Suvīra! Of what is ‘tathatā’ (suchness) a designation? Suvīra!”
Suchness (*tathatā*) refers to the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is neither that which is attained by foolish ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), nor is it different from that.

However, the nature of all phenomena is as it is seen by the Tathāgatas, their disciples, and the Bodhisattvas; because this principle of the nature of phenomena is real, eternal, and unchanging, it is called Suchness. This very Suchness is what is spoken of as the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the Bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) neither increases nor decreases in regard to all phenomena;
it is neither joined nor separated, neither deficient nor complete, neither beneficial nor harmful, and it does not undergo transference."
It is not an entrance; it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa,
neither accumulation nor disappearance, neither with signs nor signless,
neither equal nor unequal, neither conventional nor ultimate, nor is it pleasure.
It is not suffering; it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is neither pure nor impure;
it is neither self nor non-self; it is neither true nor false; it is neither an agent nor an instrument of action;
it is neither receptacle nor non-receptacle; it is neither conviction nor lack of conviction; it is not self...
It is nature, yet not non-nature; it is neither death nor birth, neither birth nor death;
it is neither emergence nor disappearance, neither continuity nor discontinuity; it is neither conjunction nor non-conjunction;
it is neither possessed of greed nor free from greed, neither possessed of hatred nor free from hatred, and neither possessed of delusion...
It is not apart from delusion; it is neither inverted nor non-inverted; it has neither an object of perception nor no object of perception;
it is neither subject to exhaustion nor inexhaustible; it possesses neither wisdom nor lacks wisdom;
it is neither of low nature nor of high nature; it is neither beneficent nor non-beneficent; it neither departs nor...
Returning again, it is neither of the nature of existence nor of the nature of non-existence;
neither affection nor aversion; neither clarity nor darkness; neither indolence nor diligence; neither empty nor not empty;
neither with signs nor signless; neither with aspiration nor without aspiration; neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
It is conditioned, neither obscured nor unobscured, neither ignorance nor liberation,
neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, neither nirvana nor non-nirvana,
neither according to principle nor contrary to principle, neither thorough knowledge nor lack of thorough knowledge, and not renunciation.
It is neither non-renunciation, nor discipline, nor lack of discipline; neither observance of precepts, nor violation of precepts;
neither distraction, nor non-distraction; neither sublime wisdom, nor unwholesome wisdom;
neither consciousness, nor non-consciousness; neither abiding, nor non-abiding; neither of the same class, nor of a different class.
It is neither existent nor non-existent; neither attained nor unattained;
neither realization nor non-realization; neither actualization nor non-actualization; neither penetration nor non-penetration.
The profound perfection of wisdom does not manifest before one for the sake of these various kinds of activities.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as a person in a dream speaks of the various natures of what they see within that dream, so too the natures of those spoken-of dream-objects do not exist at all. Why is this?
"O Suvīra! Even a dream does not exist; how much less could there be a self-nature of a dream-object that can be described!
In this same way, although this Prajñāpāramitā is conventionally said to have various self-natures, this Prajñāpāramitā in reality has no self-nature that can be found or proclaimed."
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Just as a dream does not manifest in order to display any phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not manifest in order to display any phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
It is like a phantom person describing the various natures of what is seen by a phantom; such described natures of the illusory objects do not exist at all."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Even illusion does not exist; how much less can one speak of a self-nature of illusory objects!

Thus, although this prajñāpāramitā is conventionally described as having various intrinsic natures, in reality, no intrinsic nature of this prajñāpāramitā can be found that is capable of being proclaimed.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as an illusion does not manifest for the purpose of producing phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the purpose of producing phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

Just as a person who is like a reflection or a shadow might proclaim the various intrinsic natures of reflections and shadows, yet those proclaimed intrinsic natures of reflections and shadows do not exist at all."
Why is this? O Well-Valiant One!
Since even a shadow does not exist, how much less could there be a self-nature of light and shadow that can be described!
Thus, although this perfection of wisdom is conventionally described as having various intrinsic natures, in reality, no intrinsic nature of this perfection of wisdom can be found or proclaimed.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as a reflection does not appear before one for the purpose of displaying all phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom does not appear before one for the purpose of displaying all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Just as a person might proclaim the various intrinsic natures of a mirage, yet those proclaimed intrinsic natures of the mirage do not exist at all."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Even a flame does not exist; how much less can one speak of a self-nature of a mirage!

Thus, although this prajñāpāramitā is conventionally described as having various intrinsic natures, in reality, no intrinsic nature of this prajñāpāramitā can be found that is capable of being proclaimed.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Just as a mirage does not appear before one for the purpose of displaying all phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom does not appear before one for the purpose of displaying all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
It is like a person staying within a mountain valley or similar place who hears the sound of an echo but sees nothing at all; yet when they speak themselves, they hear that sound as well."

Thus, although various words and phrases of this Prajñāpāramitā are heard, the dharmas that are heard have no intrinsic nature whatsoever; they exist only as hearing and understanding at the time of their being spoken.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Just as an echo does not appear before one in order to manifest all phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom does not appear before one in order to manifest all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
It is as if someone were to see various masses of foam and then describe the intrinsic nature of those masses of foam;
yet that described intrinsic nature of the masses of foam cannot be found at all, whether internally or externally.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Even that which is called a "mass of foam" does not exist as a reality; how much less could there be an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that can be described!
Thus, although this perfection of wisdom is conventionally described as having various intrinsic natures, in reality, no intrinsic nature of this perfection of wisdom can be found or proclaimed.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as a mass of foam does not appear for the sake of producing phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom does not appear for the sake of producing phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
It is like a person who sees a bubble arise and then speaks of the various intrinsic natures of that bubble; yet, those intrinsic natures of the bubble spoken of do not exist at all."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Even that which is described as a bubble does not exist in reality; how much less could there be an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that can be proclaimed!

Thus, although this perfection of wisdom is conventionally described as having various intrinsic natures, in reality, no intrinsic nature of this perfection of wisdom can be found that is capable of being proclaimed.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as a bubble does not appear for the purpose of bringing forth phenomena, so too the perfection of wisdom does not appear for the purpose of bringing forth phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

Just as when a person peels away the stalks of a plantain tree, although no core substance can be found, there is still the utility of its leaves; so too, although this Prajñāpāramitā has no true reality, it possesses the utility of being taught."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
It is as if, for example, there were a person who, wishing to demonstrate the great expanse of space, might say something to that effect, yet the great expanse of space cannot be demonstrated.
Thus, although this Prajñāpāramitā is taught for the purpose of being revealed, this Prajñāpāramitā cannot be revealed.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
Just as the great expanse of space may be indicated by various verbal expressions, yet within that great expanse of space no real phenomenon can be found to be indicated."
Thus, although the perfection of wisdom is revealed through various modes of expression, this perfection of wisdom has no real dharma that can be found to be revealed.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

For example, although shadows and light can be described, there is no substantial dharma therein that can be grasped; yet, while there is nothing to be grasped, they nevertheless manifest and illuminate."

Thus, although this Prajñāpāramitā is variously explained through provisional words and phrases, there is no real dharma to be grasped; yet, while there is nothing to be grasped, it illuminates all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Just as a maṇi jewel possesses great radiance, yet this radiance cannot be apprehended as being either internal or external;
so too, although the prajñāpāramitā can illuminate the nature of all phenomena, neither its interior nor its exterior can be apprehended at all."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
For example, although the light of a lamp does not abide for even a moment, it is able to illuminate so that those with eyes may behold various forms.
Thus, although this Prajñāpāramitā abides nowhere among all phenomena, it is able to illuminate and comprehend them, enabling all noble ones to perceive the true nature of dharmas.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary!
Although the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha teaches the Prajñāpāramitā, he teaches that the Prajñāpāramitā is not the perfected reality (pariniṣpanna).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna*). Why is this?

“Śāriputra! Because the five aggregates are not truly established, I say that the perfection of wisdom is not truly established; because the twelve bases and eighteen elements are also not truly established, I say that the perfection of wisdom is not truly established.”

“Śāriputra! Because ignorance is not truly established (*pariniṣpanna*), I say that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not truly established. Because volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are also not truly established, I say that the perfection of wisdom is not truly established.”

“Śāriputra! Because permanence and impermanence, pleasure and suffering, self and non-self, purity and impurity, tranquility and non-tranquility, inversion and non-inversion, the various veils and views, superimposition and denial, arising and ceasing, abiding and changing, and emergence and disappearance are not ultimately established (*pariniṣpanna*), I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not ultimately established.”

“Śāriputra! Because the self, sentient being, life-principle, creature, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, youth, agent, instigator, arouser, co-arouser, experiencer, one who causes experience, knower, one who causes knowing, seer, and one who causes seeing are not established by way of their own nature (*pariniṣpanna*), I say that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not established by way of its own nature.”

“Śāriputra! Because dharmas such as truth and falsehood, going and returning, being seen and not being seen, internal and external, and so forth, are not perfectly established (*pariniṣpanna*), I say that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not perfectly established.”

"Śāriputra! Because the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness; the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; and the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena are not perfectly established, I say that the perfection of wisdom is not perfectly established."

“Śāriputra! Because the maturation of the fruit of karma, the causes and conditions of annihilation and permanence, and the three periods of the three times are not perfectly established, I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not perfectly established.”

“Śāriputra! Because generosity and stinginess, ethical discipline and transgression of discipline, patience and malice, diligence and laziness, meditative concentration and distraction, and sublime wisdom and false wisdom—along with mind, mentation, and consciousness; the uninterrupted cycle of death and birth; and both affliction and purification—are not truly established (*pariniṣpanna*), I say that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not truly established.”

“Śāriputra! Because the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, the factors of the path, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, the attainments, the immeasurables, the supernormal powers, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are not truly established, I say that the perfection of wisdom is not truly established.”

“Śāriputra! Because virtue and non-virtue, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, the mundane and the supramundane, the faulty and the faultless, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the determinate and the indeterminate, the black and the white, and the inferior, mediocre, and sublime greed, hatred, and delusion—along with their opposites—are not truly established, I say that the Prajñāpāramitā is not truly established.”

“Śāriputra! Because seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; reliance and grasping; abiding; discursive thought and investigation; objects of focus; deception and guile; envy and stinginess; conjunction; the two characteristics; non-arising; non-activity; tranquility and insight; clear understanding; exhaustion and detachment; the cessation of defilement; relinquishment—all these depend upon the conventional and not the ultimate perfected nature—I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not the perfected nature.”

“Śāriputra! Because the dharmas of the stage of the śrāvaka, the dharmas of the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the knowledge of all-knowledge, unattached knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, unequaled knowledge, the great vows of a bodhisattva, the perfection of the śrāvaka, the perfection of the pratyekabuddha, and the knowledge of all dharmas—immeasurable, boundless, and unequaled—are not established as truly real due to the non-perception of all dharmas as they truly are, I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not established as truly real.”

"Śāriputra! Because that which is cool, real, tranquil, utterly tranquil, and supremely tranquil is not established by way of its own nature (*pariniṣpanna*), I say that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not established by way of its own nature."

“Śāriputra! Because the maturation of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-fields, the perfection of the marks and signs, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth, are not established by way of their own nature, I say that the Prajñāpāramitā is not established by way of its own nature.”

“Śāriputra! Because everything from nirvāṇa down to all phenomena—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neither—is not the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), I say that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is not the thoroughly established nature.”

“Śāriputra! Just as the great void is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, devoid of intrinsic nature, and not established by way of ultimate reality, so too is this perfection of wisdom formless, invisible, non-obstructive, devoid of intrinsic nature, and not established by way of ultimate reality.”

“Śāriputra! For example, although a rainbow manifests various kinds of wondrous colors, it lacks even a single reality; likewise, although this Prajñāpāramitā is displayed through various provisional verbal signs, that which is displayed has no intrinsic nature to be found.”

“Śāriputra! For example, although space may be measured with various kinds of cubits and spans, one has never seen even as much as five finger-breadths of it that is established by way of its own nature (*pariniṣpanna*). In the same way, although this *prajñāpāramitā* is displayed through various provisional verbal expressions, one has never seen even the slightest essence within it that is established by way of its own nature.”
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly difficult to perceive.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because that which sees cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra said:
“Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly difficult to realize.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”
"Because the one who awakens cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra said, "In this way,
the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be demonstrated."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
For it is able to manifest that dharmas are unattainable.”
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom has nothing to be revealed.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! It is not for the sake of manifesting the dharma before one's eyes.
Śāriputra said:
“Thus, this perfection of wisdom has non-existence as its nature.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has as its intrinsic nature the absence of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
it has as its intrinsic nature the absence of self-nature in all perversions (*viparyāsa*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), views (*dṛṣṭigata*), and tendencies of craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*);

and it has as its intrinsic nature the absence of self-nature in the self (*ātman*), sentient being (*sattva*), life-principle (*jīva*), living being (*jantu*), nourisher (*poṣa*), and person (*pudgala*).
Because the person (*pudgala*), the mind-born (*manuja*), the youth (*māṇava*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the instigator of action (*kāraka*), the originator (*utthāpaka*),
the co-originator (*samutthāpaka*), the experiencer (*vedaka*), the instigator of experience (*vedayitṛ*), the knower (*jñātṛ*), the instigator of knowledge (*jñāpayitṛ*), the seer (*draṣṭṛ*),
and the instigator of seeing (*darśayitṛ*) have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, [they are not established] by means of earth, water, fire, ...

Because the elements of wind, space, and consciousness have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; because the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
because the realms of desire, form, and formlessness have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
and because generosity, stinginess, ethical discipline, transgression of precepts, patience, and anger [have non-existence as their intrinsic nature].
Because diligence, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, sublime wisdom, and faulty wisdom have non-existence as their intrinsic nature,
and because the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, calm abiding and insight, the immeasurables, the supernormal powers, the meditative concentrations,
the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative attainments, and clear knowledge and liberation have non-existence as their intrinsic nature—
Because its intrinsic nature is the exhaustion of defilements, their separation, and their cessation as being without intrinsic nature;
because its intrinsic nature is the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of cessation, and the absence of intrinsic nature in nirvāṇa;

and because its intrinsic nature consists of the stages of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the Buddha, the conventional knowledge and vision, the ultimate knowledge and vision, and unattached knowledge.
"Because all dharmas, such as the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), have the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as their essential nature. Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) does not appear for the sake of accomplishing or destroying dharmas."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest for the sake of accomplishing or arising phenomena, nor for the sake of destroying or annihilating the phenomenon of non-self.”
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of conditions or as a means.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because all phenomena are not objects of cognition, there is no such phenomenon that can serve as an object for the arousal of the perfection of wisdom."
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom manifests before one without increasing or decreasing any phenomena.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be increased or decreased.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the purpose of transcending all phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be transcended.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests not for the sake of diminishing or augmenting any dharma."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
This is because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive any dharma that can be diminished or increased.”
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of joining with or separating from any phenomena.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because in the profound perfection of wisdom, no dharma is seen that can be joined or separated.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of grasping, carrying away, or disciplining dharmas.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive any dharma that can be grasped and taken away for the purpose of disciplining.
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests not because it creates enmity or favor toward dharmas.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive any dharma upon which one could bestow favor or inflict harm.”
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of the arising or non-arising of phenomena.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be brought into being, for there is no such thing as arising.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom does not manifest for the sake of even the slightest association or dissociation with phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be either associated with or dissociated from.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests not for the sake of having even the slightest co-dwelling or non-co-dwelling with dharmas."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive any dharma with which one might dwell together or with which one might not dwell together.”
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not appear for the sake of the arising or non-arising of any phenomenon."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be brought into arising or not brought into arising.”
Śāriputra said:
"This Prajñāpāramitā does not circulate within phenomena, nor does it manifest for the sake of not circulating."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be made to flow or not to flow.”
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, this prajñāpāramitā does not manifest for the sake of the activity or the instruments of even the slightest dharma.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, not even the slightest dharma is perceived that could serve as an agent for its activity or as an instrument manifested before it."
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of realizing the equality or inequality of phenomena."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that could be realized as either equal or unequal.”
Śāriputra said:
"This Prajñāpāramitā does not manifest for the sake of grasping or abandoning any phenomena.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be grasped or abandoned.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of performing any action regarding phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is perceived that could have any activity therein.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* is most profound."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
For what reason? Because—"
Śāriputra! Because the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound;
because the factors of dependent origination are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound.
Because inversion, the five hindrances, the tendencies of views, and the modes of craving are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound;
because the self, sentient beings, and so forth are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound;
because conceptual proliferation and non-proliferation are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound.

Because generosity, stinginess, ethical discipline, violation of ethical discipline, patience, anger, diligence, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, sublime wisdom, and corrupt wisdom are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound;

because the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound;
and because suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are profound, this perfection of wisdom is most profound.
Because the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are equal and profoundly deep, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound;
because the various powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are profoundly deep, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound;
and because the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are profoundly deep, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound.

Because the knowledge of all Buddha-dharmas—unattached throughout the three periods of time, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of non-action, and the knowledge of detachment from defilement—is profound, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound;
because the knowledge that abandons all hindrances is profound, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
