Just as the great ocean is deep and vast beyond measure, so too is this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) deep and vast beyond measure."
Regarding its profundity and vastness: it is that which is realized through boundless merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, just as the great ocean is immeasurable and boundless, being the accumulation of great jewels and various treasures, so too is this Prajñāpāramitā immeasurable and boundless, being the accumulation of the jewels of the Great Dharma and all dharmas."
Śāriputra said:
“This Prajñāpāramitā does not manifest for the purpose of revealing all dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because this profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be displayed, it manifests.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of having knowledge or lacking knowledge regarding phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is!
“Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, not even the slightest dharma can be perceived that could be designated as having wisdom or lacking wisdom.
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest for the sake of guarding or concealing dharmas.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive any dharma that can be guarded or concealed."
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not appear for the sake of grasping at any phenomenon.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be grasped.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom manifests without relying upon any phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can serve as a basis for reliance.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests not for the sake of grasping or storing dharmas."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be grasped or stored."
Śāriputra said:
“This Prajñāpāramitā does not manifest for the sake of grasping at any phenomenon.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive any dharma that can give rise to attachment.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of attachment to any phenomena.
The Buddha said, "It is so!"
"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive any dharma upon which one might become attached.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests for the purpose of not abiding in any dharma."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā does not perceive any dharma with which it could coexist."
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of the continuity or the interruption of dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be continued or severed.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom manifests because it does not give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion toward phenomena, and because it is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
The Buddha said: "So it is!"
“Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no phenomenon is seen that gives rise to greed, hatred, or delusion, nor that is free from greed, hatred, or delusion.
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest for the sake of producing a knower or causing something to be known regarding phenomena.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can arise as a knower or that causes one to know.”
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of perceiving the intrinsic nature or the non-intrinsic nature of phenomena."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive any dharma that can be known as having either an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or a non-intrinsic nature."
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not manifest for the sake of purifying phenomena.
The Buddha said:
“It is so! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be purified.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The profound perfection of wisdom is pure by its very nature.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”
Why is this? Śāriputra, because the aggregates,
sense bases, and elements are pure by nature, so too is this perfection of wisdom pure by nature.
Because dependent origination, the perversions, views, the courses of craving, greed, hatred, and delusion are pure by nature, so too is this perfection of wisdom pure by nature.

Because the self, sentient beings, life-principle, living being, nourisher, spirit, person, individual, mind-born, manna, agent, instigator, originator, co-originator, experiencer, one who causes experience, knower, and seer are pure by nature, so too is this perfection of wisdom pure by nature.
Because the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and the finite and infinite, are pure by nature, so too is this perfection of wisdom pure by nature.
Because generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are pure by nature, this perfection of wisdom is pure by nature;

because the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the branches of the path, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, the attainments, and loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are pure by nature, this perfection of wisdom is pure by nature.

Because all that is non-erroneous—the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; the supernormal powers; the noble paths; the stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas; the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; liberation; the knowledge and vision of liberation; and the primordial purity of nirvāṇa—is intrinsically pure, so too is this perfection of wisdom intrinsically pure.

Because the phenomena of the past, future, and present; the unattached knowledge and vision; and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are intrinsically pure, so too is this perfection of wisdom intrinsically pure.

Because the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; the realms of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness; the realm of sentient beings; and the realm of phenomena are inherently pure, this Prajñāpāramitā is likewise inherently pure.
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom is formless, invisible, and without resistance.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! In this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, not even the slightest dharma is seen to have form, to be visible, or to possess resistance.
Śāriputra said:
“Thus, this perfection of wisdom is without any conditioned activity.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”
"Because an agent who creates cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā has no destination."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma is seen that can be approached.”
Śāriputra said:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom cannot be conceptually established.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, no dharma can be apprehended for the purpose of designation.
Śāriputra said:
“Thus, this perfection of wisdom is indeed unique.
The Buddha said, “It is so!”
"Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive any dharma with which it could be associated.
Śāriputra said:
"In this way, *prajñāpāramitā* is signless (*animitta*)."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because the characteristics of all phenomena are ungraspable.”
Śāriputra said, “In this way,
the perfection of wisdom has nothing that it illuminates.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because neither the capacity to illuminate nor that which is illuminated can be apprehended. Śāriputra said:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is indeed boundless.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
Why is this? Śāriputra, because the aggregates,
bases, and elements are boundless, the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
Because dependent origination, inversions, views, tendencies of craving, attachment, aversion, ignorance, and so forth are boundless, the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
because the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit are boundless, the perfection of wisdom is also boundless;
and because generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are boundless, the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.

Because the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the factors of the path are non-perverted and limitless, the perfection of wisdom is also limitless;

because the objects of focus, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, the deliverances, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are limitless, the perfection of wisdom is also limitless;

and because the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the Buddha, the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are limitless, the perfection of wisdom is also limitless.

Because sentient beings and so forth, the desire, form, and formless realms, the immeasurables, the supernormal powers, the various hindrances, the knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present, unattached knowledge and vision, the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness, the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and so on are infinite, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also infinite.
“Śāriputra! The profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended in its beginning, middle, or end; it is likewise non-apprehendable within all phenomena.”
Śāriputra! The profound perfection of wisdom is boundless and limitless. Śāriputra!
Just as the limit of great empty space cannot be apprehended, so too the limit of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra!
Just as the limits of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, so too the limit of the perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra, you should know that the perfection of wisdom is without limit and without spatial direction at its beginning, middle,
and end. Śāriputra!"

Because the aggregates, bases, and elements; dependent origination, perversions, the hindrances, views, the modes of craving, greed, hatred, and delusion; the notions of self and sentient beings; generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the factors of enlightenment; the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments; suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; the immeasurables, supernormal powers, clear knowledges, liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and all other dharmas—whether those of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or the Buddha-dharmas—are without limit, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without limit.
Śāriputra! Because the profound perfection of wisdom has no limit that can be apprehended, it is called "limitless"; because it has no boundary that can be apprehended, it is called "boundless."
Śāriputra! Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless, it is called "limitless"; because it is limitless, it is called "boundless."
Śāriputra! Because the nature of self and the nature of grasping cannot be apprehended within this profound prajñāpāramitā, you should know that it is designated as "boundless" and "limitless."
Śāriputra! Because all phenomena are without limit, you should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also without limit.
Because the great void is without limit, you should know that all phenomena are also without limit.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 596. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Five of the Sixteenth Division on Prajñāpāramitā. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice within the various objective signs based on such dharmas?
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not even apprehend dharmas, let alone non-dharmas!"
If they do not even attain the Path, how much less could they attain what is not the Path!
Within pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), they have neither attainment nor grasping; how much less could they violate the precepts!
These Bodhisattvas do not fall into the three realms, nor do they fall into the births and deaths of the various destinies, nor do they cling to body or life, let alone external objects!
They have already reached the limit of the flow of birth and death, have crossed the great ocean, and have transcended all great perils.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
relying on such dharmas, practice within the various characteristics of objects and know that all objects are devoid of the nature of being objects."
By virtue of these causes and conditions, these noble beings have no dwelling attachment toward any object.
Just as the lion king is not attached to various objects, so too these noble beings are untainted and unmixed with all objective realms, transcending them entirely.
Just as a great caravan leader is free from obstacles, so too do these virtuous persons, relying on such a Dharma, practice amidst various objective phenomena without any attachment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
I do not see a single bodhisattva among this great assembly who does not have deep faith and understanding in such a Dharma, nor who harbors doubt or hesitation regarding such a Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All the bodhisattvas in this assembly have now forever severed all doubt and hesitation regarding such a Dharma.
These noble beings have no hesitation themselves regarding such a Dharma, and they are also able to forever sever all the doubts and hesitations of all sentient beings.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, these virtuous persons have no hesitation regarding any phenomena; they are able to definitively proclaim to sentient beings that the nature of all phenomena is entirely non-existent.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if there should be those in future ages who hear such a Dharma as this, they shall also eliminate all doubt and hesitation regarding all phenomena, and they will be able to forever sever all the doubts and hesitations of sentient beings by proclaiming the essential points of the Dharma just as I have now taught them."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I never say that sentient beings with meager roots of virtue can give rise to deep faith and understanding in this Dharma;
sentient beings with meager roots of virtue have no capacity to receive this Dharma, for such wealth of Dharma cannot be utilized by them."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Beings with meager roots of goodness do not even hear the name of such a Dharma, much less are they able to receive, uphold, contemplate, or cultivate it!

If there are those who hear such a Dharma as this, I definitively prophesy that they shall attain the Buddha-dharma; in future ages, they will be able to roar the lion’s roar amidst all the Buddha-dharmas, just as I now, within this great assembly, roar the lion’s roar, the fearless roar, the roar of a Great Man, and the roar of self-arisen wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are those who hear such profound essential teachings as these, and at the very least are able to give rise to a single heart of faith and joy without engendering slander, I also grant them the prediction that they shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because it is extremely difficult for sentient beings to hear the profound Dharma and then joyfully accept it with faith.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this profound Dharma, give rise to deep faith and joy, and are able to resolve their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—such sentient beings are even more difficult to find. I say that they have accomplished vast roots of goodness, possess great provisions, and don the great armor; they shall swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi.

If any sentient beings, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, rejoice with faith and delight, and listen to and receive it repeatedly, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless; how much more so for those who can uphold it and explain it to others!

Whether they have not yet entered or have already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), if they are not fixed in either of the two vehicles, I declare that they shall all attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future, forever without interruption or exhaustion.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If sentient beings have accomplished inferior dharmas, I do not see that they possess the capacity to receive the vast dharma; the 'vast dharma' refers to the bodhi of the Buddha."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Among the various classes of sentient beings, there are many who have accomplished inferior qualities; their faith and understanding are likewise all inferior, and they are unable to plant vast roots of virtue. Consequently, they cannot believe in or accept such profound, vast, and untainted True Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If sentient beings have accomplished the vast Dharma, their faith and understanding are likewise all vast;
they set out upon the Mahāyāna, skillfully perform their tasks, skillfully don the armor, and are well able to discern the profound meaning."
The Principle is the excellent practice of the Great Way, free from peril and perfectly upright;
it is far removed from the dense forest, its characteristics being equal, devoid of thorns, rubble, pits, or hollows; it is pure and unsullied, neither crooked nor devious;
it benefits the world, brings peace and happiness to the world, and has compassion for the world, together with the devas.
Acting for the sake of vast meaning, benefit, and happiness, he serves as a great illumination and a firm ladder for all sentient beings;
endowed with great compassion and pitying all, he desires to bring benefit to sentient beings,
desires to grant them peace and happiness, and desires to make them secure, universally bestowing upon sentient beings all requisites for well-being.
Such sentient beings are indeed bodhisattvas.

These mahāsattvas are well able to enjoy the great wealth of the Dharma; these mahāsattvas are well able to seek the great wealth of the Dharma. This most supreme wealth belongs to them and to no others.

Why is this so? Because if there are classes of sentient beings who do not draw near to virtuous friends, have not planted roots of goodness, and possess meager merit, they will have inferior inclinations and will be unable to believe in or accept such a vast, profound, and untainted True Dharma.
Based on such distinctions among these various classes of sentient beings, I have spoken with intentional meaning:
"The realms of sentient beings are diverse; according to their respective types, whether superior or inferior, they each take delight in one another."
Sentient beings of inferior inclination take pleasure in sentient beings of inferior inclination;
sentient beings of vast inclination take pleasure in sentient beings of vast inclination.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By means of what dharmas does this Prajñāpāramitā take its range of activity?”
Thereupon the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā takes boundless phenomena as its objective domain; it is like the element of wind, which moves through boundless realms.
This Prajñāpāramitā takes boundless phenomena as its objective domain; it is like the element of space, which moves through boundless realms."

Thus, this prajñāpāramitā takes boundless phenomena as its objective sphere; just as the element of wind takes the great void as its objective sphere, so too does this prajñāpāramitā take the emptiness of all phenomena as its objective sphere.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as the realm of space and the realm of wind are both without a location that can be seen, and likewise do not manifest before one as the characteristics of arising phenomena."
Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā has nothing whatsoever that can be demonstrated among all phenomena, nor does it appear before one for the sake of giving rise to the characteristics of phenomena.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as the realm of space and the realm of wind are both ungraspable, neither are they truly established, nor do they possess any material form that can be calculated.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is entirely ungraspable; it is not a perfected reality, nor can it be known through the calculation of signs such as form and so forth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as in the realm of space and the realm of wind, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is a perfected reality (pariniṣpanna) which can be manifested;
so too, in this Prajñāpāramitā, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is a perfected reality which can be manifested.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the characteristics of this prajñāpāramitā?
Thereupon, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā is entirely without marks.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as with the realm of space and the realm of wind, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is truly established such that its mark could be demonstrated."
In this Prajñāpāramitā, there is not even the slightest dharma that is established by way of its own nature (pariniṣpanna) such that its characteristics could be demonstrated.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is free from all marks; there is not even the slightest mark that can be apprehended.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, just as the realm of space has no place of obstruction or attachment, so too the perfection of wisdom has no place of obstruction or attachment. For this reason, it is said that the profound perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as its characteristic.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is not that a characteristic can be apprehended in the dharma of non-attachment; rather, it is in accordance with worldly conventions and linguistic principles that one speaks thus:
'The profound perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as its characteristic.'"
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Although it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* has non-attachment as its characteristic, because this *prajñāpāramitā* has no characteristic that can be apprehended, it cannot be said that non-attachment is its characteristic; for the dharma of non-attachment is devoid of any formal mark.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called "non-attachment" refers to attachment to omniscience, attachment to non-apprehensibility, and attachment to suchness.

It is called "non-attachment" because it is free from all inverted attachments; yet among these various attachments, no attachment can be found. For this reason, it is said to be attachment to suchness and attachment to non-apprehensibility.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which is called "non-attachment" is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*; this is described as the wisdom characterized by non-attachment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All phenomena have non-attachment as their characteristic; because the characteristics of all phenomena cannot be apprehended, they are said to have the characteristic of non-attachment.

Not even the slightest phenomenon manifests as a characteristic of arising, for within this there is no characteristic to be apprehended; thus it is called "signless. Because it is signless, it is designated as "non-attached."

If all phenomena possessed even the slightest characteristic, one would be able to find attachment therein; however, because all phenomena are entirely devoid of manifold characteristics, no attachment can be found therein. Therefore, it is said that the characteristic of all phenomena is non-attachment.
Although this has been said, it is not as it was spoken, because the mark of non-attachment is ineffable. Why is this?
Because the mark of non-attachment is non-existent, because its nature is detached, and because it cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The Dharma has no characteristic of attachment; it cannot be manifested, nor can it be fully revealed. Nevertheless, for the sake of sentient beings, it is expediently manifested as this characteristic of non-attachment; therefore, one should not cling to it."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All characteristics of defilement are themselves signless; it is not that non-defiled phenomena manifest for the sake of arising as signs.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

All defiled phenomena manifest through inversion; all that is inverted is signless (*animitta*); and all that is signless is inexpressible. Therefore, phenomena that possess signs are themselves signless.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All pure dharmas are likewise without marks. Why is this?
Since even all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) lack any characteristic (*nimitta*),
how much more so could pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) possess a characteristic!
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If one can thoroughly know the true nature of all defiled phenomena as they really are, those defilements will be found to be non-existent; yet, sentient beings give rise to these defilements due to their inversions.

All that is inverted is not real; if it is not real, then it has neither substantial entity nor real characteristic. To be able to thoroughly know things thus, according to reality, is called purification.
Since even the characteristics of various defilements cannot be apprehended, how much less could the characteristics of purity be apprehended!
Therefore, both the dharmas of defilement and purity lack any existent characteristic and are not pariniṣpanna (perfected reality).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! All phenomena are signless;
because they are not established as truly existent, they are called 'non-attachment. Therefore, it is said that the characteristic of all phenomena is non-attachment."
Because all phenomena are characterized by non-attachment, they are called "non-attached"; yet foolish ordinary beings cling to the very characteristic of non-attachment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, this is what is meant by saying that all phenomena have non-attachment as their characteristic.
This characteristic of non-attachment should be understood as the sphere of activity of wisdom (*jñāna*), and it is also the sphere of activity of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

This characteristic of non-attachment, which is the sphere of activity of wisdom, is also called *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore, it is said that the practice of *prajñāpāramitā* has an infinite range. One should know that all natures of non-attachment are designated as having an infinite range of practice.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

As for 'the sphere of activity,' you should know that this indicates what is not a sphere of activity; it is impossible to demonstrate the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as being a sphere of activity."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which is the sphere of activity should be understood as demonstrating the non-sphere of activity, because the suchness and the mode of being of all phenomena are entirely unapprehendable."
All phenomena are not the sphere of activity, because all phenomena lack the nature of being an object.
If one can thus thoroughly know all phenomena, this is called "practicing within the sphere of all objects"; yet, although it is so described, it is not as the description suggests.
If one can thus thoroughly know all phenomena such that there is no attachment whatsoever, this is called the characteristic of non-attachment.
Based on this principle, it is said that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) has non-attachment as its characteristic.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
regarding these profound essential teachings on the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom as thus described, there are very few companions who would wish to proclaim, analyze, and reveal them."

In this context, the companions consist solely of those śrāvakas who have seen the truths and are headed for great enlightenment, as well as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are already non-retrogressive, and individuals endowed with vision who no longer regress from the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

A person endowed with such vision is likewise able to practice these profound essential teachings correctly and remain free from doubt; having personally realized the stage of a bodhisattva and attained pure patience (*kṣānti*), they will certainly have no doubts regarding these essential teachings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
For foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), such a sublime Dharma is not within the range of their practice.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

This Dharma teaching associated with the profound perfection of wisdom as thus explained is extremely difficult to encounter; it shall never fall into the hands of sentient beings whose inclinations and understandings are inferior.

If there are sentient beings who have served many Buddhas in the past, who have accomplished the most supreme and pure roots of goodness, and whose faith and understanding are vast, then this teaching of the Dharma corresponding to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as here explained shall fall into their hands.

It should be known that such sentient beings have already planted immeasurable and vast roots of goodness; they have accomplished a pliant and pure intention; they have, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, planted the seeds of enlightenment, made great vows, practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva, and mounted the vehicle of the Buddha; they have drawn near to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and have questioned them regarding the profound Dharma in accordance with reality; for this reason, these teachings corresponding to the Prajñāpāramitā have fallen into their hands.

It should be known that such classes of sentient beings have either already realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), or are close to realizing it; therefore, this teaching of the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) has fallen into their hands.

It should be known that such beings will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; except for those who, through the power of compassion and vows, do not seek swift realization.
It should be known that such beings have already received a prophecy from the Buddhas, or else will receive a prophecy before long.

"You should know that such classes of sentient beings, even if they have not yet received a face-to-face prophecy from a Buddha, are as if they have already received a face-to-face prophecy from a Buddha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If there are sentient beings whose roots of virtue are not yet mature and whose merit is meager, they will not even hear the name of such a sūtra as this *Prajñāpāramitā*, let alone be able to take it in hand to read, recite, uphold, transcribe, make offerings to it, or explain it extensively for others!
It is impossible for them to be able to do so.

However, if sentient beings have matured roots of goodness and, by the power of their past vows, encounter this sutra and are able to hear it, receive and uphold it, copy it, read and recite it, revere and make offerings to it, and explain it extensively for others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If sentient beings possess flourishing roots of virtue and a well-disciplined intention, then this Dharma teaching associated with the perfection of wisdom shall fall into their hands."

I declare that those sons and daughters of good family—whether belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle or the Śrāvaka vehicle—who, having attained this Dharma, cherish it with a profound heart, will find that all the aforementioned faults previously mentioned are transformed by the power of such roots of goodness. Though they may have formerly been indolent, prone to excessive sleep, lacking correct awareness (*asamprajanya*), failing to abide in right mindfulness (*asmṛti*), or possessed of a distracted mind; though they may have been addicted to food and drink, fond of precious wealth, inclined toward coarse speech, or delighted in violence and cruelty;
though they may have harbored arrogance or possessed dull faculties and lacked understanding—all these shall be overturned through the power of their roots of goodness.

Having attained such profound essential teachings, even if they were previously śrāvakas, they now transform into bodhisattvas; they develop redoubled love and joy for the profound Dharma, remain heedful regarding all sensory objects, and take delight in the practice of all wholesome dharmas. With courageous and correct diligence, they abandon all laziness; with a single-minded focus, they collect their thoughts and guard the sense faculties. They refrain from coarse speech and do not engage in violent or evil conduct; they constantly cultivate reverence and delight in the study of extensive learning. Their vigor is blazing and free from all greedy attachments, as they are well able to discern the profound meaning of the Dharma.
If you wish to fulfill such merits, you should diligently study and practice these profound essential teachings.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if bodhisattvas or those of the śrāvaka vehicle hear these essential teachings, they will obtain a sublime fruit; that is to say, upon hearing such profound essential teachings, they will certainly never again engage in negligence, will not give rise to confidence in unwholesome dharmas, and their wholesome desire and diligence will neither decline nor diminish. They will not become lax regarding their practice, will take no pleasure in seeking out external heterodox teachings, and will not frequently manifest greed, hatred, or delusion.
Such fruits as these are immeasurable and boundless, all resulting from hearing this profound essential of the Dharma.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the profound essential of the Dharma does not constitute a fruit merely by being heard with the ears; rather, it is called a fruit when one practices with diligence and without negligence, understands reality as it is, remains far removed from all evils, and brings benefit to both oneself and others.

Furthermore, "hearing the Dharma" means to understand the essential points of the Dharma as they truly are and to apply oneself diligently to its cultivation; it does not mean developing divergent interpretations or practices regarding the True Dharma.
If one develops divergent interpretations or practices regarding the True Dharma, it should be known that such a person is not said to have heard the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
You all should apply skillful means regarding the meanings you have heard, giving rise to non-erroneous understanding and abiding in correct practice.

If one gives rise to erroneous understanding regarding the meaning of the Dharma and practices incorrectly, you should know that such a person will certainly lack the patient acceptance (kṣānti) that accords with the Buddha’s True Dharma."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Within my true Dharma and Vinaya, those who practice according to what has been taught attain "conformity-patience" (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
What is called conformity-patience refers to the initiation of correct practice through non-erroneous discernment regarding the true Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

One who possesses the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*) and abides in right practice should be known as one who will certainly not fall into the miserable destinies of hell, the animal realm, or the hungry ghosts, and will swiftly realize the supreme fruit of the True Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Sentient beings should not rely on or place their trust in meager roots of virtue, thinking that these alone can liberate them from the evil realms.

Even diligent application of effort cannot be relied upon; as long as one has not yet fully attained right view regarding the Dharma, there remains the possibility of falling back into the evil realms."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If one has attained patient acceptance (kṣānti) through the perfect cultivation and study of the true Dharma, one will no longer create karma that leads to the miserable realms, will no longer be indolent or give rise to factors conducive to regression, will not fear falling back into inferior states, and will not allow the mind to become lax or negligent regarding the practices undertaken."

Why is this? Śāriputra, because they are able to correctly and universally know the aspects of defilement and purification; they attain the vision of reality as it is and penetrate all phenomena, such that they do not give rise to attachment toward the false mental appearances produced by inversion.

Regarding the profound meaning and intent of the True Dharma, he has attained right view and is fully endowed with patient compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*); being intelligent, disciplined, and gentle, he abides in pure morality;
his observance of the rules of discipline, his correct conduct, and his adherence to the codes of propriety are all complete, having attained this patient compliance.
Even devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others show reverence to them, let alone human beings!

Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and all others should cherish, take refuge in, make offerings to, protect, and surround them, ensuring that no adverse conditions can harm their lives or their spiritual practice, let alone human beings!

Therefore, one should diligently cultivate the True Dharma and the patient acceptance that accords with it (*anulomikī kṣānti*). If one attains this patient acceptance, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others will constantly follow, protect, revere, and make offerings to one, never abandoning them for even a moment.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Why, Venerable One, do you remain silent and say nothing?
Why do you not speak of the profound perfection of wisdom?"

Now the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is present as witness; this great assembly is a true vessel for the profound Prajñāpāramitā, their intentions being pure and their aspiration to hear the profound Dharma.
Subhūti replied: "Yes, Śāriputra!"
"I do not perceive anything at all regarding all phenomena; therefore, I now remain silent and say nothing.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, I do not perceive the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do I perceive the assembly of bodhisattvas."

One does not perceive a speaker, nor does one perceive that which is spoken; furthermore, one does not perceive that it is spoken by this, for this, because of this, belonging to this, or depending upon this.
Since I perceive nothing herein, how can I proclaim the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the bodhisattvas?
Even if I were to wish to speak it?
Who is it that speaks, and what is it that is spoken?
Furthermore, one does not know by what means, for what purpose, by what cause, to what it belongs, or upon what it depends that it is spoken.
"How shall I proclaim such a profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
this profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be proclaimed, cannot be demonstrated, and cannot be conceptualized through discursive proliferation (*prapañca*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā cannot be proclaimed, cannot be demonstrated, and cannot be conceptualized through discursive proliferation."
If one can thus indicate it through skillful means, that reveals the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This profound prajñāpāramitā cannot be described by means of past characteristics, nor can it be described by means of future characteristics, nor can it be described by means of present characteristics.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the profound perfection of wisdom is signless and inexpressible.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, [it is thus].
I do not perceive any such characteristic in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by which this *prajñāpāramitā* could be proclaimed through that characteristic.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the characteristics of the three times regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements are not the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; rather, the suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity, immutability, and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) of those characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements throughout the three times is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The suchness, non-falsity, immutability, and suchness-as-it-is of all the characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements throughout the three times cannot be designated, cannot be displayed, and cannot be the subject of conceptual proliferation; they cannot be expressed by verbal activity or any other such means.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
this profound Prajñāpāramitā does not manifest by means of teaching the characteristics of all phenomena,
nor does it manifest by means of teaching the characteristics of the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements."
It manifests by way of teaching the characteristics of practice and non-practice, but it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of dependent origination;
it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of name-and-form;
it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of a self, sentient beings, and so forth; it does not manifest by way of teaching phenomena.
It manifests by way of the characteristics of the elements (*dhātu*), not by way of demonstrating the characteristics of being bound or liberated;
it does not manifest by way of demonstrating the characteristics of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);
it does not manifest by way of demonstrating the characteristics of suffering or pleasure; nor does it manifest by way of demonstrating the established (*vyavasthāna*) or the non-established.
It manifests through characteristics, yet it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of defilement and purity; it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of intrinsic nature and non-intrinsic nature;
and it does not manifest by way of teaching the characteristics of the conventional and the ultimate.
Therefore, it manifests not by way of explaining the characteristics of reality or falsity,
nor does it manifest by way of explaining the characteristics of transition or entry.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is free from all signs, it cannot be demonstrated as "this is the *prajñāpāramitā*," "in this *prajñāpāramitā*," "by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*," "for the sake of this *prajñāpāramitā*," "because of this *prajñāpāramitā*," "belonging to this *prajñāpāramitā*," or "relying upon this *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I do not perceive any dharma by which I might teach and demonstrate the Prajñāpāramitā.
Moreover, Śāriputra!"
There is not even the slightest dharma that can manifest or apprehend this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

it is not the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that manifests or apprehends the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), or the knowledge of liberation (*vidyā-vimukti*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Even the supramundane sublime wisdom that penetrates all things cannot manifestly grasp the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Since phenomena cannot be apprehended or manifested through phenomena, how can the profound *prajñāpāramitā* be explained and manifested?
Nevertheless, Śāriputra,
if one can understand the true principle of these phenomena, one will be able to understand the exposition of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
this profound perfection of wisdom does not manifest by way of revealing any phenomena."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, this profound perfection of wisdom does not manifest by way of displaying the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements;
it does not manifest by way of displaying name and form; it does not manifest by way of displaying...
It manifests because it demonstrates the phenomena of defilement and purity;
it does not manifest by demonstrating the various principles of dependent origination, nor by demonstrating the various perversions,
nor by demonstrating the self, the realm of sentient beings, and so forth, nor by demonstrating earth, water, and...
It manifests by way of the elements of fire, wind, space, and consciousness;
it does not manifest by way of displaying the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
nor does it manifest by way of displaying generosity and avarice, ethical discipline and immorality, patience and anger, diligence and laziness, or meditative tranquility...
It manifests due to vitarka, vicāra, prajñā, and dauṣprajña; it does not manifest by way of displaying the applications of mindfulness,
the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the branches of the path,
the dhyānas, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative attainments, the immeasurables, or the supernormal knowledges.
Previously, it did not manifest by way of revealing the truths, the paths, or the fruits;
it did not manifest by way of revealing the dharmas of the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas;
it did not manifest by way of revealing all knowledge of dharmas and non-knowledge; it did not manifest by way of revealing exhaustion.
It manifests because of the knowledge of non-arising and the knowledge of cessation,
rather than by way of manifesting the dharma of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Since no dharma manifests by means of the manifestation of dharmas, how shall I proclaim such a profound perfection of wisdom?
However, Śāriputra!

If one can understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught—not as something that manifests by way of displaying any phenomena—then one will be able to understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and will also be able to proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
this profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest for the sake of the conjunction or disjunction of phenomena. Why is that?
Śāriputra! This profound perfection of wisdom does not involve the conjunction or disjunction of the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements;
it does not involve the conjunction or disjunction of conditioned phenomena; nor does it involve the conjunction or disjunction of dependent origination.
It does not undergo conjunction or disjunction with inversion; it does not undergo conjunction or disjunction with the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
it does not undergo conjunction or disjunction with the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness;
it does not undergo conjunction or disjunction with the realms of self, sentient beings, and so forth; nor does it undergo conjunction or disjunction with the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
There is no conjunction or disjunction with respect to generosity or stinginess, ethical discipline or violation of precepts,
patience or anger, diligence or laziness, meditative concentration or distraction, or wisdom or faulty discernment;
nor is there conjunction or disjunction with respect to the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, or the faculties.
The powers, factors of enlightenment, factors of the path, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, attainments, immeasurables,
and supernormal knowledges involve conjunction and separation; however, they do not involve conjunction or separation for the truths,
the paths, or the fruits of the paths, nor do they involve conjunction with the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas, nor with the Dharma.
There is dispersion, yet it does not involve the union or dispersion of the equality of the three periods of past, future, and present;
it does not involve the union or dispersion of the knowledge of non-attachment, exhaustion, and non-arising;
and it manifests without involving the union or dispersion of nirvana.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
since no dharma exists that manifests through the conjunction or disjunction of dharmas, how shall I proclaim such a profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Nevertheless, Śāriputra!
Observing this meaning, I speak thus:
the profound perfection of wisdom cannot be explained or demonstrated.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

I do not perceive any such dharma that can be called the "speaker," nor the "spoken," nor that which can be said to exist by virtue of this, for this, because of this, belonging to this, or depending upon this. How then could I proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas?
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra, saying:
“Son of good family!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not engage in any activity whatsoever regarding all phenomena.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because all phenomena arise from perversion; they are not real, do not exist, and are false, deceptive, and illusory.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
For example, those who act with regard to phenomena all act in inversion and all act in unreality;
likewise, if a bodhisattva were to have any action, they would be acting in inversion and acting in unreality.
Bodhisattvas are not characterized by inverted conduct or unreal conduct, nor can bodhisattvas who practice inverted or unreal conduct practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is inverted and unreal is not the sphere of practice;
therefore, a bodhisattva does not act within it. Furthermore, Suvīra!
What is called "inversion" is precisely falsehood, that to which foolish ordinary beings are attached.
Such dharmas do not exist in the way they appear; such attachments do not accord with their true nature. Therefore, they are termed "inversions" and "unreal."
Therefore, bodhisattvas do not act with inversion and do not act with unreality; for this reason, bodhisattvas are called speakers of truth and may also be called practitioners of non-inversion.

If there is truly no inversion, then there is nothing to be practiced; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice, and the severance of all practices is called the bodhisattva’s practice.
This bodhisattva practice cannot be demonstrated as being "this," "by this," "in this," or "from this," for it is not something manifested by the practices of bodhisattvas.
Why is this? O Suvīra!

Because all bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path by bringing all conditioned activities to rest; that is to say, they practice the bodhisattva path by bringing to rest the activities of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas that involve grasping and attachment.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

In this way, a bodhisattva does not engage with the qualities of a buddha, nor does he cling to them by thinking: 'This is the quality of a buddha,' 'by means of these qualities of a buddha,' 'in these qualities of a buddha,' or 'belonging to these qualities of a buddha.'"

In this way, the bodhisattva likewise does not engage in any conceptualization or differentiated conceptualization; that is to say, bodhisattvas do not engage in conceptualization or differentiated conceptualization.
The severance of all conceptualization and distinct conceptualization is called the practice of a bodhisattva.
O Well-Valiant One!

"Conceptualization" refers to the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; "distinct conceptualization" refers to the conceptualization of the distinctions among all phenomena. No phenomenon whatsoever can be subject to conceptualization or distinct conceptualization.

Because all phenomena are beyond conceptualization and distinct conceptualization, if one were to conceptualize phenomena, one would be creating distinct conceptualizations regarding them; however, all phenomena are far removed from both conceptualization and distinct conceptualization.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

To speak of 'discrimination' is called one extreme; to speak of 'that which is other than discrimination' is the second extreme. These are not the practice of Bodhisattvas, who dwell neither in extremes nor in the absence of extremes."

If bodhisattvas do not engage with either the finite or the infinite, these bodhisattvas likewise do not perceive a middle. If they were to perceive a middle, they would be engaging in the middle; if they were to engage in the middle, they would be engaging in the finite. This is because the middle has no engagement, no manifestation, and no demonstration, as it is free from the characteristics of engagement.
Furthermore, Suvīra!
That which is called the "Middle" should be known as the Noble Eightfold Path.
This Noble Path manifests while there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended among all phenomena; this Noble Path manifests while there is absolutely nothing to be seen among all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
When there is neither cultivation nor rejection regarding phenomena, at that time it is called the path of cessation.
This path of cessation neither cultivates nor rejects any phenomenon; it transcends both cultivation and rejection, and realizes the equal, true nature of all phenomena."
Because they have realized the true nature of the equality of all phenomena, even the notion of a "path" does not exist for them, much less the perception of a path!
Furthermore, Suvīra,
those who have brought the path to rest are the Arhats, the bhikṣus whose outflows are exhausted.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because that which is abandoned is the path;

because it is neither cultivated nor abandoned, it is called "abandoned"; because that abandonment itself is non-existent, it is called "abandoned"; and because cultivation is abandoned, it is designated as "abandoned."
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

If there is one who practices 'sending away' (prahāṇa) that which is to be attained, this is not called 'sending away. Herein, 'sending away' refers to the nature of practice; because there is no practice herein, it is called 'sending away. Since practice does not exist, 'sending away' also does not exist. Although it is spoken of in this way, it is not as it is spoken."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because that which is sent forth is ineffable, for it is devoid of the nature of being sent forth.
Furthermore, what is it that is abandoned?
It is the non-arising of perverted phenomena and the non-arising of unreal phenomena. Moreover, Suvīra!
It is not that various perversions can give rise to perversion.
For that which is perverse has no real basis for its arising; it is not because there is a real arising within this that it is called perverse.
If there were a real basis for its arising within this, it would not be named perversion; it is precisely because there is no real arising that it is named perversion.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
The assembly of bodhisattvas awakens to all phenomena as being free from all inversions. Why is this so?
The assembly of bodhisattvas understands that all inversions are not truly existent, meaning that within inversion there is no nature of inversion.

Because they know that inversions do not exist in reality, and because there is no nature of inversion within non-inversion, it is said that bodhisattvas realize all phenomena as being free from all inversions.
By awakening to all phenomena as being free from all inversions, one no longer gives rise to inversions regarding phenomena;
if there are no further inversions therein, then one does not engage in any activity toward those phenomena.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
All inversions involve active engagement;
because there is active engagement, there is origination. Both active engagement and origination arise from the false conceptualization of inversions.
Regarding the dharmas they practice, all bodhisattvas are without conceptual discrimination and without mental arousal; therefore, they are said to be far removed from inversion.
Because they are without inversion, there is no practice; because there is no practice, there is no arising. Thus, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is non-practice.

To practice non-practice means that regarding all phenomena, there is absolutely no practice; one neither observes nor manifests any characteristic of practice. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice.
If one can practice in this way—practicing without anything to practice—that is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage in practice by taking form as an object, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
To practice without taking feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as an object is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? O Well-Vigorous One!

Because these bodhisattvas know that the nature of all objects of perception is remote and detached, if they know that the nature of the object of perception is remote and detached, then there is no activity; therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is the practice of non-practice.
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage in mental activity conditioned by the eye, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not engage in mental activity conditioned by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas know that the nature of all objects of cognition is not real.
If one knows that the nature of the object of focus is not real, then there is no activity; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice by taking form as an object, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
To not engage in mental activity directed toward sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? O Well-Valiant One!
These bodhisattvas know that all objects of perception arise from inversion; if they arise from inversion, they are not real.
Knowing that the nature of objects of perception arising from inversion is unreal, they have no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is "practice of non-practice."
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice by taking eye-consciousness as an object, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not practice by taking ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness as an object, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas know that all objects of perception are entirely false and illusory.
If one knows that all objects of perception are false and illusory, then there is no practice; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice by taking name-and-form as an object, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this? Because..."
"O Suvīra! These bodhisattvas awaken to the fact that all objects of cognition are of a nature that lacks any object of cognition.

If they awaken to the fact that objects of cognition lack any object of cognition, then there is no activity; therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is the practice of non-practice."

“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the practices concerning a self, sentient beings, and so forth, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?
"Excellent valor!
These bodhisattvas know, in accordance with reality, that the nature of the notions of 'self' and 'sentient beings' is not real.
If they can know that the nature of the notions of 'self' and 'sentient beings' is not real, then they do not engage in any activity whatsoever regarding conditioned phenomena."

If one does not engage in any engagement with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) at all, then one is free from all conditioned phenomena; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage in the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, up to the notion of a knower or the notion of a viewer, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas have dispelled all conceptualizations.
If one can eliminate all perceptions, then one does not engage in any perceptions at all; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is the practice of non-practice. "Suvīra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage in perversions, dogmatic views, or hindrances, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not act with perversions, dogmatic views, or hindrances as their objective referent, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas know that the objects of all perversions, views, and hindrances are entirely non-existent as real entities.

If one knows that the spheres of activity of inversion, views, and hindrances are entirely non-existent, then there is no sphere of activity; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is the practice of non-practice.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take dependent origination as an object of focus while practicing, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?
O Well-Valiant One!
These bodhisattvas thoroughly understand dependent origination and its object.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand dependent origination and its object, then there is no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva's practice is "practice through non-practice."
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take the realms of desire, form, or formlessness as an object of focus, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel all objects of perception within the three realms.

If bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel all objects of perception within the three realms, they have no sphere of activity; therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is the practice of non-practice. "Suvīra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice by taking as objects generosity and stinginess, ethical discipline and transgression, patience and anger, diligence and laziness, meditative concentration and distraction, or wisdom and false wisdom, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? O Well-Courageous One!
These bodhisattvas thoroughly know the objects of focus for everything from generosity and stinginess up to wisdom and corrupted intelligence.
If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand all such objects of focus, they have no course of action; therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is the practice of non-action.
"O Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the practices of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, branches of the path, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, meditative attainments, immeasurables, or supernormal knowledges—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas possess sovereign realization regarding all objects of focus, and they are also able to dispel them.

If bodhisattvas can freely awaken to and eliminate all objects of perception, they then have no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva's practice is the practice of non-practice.
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice by taking the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as objects of focus, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas eliminate the objects of focus regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

If one can dispel the objects of focus regarding the Four Truths, then there is nothing to be dispelled and no practice to be performed; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is a practice of non-practice. "Suvīra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice by taking illumination and liberation as objects of focus, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that? O Well-Vigorous One!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus for illumination and liberation.
If they can dispel the objects of focus for illumination and liberation, then there is no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva's practice is the practice of non-practice.
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object of focus extinction, non-arising, or unconditioned activity, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel all objects of focus regarding exhaustion, non-arising, and non-creation.
If one can eliminate all these objects of focus, then there is no activity; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva practices non-practice. "Suvīra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness while practicing, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus belonging to the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
If one can dispel all these objects of focus, then there is no activity; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas in their practice, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus belonging to the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.

If bodhisattvas are able to universally dispel the objects of focus belonging to the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas, then there is no [fixed] course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is "practice of non-practice."

“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object of focus the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or the buddha-dharmas, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus (ālambana) pertaining to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-dharma.

If bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus pertaining to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-dharma, then there is no activity; therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is non-practice.
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices without taking nirvāṇa as an object of focus, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?
"O Suvīra! These bodhisattvas fully know the object of focus of nirvāṇa.
If bodhisattvas fully know the object of focus of nirvāṇa, they have no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice."
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the pure conduct of the primary and secondary marks, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?
“Suvīra! These bodhisattvas are universally able to eliminate the object of focus that is the purity of the primary and secondary marks.

If bodhisattvas are universally able to eliminate the object of focus that is the purity of the primary and secondary marks, then there is no practice; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is non-practice.”
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take the purification of buddha-fields as an object of focus, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?
“Suvīra! These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objective referent of the purification of buddha-fields.

If bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objective referent of the purification of buddha-fields, then there is no practice; therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is non-practice.”
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the practices for the perfection of the qualities of the śrāvakas, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus associated with the perfected qualities of the śrāvakas.

If bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus associated with the perfected qualities of the śrāvakas, they then have no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s practice is the practice of non-practice.
“Suvīra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take as an object the bodhisattva’s perfected conduct of merit, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus regarding the perfect qualities of a bodhisattva.

If bodhisattvas are universally able to dispel the objects of focus regarding the perfect qualities of a bodhisattva, then there is no course of action; therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva's practice is "practice without a course of action."
“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If bodhisattvas can practice the perfection of wisdom, they practice by thoroughly knowing all objects of cognition and practice by dispelling all objects of cognition.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 597. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Sixteen: The Division on the Perfection of Wisdom (VI). "Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of form as an object, nor do they practice by taking the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as an object.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully known that the intrinsic nature of the objects of perception—from form up to consciousness—is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of the eye as an object, nor do they practice by taking the purity of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully known that the intrinsic nature of the objects of the eye up to the mind is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom. "Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of form as an object, nor do they practice by taking the purity of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or phenomena as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus—from form up to phenomena—is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of eye-consciousness as a condition, nor do they practice by taking the purity of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness as a condition."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of the eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of name-and-form as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already been able to thoroughly know that the intrinsic nature of the objective referent of name-and-form is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom. “Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of a self as an object, nor do they practice by taking the purity of a sentient being, a life-force, a soul, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a pudgala, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, one who causes to act, an originator, one who causes to originate, an experiencer, one who causes to experience, a knower, one who causes to know, or a seer, one who causes to see, as their objects.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully known that the intrinsic nature of the objects of perception—from "self" up to "those who see"—is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as their object the purity of the perversions, nor do they practice by taking as their object the purity of views or the hindrances."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of perversions, views, and hindrances is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of dependent origination as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already been able to thoroughly know that the intrinsic nature of the object-condition of dependent origination is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm as an object of focus."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already been able to thoroughly know that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus in the desire, form, and formless realms is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as their object the purity of generosity or stinginess; nor do they practice by taking as their object the purity of ethical discipline or its violation, patience or anger, diligence or laziness, meditative concentration or distraction, or wisdom or false wisdom."
Why is this? O Suvīra!

It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus for everything from generosity and stinginess up to wisdom and false wisdom is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of the earth element as an object, nor do they practice by taking the purity of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already attained thorough knowledge that the intrinsic nature of the objects of perception—from the earth element up to the consciousness element—is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as their object the purity of the past, future, or present."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully known that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus in the past, future, and present is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking non-attachment and purity as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully known that the nature of objects of focus is pure and free from attachment.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking the purity of the applications of mindfulness as an object, nor do they practice by taking the purity of the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, the branches of the path, the immeasurables, or the supernormal knowledges as an object."
Why is this? O Suvīra!

It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus—from the foundations of mindfulness up to the supernormal powers—is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as their object the purity of the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, or attainments."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus for the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as their object illumination or the purity of liberation."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of focus for both knowledge and liberation is pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as their object the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the purity of all-knowledge."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
