It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully understood that the intrinsic nature of the objects of knowledge of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and all-knowledge (*sarvajñāna*) is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking as an object the purity of all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have already fully realized that the nature of all phenomena—the objects of perception for all sentient beings—is fundamentally pure.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"O Well-Valiant One!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking anything pure as an object-condition."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
It is because these bodhisattvas have thoroughly realized that the intrinsic nature of all objects of cognition is pure.
If bodhisattvas thoroughly penetrate that the intrinsic nature of all objects of focus is pure, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, they do not perceive that "this is form" up to "this is consciousness," nor that "this arises from form" up to "this arises from consciousness," nor that "this belongs to form" up to "this belongs to consciousness," nor that "this proceeds from form" up to "this proceeds from consciousness. Because these bodhisattvas do not view dharmas such as form in this manner, they neither elevate nor deprecate form and the other aggregates; they do not give rise to them, do not extinguish them, do not engage with them, and do not observe them. They likewise do not engage with or observe the objects of perception, such as form and the rest.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not perceive that 'this is the eye' up to 'this is the mind'; nor do they perceive 'this arises by means of the eye' up to 'this arises by means of the mind'; nor do they perceive 'this belongs to the eye' up to 'this belongs to the mind'; nor do they perceive 'this proceeds from the eye' up to 'this proceeds from the mind. Because these bodhisattvas do not view the dharmas such as the eye in this manner, they neither elevate nor depress the eye and so forth; they neither produce nor extinguish them; they neither engage in nor observe them. They likewise neither engage in nor observe the objects of perception (*ālambana*) of the eye and so forth."
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not perceive that 'this is form' up to 'this is phenomena,' nor that 'this arises from form' up to 'this arises from phenomena,' nor that 'this belongs to form' up to 'this belongs to phenomena,' nor that 'this proceeds from form' up to 'this proceeds from phenomena. Because these bodhisattvas do not view phenomena such as form in such a manner, they neither elevate nor deprecate form and so forth; they neither arise nor cease; they neither engage in activity nor observe them; and they likewise neither engage in activity nor observe the objects of perception (*ālambana*) such as form."
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "O Well-Valiant One! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not perceive:

'This is eye-consciousness' up to 'this is mind-consciousness'; 'this arises from eye-consciousness' up to 'this arises from mind-consciousness'; 'this belongs to eye-consciousness' up to 'this belongs to mind-consciousness'; or 'this proceeds from eye-consciousness' up to 'this proceeds from mind-consciousness. Because these bodhisattvas do not view the phenomena of eye-consciousness and so forth in such a manner, they neither elevate nor depress, neither produce nor extinguish, neither engage in nor observe eye-consciousness and so forth; they likewise neither engage in nor observe the objects of perception (*ālambana*) of eye-consciousness and so forth."
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice that form is past, future, or present; nor do they practice that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are past, future, or present.
Then one does not practice with the eye as past, future, or present; nor does one practice with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as past, future, or present.
One does not practice with forms as past, future, or present; nor does one practice with sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena as past, future, or present.
One does not practice with eye-consciousness as past, future, or present; nor does one practice with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness as past, future, or present.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin,

if bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice with the notion that form is "I" or "mine," nor do they practice with the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "I" or "mine."
Then one does not practice the notion that the eye is "I" or "mine," nor does one practice the notion that the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind is "I" or "mine";
one does not practice the notion that forms are "I" or "mine," nor does one practice the notion that sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena are "I" or "mine";
one does not practice the notion that eye-consciousness is "I" or "mine," nor does one practice the notion that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness is "I" or "mine."
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhānavīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice with the notion that form is pleasure or suffering, nor do they practice with the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are pleasure or suffering.
Then one does not engage with the thought that the eye is pleasant or painful, nor does one engage with the thought that the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind is pleasant or painful;
one does not engage with the thought that forms are pleasant or painful, nor does one engage with the thought that sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena are pleasant or painful;

one does not engage with the thought that eye-consciousness is pleasant or painful, nor does one engage with the thought that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness is pleasant or painful.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not practice with the notion that form belongs to them and not to others, nor do they practice with the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness belong to them and not to others.

Then one does not practice with the thought that the eye belongs to the self and not to another; nor does one practice with the thought that the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind belongs to the self and not to another.

One does not practice with the thought that forms belong to the self and not to another; nor does one practice with the thought that sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects belong to the self and not to another.

One does not practice with the thought that eye-consciousness belongs to the self and not to another; nor does one practice with the thought that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness belongs to the self and not to another.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Subha-vīra!

If bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom do not practice the accumulation of form up to consciousness, nor their cessation; do not practice what is deep or shallow; do not practice emptiness or non-emptiness; do not practice with signs or signlessness; do not practice with aspiration or wishlessness; and do not practice with volitional activity or non-volitional activity; [they are practicing the perfection of wisdom].

Regarding the eye up to the mind, one does not practice their arising, nor their cessation; one does not practice them as deep, nor as shallow; one does not practice them as empty, nor as non-empty; one does not practice them as having marks, nor as being markless; one does not practice them as having a wish, nor as being wishless; one does not practice them as having volitional activity, nor as being without volitional activity. Regarding forms up to mental phenomena, one does not practice their arising, nor their cessation;

one does not practice them as deep, nor as shallow; one does not practice them as empty, nor as non-empty; one does not practice them as having marks, nor as being markless; one does not practice them as having a wish, nor as being wishless; one does not practice them as having volitional activity, nor as being without volitional activity.

Regarding visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, one does not engage in their arising, nor do one engage in their cessation; one does not engage in the profound, nor do one engage in the shallow; one does not engage in emptiness, nor do one engage in non-emptiness; one does not engage in having signs, nor do one engage in signlessness; one does not engage in having aspirations, nor do one engage in wishlessness; one does not engage in conditioned activity, nor do one engage in the absence of conditioned activity.
Why is this? O Suvīra!

All such phenomena possess grasping and attachment, fluctuation, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and inclination; that is to say: "I am able to perform such fluctuations," "I engage in such conceptual proliferation regarding this practice," "I incline toward such things by means of this practice," and "I rely upon this practice for such grasping and attachment."

In this regard, the bodhisattva thoroughly understands all reliance, grasping, mental fluctuations, conceptual proliferation, and the inclinations that harm ignorance; being without reliance or grasping, they have no activity whatsoever and no storehouse of grasping.
Because there is no storehouse of grasping, there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither instigation nor co-arising.
In this way, the bodhisattva eliminates all forms of arrogance and attachment while practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One!

When bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not engage with form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) as permanent or impermanent; they do not engage with them as pleasant or unpleasant; they do not engage with them as self or non-self; they do not engage with them as pure or impure; they do not engage with them as empty or non-empty; they do not engage with them as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection of light, or like an echo.

Regarding the eye up to the mind, one does not practice [the notion of] permanence or impermanence; one does not practice pleasure or suffering; one does not practice self or non-self; one does not practice purity or impurity; one does not practice emptiness or non-emptiness; one does not practice being like an illusion, being like a dream, being like a reflection of light, or being like an echo. Regarding forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), one likewise does not practice permanence or impermanence; one does not practice pleasure or suffering; one does not practice self or non-self; one does not practice purity or impurity; one does not practice emptiness or non-emptiness; one does not practice being like an illusion, being like a dream, being like a reflection of light, or being like an echo.

Regarding visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, one does not engage with them as permanent or impermanent; one does not engage with them as pleasant or unpleasant; one does not engage with them as self or non-self; one does not engage with them as pure or impure; one does not engage with them as empty or non-empty; one does not engage with them as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection, or like an echo.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Such dharmas possess vitarka, possess vicāra, possess saṃskāra, and possess vipaśyanā.

In this regard, a bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all formations—whether accompanied by vitarka, vicāra, saṃskāra, or vipaśyanā—are harmful to all formations; thus, by fully knowing all formations, they practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). This is what is called the proclamation of the conduct of bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the profound perfection of wisdom is inconceivable.”
Thereupon, the Buddha said to Suvīra: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said, Su-vīra!
Because form up to consciousness are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable."
Because the eye up to the mind are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because form up to phenomena are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
Because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable;
because dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable;
because affliction (*saṃkleśa*) is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable.
Because the fruits of karma are inconceivable, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because perversions, views, and hindrances are inconceivable, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
and because the realms of desire, form, and formlessness are inconceivable, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.

Because the self, sentient being, life-principle, living being, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, youth, agent, instigator, originator, co-originator, experiencer, causer of experience, knower, causer of knowledge, seer, and causer of seeing are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
Because the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;

because generosity, stinginess, ethical discipline, violation of ethical discipline, patience, anger, diligence, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, wisdom, and faulty wisdom are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
and because desire, hatred, and delusion are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.

Because the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because the immeasurables and the supernormal powers are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
and because the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
Because suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable;
because clear knowledge and liberation are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable;

and because the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of non-activity are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable.
Because the stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because the knowledge of the past, future, and present is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
Because non-attached wisdom is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable;
because *nirvāṇa* is inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable;
and because the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable.
Why is this? O Suvīra!

When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is called inconceivable because it is not produced by the mind, and it is also called inconceivable because it does not give rise to the mind.
"Furthermore, Suvīra! To say that the mind arises is an inversion;
to say that the mind does not arise is also an inversion. If one can thoroughly penetrate the fact that both the mind and mental factors are entirely non-existent, then that is not an inversion."
“Suvīra! The intrinsic nature of the mind does not have arising, origination, exhaustion, or cessation. Suvīra!”
"Associated with inversion means that the mind and mental factors arise, originate, perish, and cease.
O Suvīra, you should know that herein the mind can be demonstrated, and its arising through inversion can likewise be demonstrated."
“Suvīra! Foolish ordinary beings are unable to realize that the mind can be demonstrated, nor do they realize that it can also be demonstrated as arising from inversion.”

Because they fail to realize that which can be demonstrated, they are unable to correctly know the mind’s detachment, nor do they correctly know the detachment of its objects; consequently, they cling to the thought: "The mind is the self," "the mind belongs to me," "the mind depends upon me," and "the mind arises from me."
Having grasped that mind, they further grasp it as being wholesome, or grasp it as unwholesome; or grasp it as pleasure, or grasp it as suffering;
or grasp it as annihilation, or grasp it as permanence; or grasp it as a speculative view, or grasp it as the hindrances;
or grasp it as inversion, or grasp it as generosity, or grasp it as stinginess and greed. Or they grasp...
Holding to morality or violating morality; holding to patience or anger; holding to diligence or laziness;
holding to meditative concentration or distraction; holding to wisdom or false wisdom; holding to the three realms;
holding to dependent origination; holding to name-and-form; or holding to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Some cling to envy and stinginess; some cling to pride and so forth; some cling to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
some cling to the four great elements, space, and consciousness; some cling to sentient beings and the dharma-realm;
or some cling to the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the branches of the path.

Some cling to the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*); some cling to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
some cling to the knowledges (*vidyā*) and deliverance (*vimukti*); some cling to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);
some cling to the knowledge of non-activity (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*); some cling to the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; or some cling to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The stages of awakening, bodhisattvas, and buddhas; or clinging to the teachings of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas;
or clinging to non-attached wisdom; or clinging to parinirvāṇa; or clinging to buddha-wisdom;
or clinging to the primary and secondary marks; or clinging to buddha-fields; or clinging to the perfection of śrāvakas; or clinging to bodhisattvas.
Or they may grasp at other various defiled or purified phenomena. "Suvīra!

Bodhisattvas do not give rise to attachment toward such diverse gateways of Dharma. They know and see the inverted minds and mental factors that arise in sentient beings; thus, they never give rise to an inverted mind in any situation, nor do they rely on the mind to produce any inversions."
Why is this? O Suvīra!

When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they remain far removed from inverted minds and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma). They realize that the intrinsic nature of the mind is pure and luminous, and therein, no mind or mental factors ever arise.
“Suvīra! Foolish worldlings, relying upon objects of perception, give rise to minds and mental factors that grasp at having objects, and they grasp at the existence of all minds and mental factors.”
The assembly of bodhisattvas knows that the objects of focus and the minds and mental factors arising from them are entirely non-existent; therefore, they do not give rise to minds or mental factors.

“The Bodhisattva thus observes that the intrinsic nature of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) is pure and intrinsically luminous; yet, through the inversions of foolish beings, adventitious defilements are produced.

He further reflects: ‘Minds and mental factors arise based on objective referents (*ālambana*). Since one realizes that these referents do not exist, minds and mental factors cannot arise; and since they do not arise, they neither abide nor cease.’”
The nature of the mind and mental factors is luminously pure, free from all defilements, pristine, and delightful.
The nature of the mind does not arise, nor does it abide or cease; nor does it cause phenomena to arise, abide, and so forth. It is only that deluded worldlings falsely cling to these matters.
"In this way, the bodhisattva knows that the mind and mental factors are by nature unarisen, neither abiding nor ceasing, as they practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If bodhisattvas can practice in this manner, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom."
When practicing in this way, one does not form such thoughts:

"I am practicing the perfection of wisdom; I am now practicing the perfection of wisdom by relying on this; I am now practicing the perfection of wisdom by means of this; I am now practicing the perfection of wisdom from this."
If bodhisattvas should form such thoughts as:
"This is the perfection of wisdom; this is by means of the perfection of wisdom; this is based upon the perfection of wisdom; this belongs to the perfection of wisdom."
If one dwells upon that thought, one is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom without seeing or apprehending any of the perfections of wisdom, that is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Suvīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, it is the unsurpassed practice; when a bodhisattva...”
To practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is to practice purity;
for a bodhisattva to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way is to practice clarity;
for a bodhisattva to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way is to practice non-arising. For a bodhisattva to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way—
This is the practice of non-extinction; when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, it is the practice of transcendence.

When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, it is the practice that is difficult to subdue—namely, by all evil Māras, or the retinues of Māras, or others who possess signs, who engage in practices of apprehension, or who [cling to] a self.
...sentient beings, life-principles, born beings, nourished beings, persons, individuals,
mind-born beings, sons of Manu, agents, experiencers, knowers, and seers; all such views—
whether views of eternalism or nihilism, or views regarding the aggregates, or views regarding the sense bases, or...
Whether it be views regarding the various elements (*dhātu*), views regarding the Buddhas, views regarding the teachings (*dharma*), views regarding the Saṅgha, views regarding nirvāṇa,
or the notion of having attained realization; whether it be overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
the activities of greed, hatred, and delusion, the activities of perversion and the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), or those who set out by deviating from the path— none of these can subdue it.
"Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they transcend all worlds; none can equal them, for they are most honored and most supreme.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Suvīra: "It is so!
It is as you have said."
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
Thus, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they transcend all worlds; none can equal them, for they are most honored and most supreme."

All evil Māras—whether Māra devaputras, their retinues, or their armies—cannot subdue them; even all views that cling to the characteristics and nature of nirvāṇa cannot subdue them; and the practices of all foolish ordinary beings cannot subdue the practices undertaken by this bodhisattva.
"O Suvīra! This bodhisattva practice is not possessed by foolish ordinary beings;
it is also not possessed by those in training, those beyond training, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas."

"O Suvīra! If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas were to possess such a practice, they should not be called Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; they should be called Bodhisattvas, and they would attain the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses and other boundless qualities."
"O Suvīra! Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack this practice, they are not called Bodhisattvas, and they do not attain the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses and other boundless qualities."
“Suvīra! The profound perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattvas is the ground for the qualities of the four fearlessnesses and other virtues of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they take the realization of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and so forth as their task.
If bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will swiftly realize the qualities of a Tathāgata, such as the four fearlessnesses.

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas, before they have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, practice the profound perfection of wisdom through the power of their great vows or the power of the Tathāgatas’ protection, they will swiftly be able to gather the four fearlessnesses and other boundless qualities.”

Suvīra! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot aspire to or seek the qualities of a Buddha, such as the four fearlessnesses; nor do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, protect and sustain them so that they may realize those four fearlessnesses.
“Suvīra! By the power of their great vows and the power of the protection of all Tathāgatas, the assembly of bodhisattvas shall be able to realize the four fearlessnesses and so forth. Why is this?
“Suvīra! When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will certainly attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
What are these four analytical knowledges?”

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*): these are called the four analytical knowledges.

When the assembly of bodhisattvas accomplishes these four analytical knowledges, although they have not yet realized the sought-after unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, by the power of their great vows, they are able to encompass the qualities of a Buddha, such as the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know that he has accomplished the supreme roots of goodness of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and because they know that he has attained the ground of the merit of profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they diligently protect and mindfully attend to him with their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), causing him to receive the various Buddha-qualities such as the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to realize the four analytical knowledges and wishes to receive the roots of goodness of the qualities such as the four fearlessnesses, should study *prajñāpāramitā* and practice *prajñāpāramitā*, without giving rise to attachment.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they penetrate all phenomena— whether as cause, as origin,
as disappearance, or as cessation— and there is not the slightest phenomenon that does not accord with the perfection of wisdom."
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas understand, as they truly are, the characteristics of the cause, origin, cessation, and path of all phenomena.
Having understood the characteristics of the cause, origin, cessation, and path of phenomena, they neither cultivate nor eliminate form;
they likewise neither cultivate nor eliminate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and they neither cultivate nor eliminate the eye.
He neither cultivates nor abandons the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; he neither cultivates nor abandons forms;
he neither cultivates nor abandons sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
he neither cultivates nor abandons eye-consciousness; and he neither cultivates nor abandons ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
Nor does one cultivate or eliminate; one neither cultivates nor eliminates name-and-form, neither cultivates nor eliminates defilement or purity,
neither cultivates nor eliminates dependent origination, neither cultivates nor eliminates the perversions,
views, hindrances, or the tendencies of craving, and neither cultivates nor eliminates greed, hatred, or delusion.
One neither cultivates nor abandons the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; one neither cultivates nor abandons the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness;
one neither cultivates nor abandons the realm of sentient beings or the realm of phenomena;
and [one neither cultivates nor abandons] the self, the sentient being, the life-principle, the creature, the nourisher, or the person.

One neither cultivates nor abandons the person (*pudgala*), the mind-born (*manomaya*), the youthful (*māṇava*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the experiencer (*vedaka*), the knower (*jñātṛ*), or the seer (*draṣṭṛ*);
one neither cultivates nor abandons the views of annihilationism or eternalism;
and regarding generosity and stinginess, ethical discipline and its violation, patience and anger, and diligence...
They neither cultivate nor eliminate indolence, meditative concentration, distraction, wisdom, or faulty discernment;

they neither cultivate nor eliminate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the factors of the path;
and they neither cultivate nor eliminate the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, or meditative attainments.
They neither cultivate nor eliminate the abandonment of perversions; they neither cultivate nor eliminate [the truths of] suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they neither cultivate nor eliminate the immeasurables or the supernormal powers;
they neither cultivate nor eliminate the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of non-activity; and regarding ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—
The bodhisattva neither cultivates nor abandons the stages of a Buddha; he neither cultivates nor abandons ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or the Buddha-dharmas;
he neither cultivates nor abandons calm abiding (śamatha) or insight (vipaśyanā);
he neither cultivates nor abandons nirvāṇa; and he neither cultivates nor abandons the knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present.
One neither cultivates nor rejects the wisdom of non-attachment; one neither cultivates nor rejects the wisdom of the Buddha;
one neither cultivates nor rejects the various buddha-qualities such as fearlessness.
"Why is this? O Suvīra!
Form has no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or dispelled; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no intrinsic nature."
It cannot be cultivated or eliminated; the eye lacks intrinsic nature and thus cannot be cultivated or eliminated.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind also lack intrinsic nature and thus cannot be cultivated or eliminated. Visible forms lack intrinsic nature and thus cannot be cultivated or eliminated;
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena also lack intrinsic nature and thus cannot be cultivated or eliminated. The eye...

Consciousness has no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or eliminated; likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness have no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or eliminated.
Name-and-form have no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or eliminated;
defilement and purity have no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or eliminated; dependent origination has no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or eliminated.
Perversions, views, hindrances, and the tendencies of craving lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded;
greed, hatred, and delusion lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded; the realms of desire, form, and formlessness lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded;
and the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness [lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded].
Intrinsic nature cannot be cultivated or eliminated; the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or eliminated;
likewise, the self, sentient being, life-principle, creature, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, young brahmin, agent, experiencer, knower, and seer [cannot be cultivated or eliminated].
The absence of intrinsic nature cannot be cultivated or dispelled; the views of annihilationism and eternalism, being without intrinsic nature, cannot be cultivated or dispelled;

generosity, stinginess, ethical discipline, immorality, patience, anger, diligence, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, wisdom, and faulty wisdom—being without intrinsic nature—cannot [be cultivated or dispelled].

Cultivation and relinquishment: the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and factors of the path have no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or relinquished;
the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments have no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or relinquished;
the abandonment of inversions has no intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or relinquished; suffering...

The truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded; the immeasurables and the supernormal powers lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded;
the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of non-activity lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded;
and the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas [lack intrinsic nature and cannot be cultivated or discarded].

The absence of intrinsic nature cannot be cultivated or dispelled; the absence of intrinsic nature in ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the buddha-dharmas cannot be cultivated or dispelled;
the absence of intrinsic nature in calm abiding and insight cannot be cultivated or dispelled;
the absence of intrinsic nature in nirvāṇa cannot be cultivated or dispelled; and the wisdom and vision regarding the past, future, and present [cannot be cultivated or dispelled].
The intrinsic nature cannot be cultivated or eliminated; non-attached wisdom, being without intrinsic nature, cannot be cultivated or eliminated;

the Buddha-wisdom, being without intrinsic nature, cannot be cultivated or eliminated; and the various buddha-qualities such as fearlessness, being without intrinsic nature, cannot be cultivated or eliminated.
"Why is this? O Well-Valiant One!
Not even the slightest dharma-nature is the perfected reality; all are merely conventional designations, for within them there is not the slightest intrinsic nature."

Because they lack intrinsic nature, all things are not substantially real; all phenomena have non-existence as their very nature. Therefore, all phenomena are without reality and without arising. Why is this?
“Suvīra! All inverted phenomena are not truly existent; all phenomena arise from inversion, and all inversions lack any real nature.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, and when one seeks for an intrinsic nature, it is entirely unfindable; therefore, they all take the absence of nature as their nature.
“Suvīra! That which is without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) is called ‘without intrinsic nature’ because it is neither real nor produced.

This demonstrates that because intrinsic nature is not truly existent, it is called ‘without intrinsic nature. If intrinsic nature does not exist, then it cannot be cultivated, nor can it be eliminated.”
Because that which arises from inversion does not truly exist, it can neither be cultivated nor eliminated. Why is this?
O Well-Valiant One!

Since all phenomena have non-existence as their nature, they are devoid of intrinsic nature and are therefore not substantial entities. Because they are not substantial entities, there is neither cultivation nor elimination.

“Suvīra! When the bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell within all phenomena with the vision of reality as it is and practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they neither cultivate nor eliminate any phenomenon; this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
"O Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way and abide in this way, they will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to full completion."
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to a mind associated with the signs of form, nor do they give rise to a mind associated with the signs of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not give rise to a mind associated with the signs of the eye, nor do they give rise to a mind associated with the signs of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."

He does not give rise to a mind associated with the characteristics of unattractive forms, nor does he give rise to a mind associated with the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mental consciousness;

he does not give rise to a mind associated with the characteristics of visible forms, nor does he give rise to a mind associated with the characteristics of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects;
he does not give rise to a mind accompanied by attachment, nor does he give rise to a mind accompanied by aversion.
A mind accompanied by stinginess and greed; a mind accompanied by the arising of afflictions;
a mind accompanied by anger and resentment; a mind accompanied by indolence; a mind accompanied by distraction;
a mind accompanied by wrong wisdom; and a mind accompanied by the fetter of sensual desire—none of these arise.
He does not give rise to a mind accompanied by attachment to form; he does not give rise to a mind accompanied by attachment to the formless;
he does not give rise to a mind accompanied by sensual desire; he does not give rise to a mind accompanied by divisiveness;
he does not give rise to a mind accompanied by wrong view; he does not give rise to a mind accompanied by attachment to wealth and status; he does not...
They give rise to a mind that clings to that which accompanies wealth and nobility, but they do not give rise to a mind that clings to that which accompanies great riches or eminent lineage;
they do not give rise to a mind that clings to rebirth in the heavens, nor a mind that clings to the realm of desire, nor a mind that clings to the realms of form or formlessness. They do not...
They give rise to the mind of the stage of the śrāvaka, but do not give rise to the mind of the pratyekabuddha stage;
they do not give rise to a mind associated with attachment to the practices of bodhisattvas, nor even a mind associated with the view of nirvāṇa.

"Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished such a pure mind, although they give rise to pervasive loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings, they are able to eliminate the notion of 'sentient beings.
They abide without grasping at the notion of sentient beings, and they likewise have no attachment to the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), having accomplished sublime wisdom and skillful means."
Because they have accomplished such dharmas, they are able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without attachment and swiftly bring it to fulfillment.

Because these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and swiftly fulfill it, they neither grasp nor cling to form (rūpa); they likewise neither grasp nor cling to feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna).
They neither grasp nor cling to the eye; they likewise neither grasp nor cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There is no grasping and no clinging toward form; likewise, there is no grasping and no clinging toward sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
There is no grasping and no clinging toward eye-consciousness; likewise, there is no grasping and no clinging toward ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
There is no grasping and no clinging toward name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); there is no grasping toward defilement or purification.
Without grasping; without appropriation or grasping toward dependent origination; without appropriation or grasping toward the perversions, views, hindrances, or modes of craving;
without appropriation or grasping toward greed, hatred, or delusion;
without appropriation or grasping toward the realms of desire, form, or formlessness; [without appropriation or grasping] toward earth, water, fire, or wind.

The element of space and the element of consciousness are without grasping and without clinging; likewise, one is without grasping and without clinging toward the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

One is without grasping and without clinging toward a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a living being, a nourisher, a spirit, a person (*pudgala*), a mind-born being, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a perceiver.
The seer has no grasping and no clinging; they have no grasping and no clinging toward the views of annihilationism or eternalism;

they have no grasping and no clinging toward generosity or stinginess, ethical discipline or immorality, patience or anger, diligence or laziness, meditative concentration or distraction, wisdom or false wisdom; they have no grasping toward mindfulness...
They are without grasping or attachment toward the bases of power, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the factors of the path;
they are without grasping or attachment toward the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the attainments;
they are without grasping or attachment toward suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; and they are without grasping toward the immeasurables and the supernormal powers.
There is no grasping; one has no appropriation or grasping regarding the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of non-activity;
one has no appropriation or grasping regarding the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas;
and one has no appropriation or grasping regarding the qualities of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas.
They are without grasping or attachment toward *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; they are without grasping or attachment toward the realm of *nirvāṇa*;
they are without grasping or attachment toward the knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present; they are without grasping or attachment toward unattached wisdom;
and they are without grasping or attachment toward the Buddha’s wisdom, powers, fearlessnesses, and other boundless qualities of a Buddha.
The Dharma is without grasping and without clinging; it is without grasping or clinging toward the severance of perversions, views, hindrances, and so forth. Why is this?
"O Suvīra! Because all dharmas cannot be grasped, cannot be appropriated, and there is no one who can grasp them, nor anyone who can appropriate them. Why is this?"
"O Suvīra! There is not the slightest dharma that should be grasped or appropriated, nor is there the slightest dharma that is capable of grasping or appropriating. Why is this so?
If that which appropriates and that which is appropriated are both unattainable. Why is this?
O Well-Valiant One!
Because all phenomena are not solid or substantial, being like illusory things;
because all phenomena lack self-mastery, as a solid or substantial nature cannot be found;
and because all phenomena are like reflections and shadows, being ungraspable.
Because all phenomena are entirely false and deceptive, lacking intrinsic nature;
because all phenomena are like masses of foam, incapable of being grasped or rubbed;
because all phenomena are like floating bubbles, arising and then quickly perishing.
Because all phenomena are like a mirage, arising from inversion;
because all phenomena are like a plantain tree, lacking any solid core within;
because all phenomena are like the moon reflected in water, incapable of being grasped.
Because all phenomena are like rainbows, being products of false discrimination;
because all phenomena are devoid of functional activity, being incapable of initiation;
and because all phenomena are like empty fists, lacking any real nature or characteristics.
“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas have thus observed all phenomena, they neither grasp at, nor cling to, nor dwell upon, nor adhere to any phenomena.”

Suvīra! All bodhisattvas do not deeply rely on or trust any phenomena, do not give rise to grasping or attachment, and do not produce stubborn adherence; they practice the perfection of wisdom without any craving or affection.
“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way and abide in this way, they will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to full completion.”
"Furthermore, Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not train in form, nor do they train for the sake of transcending form;
they do not train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they train for the sake of transcending feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
One does not train for the arising of form, nor does one train for the cessation of form;
one does not train for the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one train for the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not train for the sake of disciplining form, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining form;

one does not train for the sake of disciplining feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
One does not train for the sake of subduing or transforming form, nor for the sake of entering into or abiding in form;

one does not train for the sake of subduing or transforming feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor for the sake of entering into or abiding in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not train in the eye, nor do they train for the sake of transcending the eye;
they do not train in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor do they train for the sake of transcending the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”
One does not train in the arising of the eye, nor does one train in the cessation of the eye;
one does not train in the arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does one train in the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One does not train for the sake of disciplining the eye, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining the eye;
one does not train for the sake of disciplining the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One does not train for the sake of subduing or shifting the eye, nor for the sake of entering into or abiding in the eye;
one does not train for the sake of subduing or shifting the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor for the sake of entering into or abiding in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they do not train in form, nor do they train for the sake of transcending form;
they do not train in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena, nor do they train for the sake of transcending sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena.”
One does not train for the arising of form, nor does one train for the cessation of form;
one does not train for the arising of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does one train for the cessation of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
One does not train for the sake of disciplining forms, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining forms;

one does not train for the sake of disciplining sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
One does not train for the sake of subduing or transforming form, nor for the sake of entering or abiding in form;

one does not train for the sake of subduing or transforming sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor for the sake of entering or abiding in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they do not train in visual consciousness, nor do they train for the sake of transcending visual consciousness;

they do not train in auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness, nor do they train for the sake of transcending auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.”
One does not train in the arising of visual consciousness, nor does one train in the cessation of visual consciousness;

one does not train in the arising of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness, nor does one train in the cessation of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.
One does not train for the sake of disciplining eye-consciousness, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining eye-consciousness;

one does not train for the sake of disciplining ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor does one train for the sake of not disciplining ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
One does not train for the sake of subduing or shifting the eye-consciousness, nor for the sake of entering into or abiding in the eye-consciousness;

one does not train for the sake of subduing or shifting the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor for the sake of entering into or abiding in the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 598. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Seven of the Sixteenth Section on Prajñāpāramitā: “Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they do not train in form as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, empty or non-empty, self or non-self; nor do they train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, empty or non-empty, self or non-self.

“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they do not train regarding the eye as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as empty or non-empty, or as self or non-self; nor do they train regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as empty or non-empty, or as self or non-self.”

“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not train in form as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as empty or not empty, as self or selfless; nor do they train in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as empty or not empty, as self or selfless.”

“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they do not train in visual consciousness as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, empty or non-empty, self or non-self; nor do they train in auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, empty or non-empty, self or non-self.”
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not take as their object the past, future, or present formations of form; nor do they take as their object the past, future, or present formations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not take as their object the past, future, or present activities of the eye; nor do they take as their object the past, future, or present activities of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”

“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not take as their object forms—whether past, future, or present—and they likewise do not take as their objects sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena—whether past, future, or present.”

“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas train in this way, they do not take as an object the past, future, or present activity of eye-consciousness; nor do they take as an object the past, future, or present activity of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.”
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, although they observe the past through the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness, they do not engage with the past by means of the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness;

although they observe the future through the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness, they do not engage with the future by means of the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness."
Although one observes the present by way of the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness, one does not practice emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness with respect to the present.

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, although they contemplate the past as empty, selfless, devoid of what belongs to a self, impermanent, non-eternal, and non-durable—abiding in the dharma that is unchanging and immutable—they do not practice with respect to the past in such a manner;

although they contemplate the future as empty, selfless, devoid of what belongs to a self, impermanent, non-eternal, and non-durable—abiding in the dharma that is unchanging and immutable—they do not practice with respect to the future in such a manner.”

Although one contemplates that the present is empty, selfless, devoid of "mine," impermanent, non-eternal, and non-abiding, and dwells in the dharma of immutability, one does not practice with respect to the present in such a manner.
“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way and abide in this way, they will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to full completion.”
"Excellent valor!
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, no evil Māras will be able to find an opportunity against them.
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will universally be able to recognize all demonic activities and will not be led astray or deprived by them."
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, they do not take form as an object, nor do they take feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as objects;
they do not take the eye as an object, nor do they take the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as objects.
It does not take form as its object, nor does it take sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena as its object;
it does not take eye-consciousness as its object, nor does it take ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness as its object;
it does not take name-and-form as its object, nor does it take defilement or purity as its object, nor does it take perversions, views, or hindrances as its object.
The practice of loving-kindness does not take as its object greed, hatred, or delusion; it does not take as its object self, sentient beings, and so forth;
it does not take as its object annihilationism or eternalism; it does not take as its object the finite or the infinite; it does not take as its object the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
it does not take as its object dependent origination; and it does not take as its object earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness.
Regarding the realms: it does not take the realm of sentient beings or the realm of phenomena as its object; it does not take reality or falsehood as its object;
it does not take bondage or liberation as its object; it does not take the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion as its object;
nor does it take generosity or stinginess, ethical discipline or transgression, patience or anger, and diligence or laziness as its object.
Laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, wisdom, and faulty wisdom do not take as their objects the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power,
the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the factors of the path; they do not take as their objects the abandonment of the perversions,
nor do they take as their objects the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, or attainments, nor do they take as their objects loving-kindness.
Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity do not take suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path as their object;
they do not take the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of non-activity as their object; they do not take the knowledge of non-attachment as their object;
they do not take the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas as their object; they do not take ordinary beings or śrāvakas... [as their object].
Pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-dharma do not rely on supernormal powers or knowledge-and-vision; they do not rely on liberation;
they do not rely on the knowledge-and-vision of liberation; they do not rely on nirvāṇa; they do not rely on knowledge-and-vision of the past, future, or present;
they do not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom, powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth; and they do not rely on buddha-fields.
It is pure; it does not take as its object the purity of the marks and signs, nor the perfection of the śrāvakas, nor the perfection of the pratyekabuddhas, nor the perfection of the bodhisattvas.
Why is this? O Suvīra!

Because all phenomena are not objects of cognition, because all phenomena are not subjects of cognition, and because no phenomenon possesses anything to be grasped, one cannot speak of them as having an object of cognition.

“Suvīra! If there is an object of perception, there is movement, conceptual attachment, and grasping. If there is grasping, there is sorrow and suffering, as well as the arising of intense arrows of grief, lamentation, and affliction.”
"Excellent valor!
If there is an object of perception, there is bondage and no path to deliverance; by this, all sorrow and suffering increase.
Excellent valor!"

If there is an object of perception, there is reliance and grasping, agitation and conceptual proliferation; if there is an object of perception, there are various forms of strife, quarreling, and contention; if there is an object of perception, there are various forms of ignorance and deluded darkness; if there is an object of perception, there is fear; if there is an object of perception, there is the snare of Māra and the bondage of Māra; if there is an object of perception, there is the oppression of suffering and the seeking of security.

"O Suvīra! When a bodhisattva perceives such various faults and afflictions as these, they do not take conditions upon themselves regarding all phenomena; because there is nothing to be taken as a condition, they have no grasping toward any phenomenon. Because there is no grasping, they abide without attachment toward any phenomenon."

In this way, although the bodhisattva has no object of focus, they attain mastery over meditative concentration regarding objects; and although they attain mastery over meditative concentration regarding objects, they have no reliance or attachment, nor do they abide anywhere.
"Excellent valor!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will be able to remain without攀缘 (clinging to objects), without attachment, and without contention regarding all phenomena, dwelling untainted by any phenomena."
“Suvīra! These bodhisattvas, having attained liberation from all objects of focus and phenomena, practice the perfection of wisdom.”

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way and abide in this way, they will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to completion. No evil Māras will be able to obstruct them; the hosts and retinues of Māra cannot seize them; those seeking their faults will ultimately find none, nor can they disturb them through skillful means.

Furthermore, they will be able to subdue Māra and his armies, universally recognize all demonic activities, act with sovereign mastery without following such activities, and cause the palaces of all Māras to tremble and burn.”
He is also able to subdue all non-Buddhists and cannot be subdued by non-Buddhists;
he is also able to crush and destroy all opposing doctrines and cannot be crushed or destroyed by opposing doctrines.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas practice in this way, they do not dwell in conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding form; they likewise do not dwell in conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

They do not dwell in conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the eye; they likewise do not dwell in conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."

He does not dwell on conceptualization regarding form, nor does he engage in discursive differentiation; he likewise does not dwell on conceptualization regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does he engage in discursive differentiation.

He does not dwell on conceptualization regarding eye-consciousness, nor does he engage in discursive differentiation; he likewise does not dwell on conceptualization regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor does he engage in discursive differentiation.
By reason of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding names and forms;

they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding defilement and purity; they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding dependent origination;

they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the perversions, the hindrances of views, or the tendencies of craving; and they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding annihilationism or eternalism.
They do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;

they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the realm of sentient beings or the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding greed, hatred, or delusion;
and they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding what is true or what is false.
They do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness;
they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding bondage or liberation;

and they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a living being, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, a seer, or any such notions thereof.

He does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding generosity and stinginess, ethical discipline and transgression, patience and anger, diligence and laziness, meditative concentration and distraction, or wisdom and false intelligence;

he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, or the factors of the path;
and he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the abandonment of the perversions and so forth.
They do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, or meditative attainments;

they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity;
and they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of non-activity.

He does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas; he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the dharmas of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.

He does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding supernormal powers and knowledge-vision; he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding knowledge-vision of the past, future, and present;
he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding unattached knowledge-vision.
They do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding clarity and liberation;
they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas.
He does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the purity of the primary and secondary marks;
he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the purity of the Buddha-field;
he does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the perfection of the śrāvakas.
One does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the perfection of the Pratyekabuddhas;
one does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding the perfection of the Bodhisattvas.
"Why is this? O Suvīra!
Where there is conceptualization, there is differentiation; where there is no conceptualization, there is no differentiation."

All foolish ordinary beings arise from conceptual construction; their perceptions all arise from divergent conceptualization. Therefore, the bodhisattva does not give rise to conceptual construction, nor does he have divergent conceptualization.
“Suvīra! To speak of conceptualization is the first extreme;

to speak of non-conceptualization is the second extreme. Where one does not give rise to conceptualization and there is no non-conceptualization, in that place one is far removed from both extremes, and even a middle does not exist.”
"O Suvīra! If one says that 'existence' exists, this too is conceptualization; to conceptualize existence is also to fall into the extreme of existence.

Wherever there is conceptualization, there is also divergent conceptualization. For this reason, there is no cessation of conceptualization, nor does the meaning of divergent conceptualization cease."

If there is no conceptualization regarding a certain object, then there is no discursive differentiation regarding that object; by virtue of this causal condition, there is the sense of having abandoned both conceptualization and discursive differentiation.
"O Suvīra! That which is called 'the severance of conceptual discrimination' means that within this there is nothing at all to be severed. Why is this? "

“Suvīra! Because inversion is initiated by the power of non-existence, falsehood, discrimination, and false discrimination, when these are stilled, inversion also ceases to exist; since inversion does not exist, there is nothing at all to be abandoned.”

“Suvīra! That which is ‘nothing to be abandoned’ should be understood as a designation for the abandonment of suffering; that is to say, because there is not even the slightest suffering to be abandoned therein, it is called the ‘abandonment of suffering.’”

If the intrinsic nature of suffering possessed even the slightest bit of reality that could be severed, then there would be something to be severed; however, because the intrinsic nature of suffering lacks even the slightest bit of reality, there is nothing to be severed. Rather, seeing that suffering is non-existent is what is called the "severance of suffering. This means that because one thoroughly knows that suffering has no intrinsic nature whatsoever and not even a fraction of it can be found, it is termed the "severance of suffering."

"O Subhānavīra! That which consists in the total absence of conceptualization and the absence of discursive differentiation regarding suffering is called the 'pacification of suffering'; this means that suffering is not allowed to arise."
If bodhisattvas can see in this way, they will not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding any phenomena.
O Well-Vigorous One!
This is called a bodhisattva’s thorough knowledge of the nature of conceptualization and discursive differentiation, as they practice the perfection of wisdom.

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way and abide in this way, they will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to fulfillment. No evil Māras will be able to create obstacles; they will be able to recognize all the activities initiated by the hosts of Māras; and in whatever they do, they will not follow after the deeds of Māra but will act with sovereign mastery, causing the evil Māras to naturally retreat and disperse. They will crush those armies so that they gradually diminish, and with body and mind at ease, they will be free from all fear, such that the hosts of evil Māras cannot disturb or afflict them.”
He brings to rest all causes for rebirth in the evil destinies and cuts off all the crooked paths of the world.
Free from all darkness, he crosses over the torrential floods and attains the pure eye regarding all phenomena.
They act as a great light for all classes of sentient beings, upholding the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken.
Having realized the true path and the equality of all phenomena, they give rise to the pure Dharma-eye out of compassion for sentient beings.

Endowed with diligence, they abandon all laziness; having attained patience, they distance themselves from a mind of anger. Entering superior meditative concentration, they remain without dependence; attaining true *prajñā*, they achieve penetrating wisdom. They dispel regret and distance themselves from the hindrances and entanglements; escaping the snare of evil Māras, they sever the web of craving. Abiding in right mindfulness, they forget nothing.
Having attained pure ethical discipline, they reach the further shore of pure precepts;
abiding securely in merit, they are free from all faults and afflictions.
Having attained the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, they are immovable, and no other doctrines can overcome them.
They attain the purity of all phenomena, never again to fall away; they proclaim all phenomena and thereby attain fearlessness.
Entering into great assemblies, their minds are free from timidity; they bestow the sublime Dharma without any secrecy or stinginess.
By means of the path of equality, one purifies all paths; one vows to leave the wrong paths and cultivates that which ought to be cultivated.
One perfumes that which ought to be perfumed with pure dharmas, and purifies that which ought to be purified with pure wisdom.

His capacity and magnanimity are as deep and vast as the great ocean; serene and unmoving, they are difficult to fathom. This ocean of Dharma is boundless, exceeding all measure and calculation. O Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, they will accomplish these and other boundless merits; such merits are so difficult to fathom that none can know their limit except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, their exquisite form does not diminish, their wealth and status do not diminish, their retinue does not diminish, their lineage does not diminish, their family does not diminish, and their realm does not diminish;
they are not born in border regions, they do not encounter the states of non-leisure, they do not dwell together with defiled and evil sentient beings, nor do they associate with impure occupations."
One's own mind does not regress, and wisdom does not diminish;
having heard various Dharma gates from others, one is able to integrate them all into the nature of equality;
one succeeds to and flourishes the lineage of the Buddhas and the knowledge of omniscience, causing it to always thrive without interruption.

Having already attained illumination regarding all Buddha-dharmas and having drawn near to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), if an evil Māra should come to them with the intent to cause disturbance, he shall reduce that Māra and his entire retinue to ashes; their eloquence will suddenly vanish and their snares will be utterly severed.
Even if ten million Māras and their armies should come together to harass them, their minds remain unshakable.
Thereupon, the evil Māra and his hosts fled in terror and scattered, thinking to themselves:

"This Bodhisattva has now transcended my realm; he shall no longer traverse it, nor dwell within it, nor be attached to it. He will cause all other sentient beings to likewise emerge from my domain and attain a state of serene liberation."
At that time, having formed this thought, the various evil Māras were filled with grief and lamentation, and said to one another:
"Now this Bodhisattva is diminishing our kinsmen and factions, rendering us powerless."
Having spoken thus, each gave rise to sorrow, suffering, regret, and remorse.
"Furthermore, Subhānavīra!
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, cultivates the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and assembles with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*..."

At that time, the palaces of Māra all lost their majestic radiance, and everywhere signs of smoke and flames gradually arose. The evil Māras were struck with terror, grief, and anguish; as if their hearts were wounded by blades or pierced by poisoned arrows, they all lamented together, saying these words:
"Now this Bodhisattva shall cause sentient beings not to be incited by us;
now this Bodhisattva shall cause sentient beings to exit our realm; now this Bodhisattva shall cause sentient beings to be liberated..."
"In our realm, this Bodhisattva shall now cause sentient beings not to dwell within the sphere of 'I';
this Bodhisattva shall now cause sentient beings to sever and extinguish the realm of 'I'; this Bodhisattva shall now cause sentient beings to destroy the snare-net of 'I';
this Bodhisattva shall now uproot sentient beings and cause them to emerge forever from the mire of all desires."
Now this bodhisattva shall cause sentient beings to be liberated from the net of all views;
now this bodhisattva shall cause sentient beings to emerge from the deviant paths of the hindrances; now this bodhisattva establishes sentient beings, causing them to abide in the true path;
now this bodhisattva leads all sentient beings, causing them to forever emerge from the dense forest of all views.
"O Suvīra! When those evil Māras see that this bodhisattva possesses such superior and ultimate benefits, they become distressed and afflicted with grief, as if an arrow had pierced their hearts."
For example, just as a person who has lost a great treasure trove achieves vast sorrow, anxiety, and distress;
