so too does this evil Māra, with deep regret in his heart, feel as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, suffering from sorrow and distress, remaining in a state of alarm day and night, finding no joy in his own seat.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!
When a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, cultivates the profound perfection of wisdom, and assembles with the profound perfection of wisdom..."
At that time, all the evil Māras gathered in one place and, contemplating means to destroy the Bodhisattva, said to one another:
"What stratagem should we now devise, and what deed should we perform, to ruin the right practice cultivated by this Bodhisattva?"

At that time, the host of evil Māras harbored doubts and confusion; distressed and joyless as if pierced by poisoned arrows, they exhorted one another to go to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling to watch for his vulnerabilities and manifest terrifying sights.

By virtue of the majestic power of this Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), even if all the hosts of evil Māras were to exhaust their supernatural powers, they would not be able to move even a single hair-tip of the Bodhisattva, much less cause any alteration in the Bodhisattva’s body or mind.

At that time, the various evil Māras realized that the Bodhisattva was free from such things as alarm, terror, and horripilation; thus, they employed further expedients of various kinds of enchantments. However, because their own minds and spirits were both weakened by harboring fear, none of these enchantments could succeed.
At that time, the Evil Māra thought to himself:
"I am not even able to destroy this Bodhisattva, much less my own retinue or anyone else!
Having thought this, his fear and terror grew as his strength failed and his stratagems were exhausted; he returned to his own palace and remained there dwelling in sorrow and anxiety."

When a bodhisattva thus practices the perfection of wisdom and possesses such great power, even the retinues of Māra cannot cause their mind to become confused for as long as a finger-snap; how much less could they create any other obstacles!
“Suvīra! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they accomplish such merit, wisdom, and great majestic power.”

Even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to transform into Māras, and each of them were to lead a host of Māras equal in number to that total, coming before the Bodhisattva for the purpose of causing disturbance, they would be unable to obstruct the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) even by exhausting their supernatural powers.
Why is this? O Well-Vigorous One!

At that time, because the bodhisattva has accomplished such a sword-like power of profound prajñā, and has likewise accomplished the inconceivable, immeasurable, and unequaled power of prajñā, he cannot be overcome by any of the violent and evil māra armies.
"O Suvīra! That which is called the great sword is the sword of prajñā;
that which is called the great blade is the blade of prajñā."
Now, that which is called "great power" refers to the power of *prajñā*.
Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is not a sphere within which the various Māras can operate.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!..."

There are certain external sages who have attained the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, transcending the realm of the Māra of desire to be born in the various Brahma heavens and the stages of the four formless realms.
Even the mundane sublime wisdom constantly accomplished by Bodhisattvas is not within their range of activity, let alone the true Prajñāpāramitā!
How much less could Māra act within this sphere!

Even for those external seers who have attained the meditative concentrations of the form and formless realms and possess sublime wisdom, this is not within their range of activity, let alone for the Prajñāpāramitā!
"O Suvīra! When a bodhisattva accomplishes the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), at that time the bodhisattva is said to be one who has accomplished great majestic power;
if one accomplishes the power of wisdom, they are said to be one who has accomplished the sword of sharp intelligence."
If one achieves the sharp sword of prajñā, they are said to have achieved the sharp sword of wisdom.
Such a person cannot be subdued by any of the demonic armies, but can instead subdue all demonic hosts.
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas accomplish the sword of sharp wisdom—the perfection of prajñāpāramitā—and possess great power, these bodhisattvas have no point of reliance in any place, and they likewise have no reliance in whatever they do."
Why is this? O Suvīra!
If there is a basis, there is shifting; if there is shifting, there is agitation; if there is agitation, there is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"O Suvīra! If sentient beings have dependence, movement, agitation, and conceptual proliferation, those sentient beings follow the course of Māra’s power and have not escaped the realm of Māra."

“Suvīra! Even if sentient beings should be reborn as high as the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), remaining dependent upon it and bound to that basis, support, and locus, they will inevitably fall back into the realm of Māra; they have not yet escaped the snares of the evil Māra, and the threads of Māra’s noose constantly pursue them.”
Such as the son of Mṛgāra and Ārāḍa Kālāma, along with all other sages and non-Buddhists who rely on the formless, and who are bound to their respective supports, bases, and locations.
Suvīra! If bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom, and assemble with the profound perfection of wisdom.
These bodhisattvas have no point of reliance in any place, nor do they rely on anything in whatever they do. "Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom with courageous diligence and abide in accordance with it, at that time the bodhisattva does not rely on form, nor does he rely on feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness."
They do not rely on the eye, nor do they rely on the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not rely on forms, nor do they rely on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects;
they do not rely on eye-consciousness, nor do they rely on ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
Not relying on name-and-form; not relying on perversions, views, the hindrances, or various tendencies of craving;
not relying on dependent origination; not relying on the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
not relying on a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, or a person.

The person (*pudgala*), the mind-born (*manuja*), the youth (*māṇava*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the experiencer (*vedaka*), the knower (*jñātṛ*), the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), and all such conceptualizations do not rely upon the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness;
they do not rely upon the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) or the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); nor do they rely upon the first dhyāna...
Reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one does not rely on the craving for existence, nor rely on the craving for non-existence;
one does not rely on annihilationism or eternalism, nor rely on existence, nor rely on non-existence;
one does not rely on generosity or stinginess, nor on ethical discipline or transgression, nor on patience or anger.
Vigor, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, wisdom, and faulty wisdom;
not relying on the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the branches of the path;
not relying on the abandonment of perversions, nor relying on the meditative concentrations, liberations, or meditative absorptions.
...the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); not relying on suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path;

not relying on the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), or the knowledge of non-activity (*anabhisaṃskārajñāna*); not relying on the vision of unattached knowledge (*asaṅgajñānadarśana*);
not relying on clarity (*vidyā*) and liberation (*vimukti*); not relying on the vision of the knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*); and not relying on ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The stages of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and buddha do not rely upon the dharmas of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas;
they do not rely upon nirvāṇa; they do not rely upon knowledge and vision regarding the past, future, or present; they do not rely upon the equality of the three times; they do not rely upon—
The Buddha’s wisdom, powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, do not rely upon the knowledge of all modes, do not rely upon the perfection of the marks and signs,
do not rely upon the perfection of the buddha-field, do not rely upon the perfection of the assembly of śrāvakas,
do not rely upon the perfection of the assembly of bodhisattvas, and do not rely upon any phenomena. They do not rely...
He ceases transmigration; he does not rely on agitation, nor does he rely on conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Through non-reliance, he dispels everything; yet he does not cling even to the path of non-reliance, nor does he depend upon or grasp at non-reliance. He does not apprehend this as reliance, nor apprehend abiding in this reliance, nor apprehend belonging to this reliance, nor apprehend relying upon this reliance; even toward that which is relied upon, there is no dependence or grasping.

In this way, the bodhisattva dwells with respect to all bases (āśraya) without reliance, without attainment, without grasping, without appropriation, without discourse, and without delight; being unattached, they are not defiled by any base, nor do they encounter any obstruction regarding those bases, and they realize the pure dharmas of all bases.

“Suvīra! These bodhisattvas, relying upon all dharmas and depending upon pure, subtle wisdom and vision, practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). By this means, evil Māras cannot find an opportunity, and the hosts of Māra’s armies cannot subdue them; rather, they are able to subdue all the armies of Māra.”

"Furthermore, Suvīra! If bodhisattvas have not yet generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they should first accumulate immeasurable and innumerable provisions of roots of goodness; they should extensively make offerings to the Buddhas and serve many spiritual friends; they should inquire about the essential points of the Dharma at the abodes of many Buddhas; they should be fully endowed with the aspiration and resolve for great vows; they should delight in practicing generosity toward all sentient beings; they should revere and uphold pure ethical discipline; they should be fully endowed with patience and gentleness; they should possess courageous diligence free from all laziness; they should revere the cultivation of pure, stainless meditative concentration; and they should respectfully study and train in pure wisdom."

Once these bodhisattvas have generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should furthermore diligently train in the perfection of wisdom, using the power of their wisdom to subdue all hosts of Māras.
He constantly maintains this thought:
"May no evil Māra seek out my vulnerabilities to create disturbances.
By the power of this, he ensures that no evil Māras can find an opportunity to obstruct his practice, nor does he cause the hosts of Māras to give rise to such thoughts:
"I shall watch for an opportunity to find a flaw in this bodhisattva, so as to create disturbances and obstacles to his practice.
As soon as such a thought arises, he immediately brings himself to awareness:
"If I do this, I will surely encounter great suffering."
Thereupon, he gave rise to a sense of great terror, thinking:
"Lest I now lose my life, I must cease this agitated mind.
Thus, the evil intent of Māra’s army vanished.
Suvīra! For this reason, the hosts of Māra cannot obstruct the bodhisattva’s training in the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to pure desire and superior resolve, deeply respect it with their whole hearts, praise its merits, and regard it as the Great Teacher;
and if, upon hearing the teachings corresponding to the six *pāramitās*, they likewise do not give rise to hesitation or doubt;
Upon hearing the profound Dharma, their minds are not deluded or mistaken, nor do they give rise to hesitation or doubt;
they never perform actions that would result in the deprivation of the Dharma, nor do they conceive a mind that seeks such deprivation;
they exhort immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to believe in, accept, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
They exhort and encourage immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to believe, accept, and practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

These bodhisattvas first purify their mental dispositions (*āśaya*); all their intentions are free from defilement. No hosts of Māras can obstruct them, nor can they find an opportunity to exploit them. They are able to recognize all the activities of Māra; no evil Māras can lead them astray or deprive them [of their resolve], and they do not act according to the power of Māra’s mastery.
“Suvīra! For this reason, the retinues of Māras cannot disturb these bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Suvīra!”

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice with the mark of conjunction regarding form, nor do they practice with the mark of separation regarding form; they do not practice with the mark of conjunction regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they practice with the mark of separation regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

they do not practice with the mark of conjunction regarding the eye, nor do they practice with the mark of separation regarding the eye; they do not practice with the mark of conjunction regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor do they practice with the mark of separation regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;

they do not practice with the mark of conjunction regarding forms, nor do they practice with the mark of separation regarding forms; they do not practice with the mark of conjunction regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena, nor do they practice with the mark of separation regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena.
One does not practice the conjunction or separation of eye-consciousness; one does not practice the conjunction or separation of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

One does not practice the conjunction or separation of the characteristics of form; one does not practice the conjunction or separation of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

One does not practice the conjunction or separation of the characteristic of the eye; one does not practice the conjunction or separation of the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

They do not practice with respect to the signs of conjunction or separation regarding forms; they do not practice with respect to the signs of conjunction or separation regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas;

they do not practice with respect to the signs of conjunction or separation regarding eye-consciousness; and they do not practice with respect to the signs of conjunction or separation regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
"One does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding form; one does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding the eye; one does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding forms; one does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena."

They do not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding eye-consciousness; they do not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

They do not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding forms as objects; they do not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding feelings, perceptions, formations, or consciousness as objects.

They do not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding the eye as a condition; they do not engage with the signs of purity or impurity regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as conditions.

They do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity regarding forms; they do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.

They do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity regarding eye-consciousness; they do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

"One does not engage in the arising of the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding form; one does not engage in the arising of the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

One does not engage in the arising of the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding the eye; one does not engage in the arising of the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

One does not engage in the arising of the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding forms; one does not engage in the arising of the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena."

They do not engage in the arising of the marks of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding eye-consciousness; they do not engage in the arising of the marks of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

"One does not practice by taking as an object the characteristics of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of form; one does not practice by taking as an object the characteristics of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

One does not practice by taking as an object the characteristics of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of the eye; one does not practice by taking as an object the characteristics of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

One does not practice by taking as an object the characteristics of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of forms; one does not practice by taking as an object the characteristics of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena."

One does not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding the intrinsic purity or impurity of eye-consciousness; one does not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding the intrinsic purity or impurity of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

"One does not practice with regard to the characteristics of conjunction or separation concerning whether the intrinsic nature of form is pure or impure; one does not practice with regard to the characteristics of conjunction or separation concerning whether the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is pure or impure.

One does not practice with regard to the characteristics of conjunction or separation concerning whether the intrinsic nature of the eye is pure or impure; one does not practice with regard to the characteristics of conjunction or separation concerning whether the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind is pure or impure.

One does not practice with regard to the characteristics of conjunction or separation concerning whether the intrinsic nature of forms is pure or impure; one does not practice with regard to the characteristics of conjunction or separation concerning whether the intrinsic nature of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena is pure or impure."

They do not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding whether the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness is pure or impure; they do not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding whether the intrinsic nature of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness is pure or impure.

They do not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding whether the intrinsic nature of the objects of form is pure or impure; they do not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding whether the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness is pure or impure.

They do not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding whether the intrinsic nature of the eye as a condition is pure or impure; they do not engage with the characteristics of conjunction or separation regarding whether the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as conditions is pure or impure.

They do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of form; they do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena.

They do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness; they do not practice by taking as their object the signs of purity or impurity, or of conjunction or separation, regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

"One does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding form (*rūpa*) of the past, future, or present; one does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the past, future, or present.

One does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding the eye of the past, future, or present; one does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind of the past, future, or present.

One does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding forms of the past, future, or present; one does not engage with the signs of purity or impurity, of conjunction or separation, regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharma*) of the past, future, or present."

They do not engage with the signs of conjunction or separation regarding the purity or impurity of past, future, or present eye-consciousness; they do not engage with the signs of conjunction or separation regarding the purity or impurity of past, future, or present ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

They do not engage with the signs of conjunction or separation regarding the purity or impurity of past, future, or present forms as objects of perception; they do not engage with the signs of conjunction or separation regarding the purity or impurity of past, future, or present feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as objects of perception.

They do not engage with the signs of conjunction or separation regarding the purity or impurity of past, future, or present eyes as bases of perception; they do not engage with the signs of conjunction or separation regarding the purity or impurity of past, future, or present ears, noses, tongues, bodies, or minds as bases of perception.

One does not engage with the signs of union or separation regarding the past, future, or present purity or impurity of form; one does not engage with the signs of union or separation regarding the past, future, or present purity or impurity of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or phenomena.

One does not engage with the signs of union or separation regarding the past, future, or present purity or impurity of eye-consciousness; one does not engage with the signs of union or separation regarding the past, future, or present purity or impurity of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas are able to practice in this way, they neither unite with nor separate from form; they likewise neither unite with nor separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
They neither unite with nor separate from the eye, and they likewise neither unite with nor separate from the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”
It neither conjoins with nor separates from form; it neither conjoins with nor separates from sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharma*);
it neither conjoins with nor separates from eye-consciousness, nor does it conjoin with or separate from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness;
it neither conjoins with nor separates from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), nor with the perversions, views, or hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, it neither joins with nor separates from various modes of affection; it neither joins with nor separates from the realms of desire, form, or formlessness;
it neither joins with nor separates from greed, hatred, or delusion;
and it neither joins with nor separates from the notions of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a creature, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, or a soul.
It is neither conjoined with nor separated from birth, the youth, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, or the seer;
it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the notions of existence or non-existence; it is neither conjoined with nor separated from annihilation or permanence;

it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the elements (*dhātu*) or the sense-bases (*āyatana*); it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) or the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). It is not...
It neither unites with nor separates from the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness;
it neither unites with nor separates from dependent origination; it neither unites with nor separates from the five objects of sensory desire;
it neither unites with nor separates from affliction or purification; it neither unites with nor separates from generosity, stinginess, or ethical discipline.
Whether combined with or separated from transgression of the precepts, patience, anger, diligence, laziness, meditative concentration, distraction, sublime wisdom, or false wisdom;

whether combined with or separated from the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, or the factors of the path; it is not combined with or separated from the abandonment of perversions.
It is neither conjoined with nor separated from inversion and so forth; it is neither conjoined with nor separated from dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, or samāpatti;
it is neither conjoined with nor separated from suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path;
it is neither conjoined with nor separated from śamatha and vipaśyanā; it is neither conjoined with nor separated from vidyā and vimukti.
It is neither conjoined with nor separated from the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the immeasurables or the supernormal powers;
it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas;
[it is neither conjoined with nor separated from] the qualities of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas.

Whether conjoined or separated, it is neither conjoined nor separated from the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), the knowledge of non-activity (*anabhisaṃskārajñāna*), or the knowledge of non-attachment (*asaṅgajñāna*).
It is neither conjoined nor separated from saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;

it is neither conjoined nor separated from the Buddha-knowledge, the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth; nor is it conjoined with or separated from the perfection of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇavyañjanapariniṣpatti*).
Whether in conjunction or separation, it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the adornment of Buddha-fields;
it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the perfection of śrāvakas; it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the perfection of pratyekabuddhas;
it is neither conjoined with nor separated from the perfection of bodhisattvas. Why is this?
"Excellent valor!
Because all phenomena are without conjunction or disjunction.
Excellent valor!"
No phenomena manifest because of being either conjoined or separated. O Suvīra!
"Conjoined" refers to permanence; "separated" refers to annihilation.
Suvīra! The nature of all phenomena does not involve conjunction or separation through investigation. Suvīra!
The nature of all phenomena does not manifest through conjunction or separation. Suvīra!

If the nature of phenomena were to manifest through conjunction or separation, then one would be able to find among phenomena an agent and one who causes to act, an arouser and one who causes to arouse, an experiencer and one who causes to experience, a knower and one who causes to know, a seer and one who causes to see, a conjoiner and one who causes to conjoin, and a separator and one who causes to separate; likewise, the Tathāgata would also have to designate among phenomena that "this is the agent," "this is the one who causes to act," and so on, up to "this is the separator" and "this is the one who causes to separate."

“Suvīra! Because the nature of all phenomena does not manifest as either conjoining or separating, and because among all phenomena there is not even the slightest portion of an agent or one who causes another to act, nor of one who separates or one who causes another to separate—neither being obtainable nor unobtainable—the Buddha does not establish such designations.”
"O Suvīra! All phenomena arise from inversion; yet these inversions neither join nor separate.
Why is this? O Suvīra!"
Not even the slightest thing among these inverted phenomena can be found, nor can a truly existent nature of their arising be found. Why is this?
O Well-Vigorous One!
Inversions are unreal, false, deceptive, empty, and non-existent; within them there is not even the slightest real dharma that could be called an "inversion."

“Suvīra! That which is inverted deludes and confuses sentient beings and establishes the designation of ‘sentient beings. These various classes of sentient beings are manifested through false conceptualization, causing them to give rise to groundless attachment, agitation, and frivolous proliferation.”
Suvīra! It is just as when an empty fist deceives a young child; because of his ignorance, the child believes there is a real object within it.

So too it is with foolish ordinary beings: deceived by false inversions, they falsely perceive the nature of all phenomena—which is neither joined nor separated—as being joined or separated, and thus claim they truly exist.

Fools and deluded, they give rise to the perception of reality within that which is unreal, making liberation difficult; therefore, all foolish ordinary beings, through false views of conjunction and separation, are bound by inversion and wander through birth and death—namely, through conjunction with attainment, conjunction with dwelling, conjunction with views, and conjunction with grasping.
Because there is conjunction, one grasps at disjunction, thinking that disjunction is attained by means of eliminating conjunction.
O Well-Valiant One!

Wherever there is conjunction, there is disjunction; yet if, within conjunction, one neither attains nor relies upon it, does not give rise to attachment, and likewise does not perceive disjunction, [then one is free].

"O Suvīra! If one perceives attainment within the state of detachment, relies upon it, or gives rise to attachment toward it, that person will then be subject to conjunction; they shall not yet be able to separate from the suffering of birth and death."

“Suvīra! Because these bodhisattvas contemplate this meaning, they are neither conjoined with nor separated from the nature of all phenomena; nor do they act or engage in cultivation as if conjoining or separating themselves from phenomena.”
“Suvīra! These bodhisattvas thoroughly understand conjunction and disjunction as they practice the perfection of wisdom. Suvīra!”
In this way, a bodhisattva dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom can swiftly fulfill all the qualities of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice attachment to or non-attachment to form; they do not practice attachment to or non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not practice attachment to or non-attachment to the eye; they do not practice attachment to or non-attachment to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not practice attachment to or non-attachment to forms; they do not practice attachment to or non-attachment to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena.
One does not practice attachment to or non-attachment to eye-consciousness; one does not practice attachment to or non-attachment to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
One does not practice the purity of attachment to or non-attachment to forms; one does not practice the purity of attachment to or non-attachment to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
One does not practice the purity of attachment to or non-attachment to the eye; one does not practice the purity of attachment to or non-attachment to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

They do not practice attachment to form, nor do they practice non-attachment and purity; they do not practice attachment to sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena, nor do they practice non-attachment and purity;

they do not practice attachment to eye-consciousness, nor do they practice non-attachment and purity; they do not practice attachment to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor do they practice non-attachment and purity.

"One does not practice attachment to form, nor does one have an object of attachment; one does not practice attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one have an object of attachment.

One does not practice attachment to the eye, nor does one have an object of attachment; one does not practice attachment to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does one have an object of attachment.

One does not practice attachment to forms, nor does one have an object of attachment; one does not practice attachment to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does one have an object of attachment."

They do not practice attachment to eye-consciousness, nor do they practice attachment to the objects of that non-attachment; they do not practice attachment to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor do they practice attachment to the objects of that non-attachment.

"One does not practice attachment to form, nor the union with non-attachment, nor separation from it; one does not practice attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the union with non-attachment, nor separation from them.

One does not practice attachment to the eye, nor the union with non-attachment, nor separation from it; one does not practice attachment to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor the union with non-attachment, nor separation from them.

One does not practice attachment to forms, nor the union with non-attachment, nor separation from them; one does not practice attachment to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, nor the union with non-attachment, nor separation from them."

One does not practice with attachment to eye-consciousness, nor with non-attachment, nor with their conjunction or separation; one does not practice with attachment to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor with non-attachment, nor with their conjunction or separation.

"One does not practice attachment to form, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or separation; one does not practice attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or separation;

one does not practice attachment to the eye, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or separation; one does not practice attachment to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or separation;

one does not practice attachment to forms, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or separation; one does not practice attachment to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or separation."

One does not practice attachment to eye-consciousness, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or disjunction; one does not practice attachment to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness, nor non-attachment, purity, conjunction, or disjunction.

"One does not engage in the purity, conjunction, or separation regarding the object of form; one does not engage in the purity, conjunction, or separation regarding the objects of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

One does not engage in the purity, conjunction, or separation regarding the object of the eye; one does not engage in the purity, conjunction, or separation regarding the objects of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

One does not engage in the purity, conjunction, or separation regarding the object of forms; one does not engage in the purity, conjunction, or separation regarding the objects of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena."

One does not engage with the purity, conjunction, or separation of the objects of visual consciousness; one does not engage with the purity, conjunction, or separation of the objects of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.
"Why is this? O Suvīra!

All such things involve transition, grasping, and fluctuation, whether they be activities or observations. The Bodhisattva thoroughly knows all such things as these, and no longer engages in them through either activity or observation."
"Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present of form; they do not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

they do not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present of the eye; and they do not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."

One does not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present forms; one does not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena;

one does not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present eye-consciousness; and one does not practice attachment or non-attachment regarding the past, future, or present ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.

"One does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of form in the past, future, or present; one does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness in the past, future, or present.

One does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of the eye in the past, future, or present; one does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind in the past, future, or present.

One does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of forms in the past, future, or present; one does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena in the past, future, or present."

One does not practice with regard to the purity or impurity of visual consciousness in the past, future, or present; nor does one practice with regard to the purity or impurity of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness in the past, future, or present.

"One does not practice attachment or non-attachment toward the past, future, or present form, nor toward its object being pure or impure; one does not practice attachment or non-attachment toward the past, future, or present feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor toward their objects being pure or impure;

one does not practice attachment or non-attachment toward the past, future, or present eye, nor toward its object being pure or impure; one does not practice attachment or non-attachment toward the past, future, or present ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor toward their objects being pure or impure;

one does not practice attachment or non-attachment toward the past, future, or present forms, nor toward their objects being pure or impure; one does not practice attachment or non-attachment toward the past, future, or present sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena, nor toward their objects being pure or impure."

One does not engage with eye-consciousness by way of attachment or non-attachment to the past, future, or present, nor regarding its object as pure or impure. One does not engage with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness by way of attachment or non-attachment to the past, future, or present, nor regarding their objects as pure or impure.
"Why is that? O Suvīra!
These bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom do not perceive at all any dharma of either practicing or non-practicing."
“Suvīra! These bodhisattvas have no practice whatsoever; they skillfully penetrate and fully comprehend all conditioned phenomena as they cultivate the perfection of wisdom.”
"O Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will swiftly fulfill all the dharmas of omniscience.

One does not practice the essential nature of form as being either distant or not distant; one does not practice the essential nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either distant or not distant.

One does not practice the essential nature of the eye as being either distant or not distant; one does not practice the essential nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being either distant or not distant.

One does not practice the essential nature of forms as being either distant or not distant; one does not practice the essential nature of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena as being either distant or not distant.

One does not practice regarding the nature of visual consciousness as being either distant or not distant; one does not practice regarding the natures of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness as being either distant or not distant.

One does not engage with form—past, future, or present—as being pure or impure by nature, revealed or unrevealed, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached; nor does one engage with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—past, future, or present—as being pure or impure by nature, revealed or unrevealed, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached.

One does not engage with the eye as being pure or impure, manifest or unmanifest, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached, whether past, future, or present; nor does one engage with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being pure or impure, manifest or unmanifest, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached, whether past, future, or present.

they do not cling to the eye, nor do they cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."

"One does not cling to the purity of the objects of visual consciousness; one does not cling to the purity of the objects of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness. O Suvīra!..."
If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will swiftly fulfill all the qualities of omniscience. "Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will be close to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will draw near to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs; their bodies will be of a true golden color with boundless radiance; they will gaze like dragon-elephants, and no one will be able to see the crown of their heads.”

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will be in close proximity to the unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present; they will also be in close proximity to the instructions, exhortations, and guidance of the Tathāgata; and they will be in close proximity to the unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision of the past, future, and present, receiving the definitive prediction of enlightenment.”

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will swiftly realize the purity of all Buddha-dharmas; they will swiftly be able to realize the purity of the buddha-field; they will swiftly be able to gather a perfect assembly of śrāvakas; and they will swiftly be able to gather a perfect assembly of bodhisattvas.”
“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they do not abide in form; they do not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not abide in the eye; they do not abide in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”
They do not dwell in form; they do not dwell in sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
they do not dwell in eye-consciousness; they do not dwell in ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness;
they do not dwell in name-and-form; they do not dwell in perversions, views, hindrances, or the conduct of craving; they do not dwell [in any of these].
The realms of desire, form, and formlessness; not abiding in the realm of sentient beings or the realm of phenomena;
not abiding in the realms of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness;
and not abiding in [the notions of] self, sentient being, life-principle, living being, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, or human.
The child, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, the seer, and all such conceptualizations do not abide in annihilationism or eternalism;
they do not abide in defilement or purity; they do not abide in dependent origination;
and they do not abide in generosity or stinginess, ethical discipline or transgression, patience or anger, diligence or laziness.
...meditative concentration, distraction, sublime wisdom, and faulty wisdom;
not abiding in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, or the factors of the path;
not abiding in the abandonment of the perversions, nor abiding in meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, or attainments; and not abiding in clarity or release.
Liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation do not abide in the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of non-activity, or unattached knowledge;
they do not abide in calm abiding or insight; they do not abide in the immeasurables or the supernormal powers;
they do not abide in suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; and they do not abide in the state of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
The bodhisattva and the stage of buddhahood do not abide in the states of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or the buddha-dharmas;
they do not abide in saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; they do not abide in the buddha-knowledge, powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth;
they do not abide in the knowledge and vision of the past, future, or present; and they do not abide in the perfection of the buddha-fields.
One does not abide in the perfection of the assembly of śrāvakas, nor does one abide in the perfection of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Why is this? O Suvīra!
Because all phenomena are non-abiding. "Suvīra!
There is no sense in which any phenomenon can be an object of abiding."
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without a place of attachment or storage; because there is no place of attachment or storage, there is nothing upon which one can dwell.
O Well-Valiant One!

If any phenomena were such that they could be dwelt upon, then it should be possible to demonstrate that this is what is to be grasped and stored, and that this phenomenon is eternally abiding; likewise, the Tathāgata would also abide within all phenomena, demonstrating that these phenomena are what is to be grasped and stored, and what is to be accumulated.
"O Suvīra! Because all phenomena cannot be established, cannot be stored, and cannot be accumulated, therefore no phenomenon is permanent."
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not abide in phenomena, nor does he manifest that "this is to be grasped and stored" or "this is to be accumulated. O Subhānavīrya!

There is not even the slightest phenomenon that can truly arise; because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can truly arise, there is nothing whatsoever in which to abide. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena have no basis for abiding.
“Suvīra! Because they employ the skillful means of neither abiding nor non-abiding, it is said that all phenomena are entirely without abiding. Suvīra!”

There is not even the slightest dharma that can be said to abide; just as the four great rivers flow from Lake Anavatapta and have no possibility of stopping until they enter the great ocean, so too with all dharmas—even those without volitional construction—there is no possibility of abiding until all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted.

"O Suvīra! One who performs no action means that within this state there is neither abiding nor non-abiding, and no obstruction; all such things are spoken of merely by way of conventional designation. In reality, there is no abiding, no obstruction, no finality, and likewise no non-abiding."
“Suvīra! There is no agent of action;

this is spoken according to worldly convention. Just as sentient beings perceive in the mundane world, there is no truly existent abiding or one who creates obstacles, nor is there any ultimate state, yet there is also no non-abiding.”

Since there is no one who dwells in reality without having performed formative actions, it can be said that all phenomena lack the quality of dwelling, being spoken of only in reliance upon conventional designations. "O Suvīra!
In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on the skillful means of non-abiding in all phenomena.
O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will swiftly fulfill all dharmas of omniscience, draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, quickly be able to sit upon the sublime seat of awakening, quickly realize the wisdom of all-knowledge, quickly fulfill the wisdom-vision of the three times, and quickly fulfill the discernment of the various mental activities of all sentient beings, because of their pervasive knowledge of sublime wisdom.
“Suvīra! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas wish to universally benefit all sentient beings,
wish to satisfy all sentient beings with material gifts, and wish to provide all sentient beings with the gift of the Dharma— ”

may they universally bestow upon all sentient beings the great wisdom of the Buddha-wisdom; may they universally have compassion for all sentient beings;
may they universally benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings; and may they cause all sentient beings to be abundantly provided with the gift of wealth and the gift of Dharma.
