he desires to cause all sentient beings to be abundantly endowed with patience and gentleness; he desires to cause all sentient beings to be abundantly endowed with courageous diligence;
he desires to cause all sentient beings to be abundantly endowed with pure meditative concentration; he desires to cause all sentient beings...
Abounding in subtle and wondrous *prajñā*, he desires to cause all sentient beings to abound in ultimate liberation;
he desires to cause all sentient beings to abound in the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he desires to cause all sentient beings to abound in rebirth in the higher realms; he desires to cause all sentient beings to abound in clarity and liberation.
To cause all sentient beings to be abundantly endowed with ultimate *nirvāṇa*;
to cause all sentient beings to be abundantly endowed with the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas; to cause all sentient beings to be abundantly endowed with and perfected in all virtues;
and to turn the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma—before all the world’s śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, and māras.
None of the non-Buddhists are able to turn the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the truth.

If one wishes to proclaim the sublime Dharma in the world; if one wishes to be able to correctly explain the stages of the Buddhas (*buddhabhūmi*); if one wishes to be able to correctly explain the stages of the Bodhisattvas (*bodhisattvabhūmi*); if one wishes to be able to correctly explain the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas (*pratyekabuddhabhūmi*); if one wishes to be able to correctly explain the stage of the Śrāvakas (*śrāvakabhūmi*); and if one wishes to awaken the roots of virtue and original vows of all classes of sentient beings, one should study this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with courageous diligence, uninterrupted and constant, and one should diligently train in reliance upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* without any attachment or concern for the self.

“Suvīra! I do not see any other dharmas whatsoever that can cause a bodhisattva to so swiftly fulfill the unsurpassed, sublime dharmas of a Buddha as this profound *prajñāpāramitā* that has been taught.”
If bodhisattvas abide in this profound perfection of wisdom and practice it with diligent application without even momentary abandonment, they will swiftly fulfill all the qualities of omniscience.

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and are able to reach its ultimate consummation, those bodhisattvas are certain to be in close proximity to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; of this there is no doubt.”

"O Suvīra! If sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, receive it with joy and faith and give rise to the perception of its reality, I declare that such persons will be able to draw forth unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and their sublime roots of goodness will swiftly reach ultimate consummation."
These sons and daughters of good family, having gathered roots of virtue, will certainly be able to accumulate the provisions for great wisdom.
O Well-Valiant One!

If bodhisattvas hold in their hands such profound teachings on the perfection of wisdom associated with skillful means, it should be known that even if these bodhisattvas have not yet received a prophecy from a Buddha in their presence, they are already close to receiving one, or will receive a prophecy from the Buddhas in their presence before long.

“Suvīra! For example, if there were a person who, having diligently studied the ten paths of wholesome action, had reached their ultimate perfection, you should know that this person’s roots of goodness are matured and they have already attained proximity to rebirth in Uttarakuru.

In the same way, if a bodhisattva holds this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their hands, you should know that they are in close proximity to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, and there is certainly no doubt about it.”

“Suvīra! For example, suppose there is a person who delights in practicing generosity, having no regard or stinginess for any wealth or treasures; who constantly gathers in sentient beings through giving, kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation; and who maintains ethical discipline and cultivates patience to subdue pride. When such a person has practiced these deeds to their ultimate conclusion, they will swiftly obtain great wealth and be born into a noble family.
In the same way, if a bodhisattva receives this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with their own hands, you should know that they are close to the stage of non-retrogression.”

“Suvīra! For example, suppose there were a person who delighted in cultivating generosity, the ethical discipline of śīla, and patience, being fully endowed with them all; who, out of compassion for sentient beings, exhorted others to uphold pure precepts, and furthermore was able to perform deeds that bring about superior karmic results—it should be known that such a person would swiftly attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).

In the same way, if a bodhisattva should receive this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in their hands, it should be known that they will swiftly sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).”

“Suvīra! Just as when a wheel-turning monarch is about to ascend the great throne, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed and observed the fast, he ascends the lion throne in the great hall and sits facing east; then a great wheel-treasure descends from the sky. You should know that this king has received the rank of a wheel-turner and will before long obtain the perfection of the seven treasures.
In the same way, when a bodhisattva receives this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their hands, you should know that they will swiftly attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Suppose there are beings who have cultivated superior roots of goodness, who always delight in practicing pure conduct, who possess vast faith and understanding, who feel weary of the human condition, who are endowed with pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), and who take pleasure in managing communal affairs; whose minds long for rebirth in the heavens through their aspirations, and who constantly act as protectors for the people of the four continents—it should be known that such beings will before long become the Four Great Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājika*) who guard the realms of the four continents.

Likewise, if a bodhisattva, by means of teachings corresponding to the *prajñāpāramitā*, bestows them upon sentient beings with a heart free from stinginess, it should be known that before long they will become a Dharma King, attaining mastery over all phenomena.”

“Suvīra! Suppose there are sentient beings who have cultivated superior roots of goodness, purer than those previously accomplished; who first bestow their acquired wealth and treasures upon others before using them themselves; who first attend to the affairs of sentient beings before attending to their own; who constantly guard themselves against being defiled by unrighteousness or unequal greed; whose hearts long for the position of Lord of Devas throughout the night; and who are firm in mind regarding the virtues they cultivate—know that such individuals will, before long, certainly be born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as Śakra, the Lord of Devas.

Likewise, if a bodhisattva, through the essential teachings associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, gives to sentient beings without regard or stinginess, know that before long they will certainly become a Dharma King, attaining great mastery over all phenomena.”
“Suvīra! Just as when someone attains the four Brahma-abodes, it should be known that they will before long be born in the Brahma-heaven;

so too, if a bodhisattva gives to sentient beings through the essential teachings associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without regard or stinginess, it should be known that they will before long turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, bestowing benefit and peace upon all sentient beings.”

“Suvīra! It is just as when the great earth reaches the season of the rains: one sees dense, moisture-laden clouds in the sky above; as twilight approaches, a great rain gradually falls, so that ponds, lakes, and marshes overflow everywhere. The plains and lowlands of the great earth, both high and low, become moistened; the thick clouds hang down and cover all, and the sweet rain universally saturates everything, causing all medicinal herbs, grasses, trees, groves, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits to flourish. The waters, lands, mountains, and rivers are fragrant and aromatic; everywhere there are flowers, fruits, springs, and pools. At such a time, the great earth is most delightful, and humans and non-humans alike rejoice upon seeing it, gathering and plucking the flowers and fruits, smelling their fragrance, and tasting their flavor.”

When Bodhisattvas thus diligently practice and study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in the present, it should be known that these Bodhisattvas will, before long, be moistened by the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); they will be well able to enter into the knowledge of all modes, and they will be able to reveal and manifest the knowledge of all modes. Through this, they will nourish and satisfy all sentient beings, distinguishing and elucidating the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
“Suvīra! Just as within the palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta, once sentient beings are born there, four great rivers emerge and each flows toward a different direction to fill the great ocean;

so too, when a bodhisattva obtains this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their hands and further applies themselves with diligence to its cultivation, they are able to bring forth great streams of Dharma and satisfy sentient beings with the gift of the Great Dharma.”
“Suvīra! Just as various birds, though differing in form and species, become one color when they rely upon Mount Sumeru;

so too, when Bodhisattvas obtain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their hands, they all follow the same course through faith, acceptance, and practice—that is, they proceed toward the omniscience of the Tathāgata.”

“Suvīra! Just as the great ocean is the support for all waters and is the destination to which all streams flow, so too the bodhisattva who has obtained this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in his hands, by diligently practicing and studying it until it is thoroughly mastered, will before long become a sea of all dharmas and swiftly become a vessel for all dharmas; he shall be the destination to which all dharmas flow, and worldly dharmas will be unable to disturb him.”
“Suvīra! Just as the orb of the sun eclipses all other lights, so too,
when the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva appears in the world, all non-Buddhist paths are completely obscured.”
"O Suvīra! When the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by bodhisattvas appears in the world, it acts as a lamp that illuminates for the classes of sentient beings."
“Suvīra! When bodhisattvas appear in the world, they illuminate the roots of goodness for all sentient beings and serve as pure fields of merit for them;
all sentient beings should make offerings to them, all sentient beings should take refuge in them, and all sentient beings should praise them.”
"Furthermore, Suvīra!

If bodhisattvas are able to train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), this is the most supreme training among all trainings; those who train in this way universally clear the path to nirvāṇa for all sentient beings."
Why is this? O Suvīra!

If one studies the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it is the most excellent and foremost among all trainings; it is sublime, most subtle, supreme, unsurpassed, peerless, and equal to the unequaled.

“Suvīra! If bodhisattvas are able to study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they bring all their studies to ultimate completion; they are universally able to uphold everything that is to be studied, they are able to elucidate all that is to be studied, and they subdue all heterodox arguments and false teachings.”

"O Suvīra! If bodhisattvas are able to train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will then be able to practice the conduct of all buddhas and bodhisattvas of the three periods of time."

“Suvīra! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have already, are now, and will in the future train in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* of training, abiding therein with supreme skill; for the sake of all sentient beings, they have already, are now, and will in the future expound such unsurpassed, pure dharmas of training.”
Suvīra! This profound perfection of wisdom as thus studied surpasses all that is studied in the world; it is the most honorable and the most supreme.
Suvīra! This profound perfection of wisdom as thus studied is a study that is spontaneous; none in all the worlds can equal it.

“Suvīra! If one studies the perfection of wisdom, there is nothing at all to be studied among all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, faulty or faultless. One does not give rise to attachment toward any such categories of phenomena; dwelling without attachment toward all phenomena, one correctly reveals to all sentient beings the unsurpassed, pure dharma of training.”
Why is this? O Suvīra!

Because all phenomena are without attachment and without bondage; not even the slightest phenomenon appears as something to be attached to or bound by, and for this reason, there is also no meaning of attaining liberation.

“Suvīra! Form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
the eye is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; the ear, the nose...”
The tongue, body, and mind are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; forms are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
eye-consciousness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; [and likewise] the ear, nose, tongue, and body...
Consciousness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; name-and-form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
the perversions, views, hindrances, and tendencies of craving are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
greed, hatred, and delusion are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; desire—

The realm of form and the formless realm are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; the realm of sentient beings and the realm of phenomena are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
and the self, sentient being, life-principle, living being, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, youth, and agent—[are likewise without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation].
The feeler, the knower, the seer, and those various perceptions are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
dependent origination, defilement, and purification are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; giving—

Avarice and greed, ethical discipline and its violation, patience and anger, diligence and laziness, meditative concentration and distraction, wisdom and false wisdom—these are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—these are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. The foundations of mindfulness...

The right abandonments, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the factors of the path are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
the elimination of perversions and so forth is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the meditative attainments are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; the immeasurables...

The supernormal powers (abhijñā) are without attachment, without bondage, and also without liberation; the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), the knowledge of non-activity (anabhisaṃskārajñāna), and the knowledge of non-attachment are without attachment, without bondage, and also without liberation;

clarity (vidyā) and liberation, as well as the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuktijñānadarśana), are without attachment, without bondage, and also without liberation; [and so are] ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
The stages of the bodhisattva, the bodhisattva himself, and the Buddha are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;
ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-dharmas are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation;

saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; and the Buddha’s wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are likewise without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.

They are equal in being without attachment, without bondage, and also without liberation; the knowledge and vision regarding the past, future, and present are without attachment, without bondage, and also without liberation. Why is this?

“Suvīra! Because attachment to all phenomena cannot be apprehended and bondage cannot be apprehended, and since both attachment and bondage do not exist, even liberation from them cannot be apprehended.”
“Suvīra! What is called ‘attachment and bondage’ refers to the attachment and fettering to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Since the nature of phenomena is non-existent, it cannot be said that there is attachment or bondage.”
As for what is called "liberation," it refers to being freed from attachment and bondage; since those two do not exist, there is no liberation.
O Well-Valiant One!

"No liberation" means that among all phenomena, there is absolutely no nature that can attain liberation. If one can view all phenomena in this way, it is called the wisdom and vision of non-attachment.
"O Suvīra! That which is called 'non-attachment' means that within this state, attachment cannot be found.
Because it is the nature of non-attachment and the nature of the absence of reality, it is called non-attachment."

Because within this, that which clings, that which is clung to, that by which one clings, that for which one clings, that because of which one clings, and that to which one belongs—all these are unapprehendable—it is called "non-attachment."
"O Suvīra! That which is called 'unbound' means that within this state, no binding can be apprehended.
Because the nature of binding is non-binding and the nature of binding is unreal, it is therefore called 'unbound.'"

Because within this, that which binds, that which is bound, by means of which, for the sake of which, on account of which, and to which it belongs—all these are unfindable—it is therefore called "unbound."
“Suvīra! If there is neither attachment nor bondage regarding all phenomena, how can one speak of liberation with respect to phenomena? Suvīra!”
Without attachment, there is no bondage, and likewise no liberation; freedom from fetters, coolness, and tranquility is called true liberation.
O Well-Valiant One!

If one has no clinging toward any phenomena, then there is no bondage; if one has no fettering toward any phenomena, then there is no liberation. To be far removed from these three things—freedom from fetters, coolness, and tranquility—is called true liberation.

"O Suvīra! In this way, a bodhisattva enters into all phenomena as being without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation, thereby attaining true wisdom and vision and practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
"O Suvīra! If bodhisattvas can practice in this way, they will draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes."

“Suvīra! By means of this subtle Dharma-seal of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, I seal all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to sever the net of doubt and to apply themselves with diligence to the study of the profound Prajñāpāramitā so that they may swiftly reach the ultimate goal.”
"O Suvīra! I now personally uphold such a Dharma-seal, causing it to abide long in the world for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings. Why is this so?

My assembly of śrāvakas possesses unsurpassed supernormal power, capable of upholding the subtle dharma-seal of the Prajñāpāramitā, so as to benefit sentient beings in the future time, the final period, and the last five hundred years after my parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, with Bhadrapāla and Nāyaka as the chief among five hundred leading Bodhisattvas, as well as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvikrāntavikramin, saying: "Good sons!

You should train yourselves in this way: the profound perfection of wisdom, which has been cultivated and accumulated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons, serves as the foremost [of all practices].

This is that which flows forth from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, this unsurpassed treasury of Dharma established by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should uphold such a treasury of Dharma; after my parinirvāṇa, in a future time, a future period, during the final five hundred years when the unsurpassed True Dharma is about to perish and its era is turning, you should extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings, so that upon hearing it, they may obtain great benefit and happiness.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, all the bodhisattvas rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We should train ourselves in this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which has been cultivated and accumulated by the Tathāgatas over immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons, and which serves as the foremost [of all practices].

This unsurpassed treasury of Dharma has flowed forth from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and is established by the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. We shall uphold such a treasury of Dharma; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the later time, the later period, during the final five hundred years, when the unsurpassed True Dharma is about to perish and its decline begins, we shall extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings, so that upon hearing it, they may obtain great benefit and happiness.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, there will be great terror, great peril, and great violence.
At that time, for the most part, sentient beings will have accomplished the karma of being destitute of the Dharma, and their minds will be largely... [corrupt/fragmented]"
Corrupted by sensual desire, improper greed, and unrighteous craving; their minds bound by stinginess and envy;
prone to anger, ferocity, and harsh speech; deceitful, fraudulent, and delighting in unrighteous conduct;
full of contempt, contentious, and discordant; they dwell in [unwholesome states].
Obscured by ethical discipline and worldly indulgence, with laziness predominant and diligence inferior,
they lose right mindfulness and dwell in non-awareness; their mouths are harsh and their beaks long, they are haughty and arrogant, delighting in the performance of evil deeds,
concealing their inner thoughts, and increasing greed, hatred, and delusion while their roots of goodness are meager— thus they become [unwholesome].
Obscured by the shell of ignorance, all their actions accord with the faction of Māra; they constantly act as enemies and harmers toward the profound Dharma and Vinaya,
serving as great thieves within the treasury of the Dharma-jewels, and being of a naturally base and evil disposition, they are difficult to associate with.
“World-Honored One!

We are now determined to uphold such an unsurpassed treasury of Dharma, accumulated through the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata over immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, and thereby bring great benefit to those sentient beings.”
"Bhagavān!

At that time, there will be a small number of sentient beings who diligently seek and delight in studying this treasury of Dharma. Their nature will be upright, free from flattery and deceit; they would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than act as enemies of the Dharma, nor will they slander, revile, or turn their backs upon it."

I shall bring benefit to such persons as these by revealing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them with this profound Dharma, so that they may apply themselves diligently to its study and practice.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately employed his supernormal powers to protect and sustain this subtle, profound, and unsurpassed Dharma-treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, ensuring that the hosts of evil Māras could not destroy or extinguish it.

Furthermore, by means of his majestic power, he protects those who are able to receive, uphold, and diligently practice this treasury of the Dharma, causing them to sever the snares of Māra and attain serene liberation, so that they may swiftly reach the ultimate consummation of their practice.
At that time, the Buddha smiled and emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm.
Sentient beings in both the human and celestial realms were able to see one another because of the Buddha’s light.

At that time, the assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other hosts of deities, all holding various kinds of celestial, exquisite flowers and incense, scattered them over the World-Honored One as an offering, and further raised voices of vast praise and hymn, saying:
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!"
Tathāgata!
You possess great majestic spiritual power!

You protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma and those who practice it, ensuring that the armies of evil Māras cannot destroy them; you sever all snares of Māra so they attain great sovereignty, and cause them to swiftly reach the ultimate consummation of their practice.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who possess pure faith and who receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this Dharma-gate for others, they shall no longer fear the armies of all evil Māras.
If bodhisattvas uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this Dharma-gate to others, they will be able to subdue all the armies of Māra, and no evil Māras will be able to create obstacles.
At that time, the Buddha said to Suvīra: “So it is! So it is!”
As stated by the gods and others: "O Suvīra!

The Tathāgata has established a boundary around this unsurpassed Dharma-gate for the sake of all evil Māras, so that the snares of the hosts of evil Māras shall be unable to create any obstruction to this Dharma-gate."
"O Suvīra! It is by relying on this Dharma-gate that the Tathāgata now destroys all the power of the evil Māras. O Suvīra!"
The Tathāgata now protects this Dharma-gate, restraining all evil Māras so that they may not cause harm or destruction.
O Well-Valiant One!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family with pure faith who receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this Dharma-gate to others, no evil Māras will be able to disturb them, and they shall be able to subdue all evil Māra-enemies.

If any bodhisattvas uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this Dharma-gate to others, they will be able to universally subdue all demonic armies and bestow benefit and peace upon all sentient beings.
"O Suvīra! This Dharma-gate cannot be grasped by the hands of those sentient beings who are defiled by various impurities. O Suvīra!"
Such a Dharma gate is the domain of those who are not bound by the snares of Māra.
O Well-Valiant One!
Such a Dharma gate is the domain of those whose nature is well-tamed and who possess supreme intelligence.
“Suvīra! Just as a most well-trained and wise elephant or horse is not ridden by minor kings, nor does it appear during an evil age, but is used only by a universal monarch;
so too, because such a one who is well-trained and extremely wise is able to utilize this profound dharma-gate when it appears in that world, this dharma-gate falls into his hands.”

“Suvīra! For example, the dragon kings Śuci-vrata, Susthita, and Airāvaṇa do not manifest themselves for the sake of being enjoyed by humans or for the sake of being seen by them; nor do they manifest themselves for the sake of being enjoyed by other classes of devas. They manifest themselves solely for the sake of being enjoyed by those devas who are well-disciplined and wise!”

Just as Śakra, the Lord of Devas, thinks of going to a place of recreation with the host of devas and adorns it, so too does that nāga manifest such forms and appear before him for the sake of being enjoyed by the Lord of Devas and the others.

Thus, if there are noble persons who are capable of utilizing this profound Dharma-gate—meaning they can hear it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and explain and analyze it for the sake of sentient beings—[they shall attain such merit].

In these teachings, they constitute a great adornment; they are able to cause them to circulate widely, act as a great illumination of the Dharma, achieve great joy in the Dharma, and experience the great bliss of the Dharma.
"O Well-Valiant One!

If one upholds even a single verse of this profound Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one shall yet obtain immeasurable and boundless merit; how much more so for one who is able to fully uphold, recite, transcribe, make offerings to, disseminate, and extensively explain this great *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to others—the merit such a person obtains is inconceivable!

"O Suvīra! Only those whose nature is disciplined, gentle, and supremely wise are able to embrace such a Dharma-gate; for those who are not disciplined, gentle, and supremely wise, this profound Dharma is not within their sphere."
"O Suvīra! It is for the sake of severing the doubts of sentient beings that I have preached this Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.

When this Dharma was spoken, immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and furthermore, boundless classes of sentient beings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata gave the prophecy that he would certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the great bodhisattvas such as Suvīra, along with the other four assemblies, and the entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Six Hundred: The Heart Mantra of the Mother of Prajñā. The Heart Mantra of the Mother of Prajñā: *tadyathā oṃ gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. The Inner Heart Mantra of the Mother of Prajñā: *oṃ prajñe prajñe mahāprajñe svāhā*.
